THERE are two sides to every question—ours and the wrong side. THAT "music hath charms to soothe the savage breast" is doubtless the reason why African ex- plorers usually go in bands. CONTENTMENT is the sweet satisfaction of know- ing you have more than you can possibly use. JASPER: "Jones is a man who grows on people." _ _ _ . .
JumpFpre: "Well, I consider hirn a miglity Poor
THE STRONGEST OF REASONS.—Quericus : "What prompted them to move?" Cynicus : "The land- lord." _

"TALKING about marvellous memories." said Wilkes, "there was Julius Caesar. He could repeat eight thousand lines of poetry." "No wonder they killed him !" said Darrow. "THAT'S a curious typographical error," said Mrs. Partridge. "The title of this new book is printed The Viking Age.'" "Well, why not ? " asked Partridge. " What ought it to be?" "Why—Biking, oughtn't it?" VERY DIFFERENT.—HeIen: "1)o you think a woman ought to work for her husband ? " Kitty: "I don't know; a little perhaps." Helen: "I mean after she gets him?" Kitty : "The idea! Certainly not !" Now OR NEVER.—He "Why does your mother insist on your having an elaborate wedding?" She: "She says it's the last chance I shall ever have to show off in good clothes." ONE TOO MANY.—Wife : "Well, Eugene, dear, do you ever regret being a married man ? " Hus- band: "Only when I sit down to a roast chicken just big enough for one. THE man who boasts that he works with his head instead of his hands is respectfully reminded that the woodpecker does the same and is the biggest kind of a bore. WIFE (up stairs) : "John, I left a scuttle of coal there for you to bring up with you." John: "Yes, I've found it."

No FOOTBALL GAME.—Two burly bricklayers were fighting furiously. At last one got the other down on the ground and began jumping on his chest. "Here, Bill," gasped the man on the ground, "that ain't fair. This is nothin' but a fight—it ain't football !" A FORECAST.—Dick: "One of those forecasts of possibilities with which the world is infested just now thinks that eventually the lunnan race will -dispense with speech." Ted: "He anticipates the extermination of woman—does he?" _ _

PRACTICAL SYMPATHY.—We have heard of a kind gentleman who one day prevented some boys from stoning a pigeon fastened by the leg. Extri- cating it with much trouble, he put it tenderly into his bosom. The next day he remarked that it made a much nicer pie than he expected. HIGBEE : "Are you ready, dear?" Mrs. Higbee: " No ; I can't think of anything I have forgotten." GAVE IT UP.—Mrs. Urban: "So you feared to remain in the country any longer? Were you afraid of tramps?" Mrs. Lawnville : "No ; I was afraid of the terrible dogs we had to have to scare tramps." ENCORE. —The bicyclist who was riding a very high wheel took a genuine header and turned an almost complete somersault. After he had re- covered himself and wiped the dirt from his face and clothes, he was very much astonished to hear one of two small boys on the sidewalk say: "Mister, do that agin, will yer ? This feller didn't see it." FRIENDIX SYMPATHY.—Friend: "Got a cold, I see." Jinks : "Yes, a little one." " You ought to be very careful. That cough needs attention." "Think so?" "It has a regular graveyard sound." "Good gracious!" "Awful dangerous time for people with colds—influenza, pneumonia, and quick consumption everywhere." "Eh ?" "Yes. A friend of mine took a cold, not half so bad as yours, last week, and in three days he was dead." "My stars !" "Fact. The doctor said my friend might have pulled through if he hadn't worried so much. Take my advice and try not to think about it." LIKE AN OFFlCER.—Evidenee made on the spur of the moment has not infrequently a meaning which was not quite what the speaker wished to convey. For instance, a matter-of-fact corporal during a Volunteer encampment last season was compelled to "run in" a refractory private before the adjutant, and his (the corporal's) account of the delinquent ended in this way: "Why, you see, -sir, he thinks he can go out whenever he likes, and come in when he likes, swagger about, smoke cigars, get tipsy, and, in fact, sir, behave just as if he was an officer." SETTING THE EVENTS TO Music.—The cricket matches between Mr. Stoddart's team and the Australians seem to have been humorous at times. The bandsmen had certainly a pretty wit at the matches in question. At Brisbane Mr. Stoddart skied the ball clean over the shed, and the band at once struck up: "After the Ball is Over." At Adelaide one of the English team was chasing a ball in a very limp sort of way, when the band set the crowd laughing by playing: "'E Dunno Where 'E Are ; " while at Melbourne one of the Austra- lians lost his wicket first ball, and was ushered back to the pavilion by: "Down Among the Dead Men." TIME FOR DISCRETION.—" John," said his spouse thoughtfully, ". of course it is well to be proud of your daughter's success at the seminary, but— but— " "But what, my dear ? " he asked. "Well, it seems to me that you are a trifle thought- less at times." "I don't quite understand you," .he said. "It's all right to speak of her standing in her class," she explained, and it is all right , to be proud of her social accomplishments. Talk of her taste if you wish to, her cooking and her singing lessons, her vivacity, her knowledge of modern languages and her 'sunny disposition, but— but— " "Well, what is it? Where have I made any mistake ? " "Why, it's about time to find a husband for her, and I would suggest, John, that you say nothing about her gymnasium work, or the fact that she played centre forward in the college football team. I have noticed that that has very often a tendency to discourage young men." . .

BUT NOT THE EMPEROR.—A celebrated antiquary was ardently engaged in searching for Roman relics in a certain part of England, when an old inhabitant informed him that on a by-road a little way out was a stile locally known as " Cwsar's Stile." Ah ! I thought as much," soliloquised the anti- uary : "a road, referred to by Antoninus, evi- aently touched that spot, and the name of that stile confirms me in my opinion that the place was once a, Roman camp:' He went off immediately and studied the sacred spot. Whilst thus engaged, an aged cottager approached him. The ardent antiquary addressed him as follows :—" I believe this is known as Gesar's Stile, is it not? "Aye, sir," said the man; "they do call it after old Le etesar, the carpenter. I helped him build it when I wor a wee lad." THEY DIDN'T SPEAK ENGLISH.—Few attractions drew larger audiences at a certain exhibition in London than a Japanese troupe of handbell ringers. The skill of these performers was remarkable, and secured for them a golden harvest. Among those who visited them, were a couple of Yorkshire weavers, who had expended a portion of their savings in a trip to the metropolis. To the astonishment of these good folk, both of whom were themselves handbell ringers, the tunes they listened to were ones which they were well accus- tomed to. Drawing a little closer to the players, they discovered, under Japanese attire, the faces of several old Yorkshire friends. During a pause in the performance, one, of the two strode up to the leader and remarked—" Jabez, I thowt I knowd thy face." "Whist," retorted Jabez, "we talk nowt but Japanese here." ANSWERED. —At a police-court one day the presiding magistrate complained that he did not believe in a particle of the evidence given by some witnesses in a certain ease that had been brought before him. "I believe that they have every one of them told lies," said he. Up rose a lawyer in the court. "Your worship," said he, "I have yet to call a witness on whose veracity the court may rely." A boy was then placed in the witness- box who stared around him like a wild animal. "My boy," said the lawyer, "you arc expected to tell the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth. Do you understand?" Boy : Yes, sir." Lawyer : "Tell thu court, now, where wicked people go to who don't tell the truth." Boy (staring nervously round him, and looking up at the magistrate) : " They come here, sir."

Appropriately enough at Eastertide, there comes news from China which will be welcomed through- out all Christian communities. In a circular ad- dressed to the consuls of the United States in China the American Minister at Pekin informs them that

his Excellency M. Gerard, Minister of . France has recently procured from the Tsung Lt Yamen by virtue of the French Treaty of 1858 an order direct- ing the local authorities to expunge. from all edi- tions and compilations of the Chinese Code all clauses placing restrictions upon the propagation of the Christian religion. "It gives me pleasure to add," says the Minister, " that the Minister of France is entitled to the gratitude of the Christian world for his action in this important matter."

The feeling that Sir Jacobus de Wet is not alto- gether the right man in the right place. as our re- presentative at Pretoria, seems to be growing. This may arise to some extent from impatience at the persistent doggedness with which Oom Paul seems , to be "slow-timing" us, and from the notion that either Sir Jacobus is being befooled or that his sympathies are more with the Boers than with England. Anyhow, we get "no forrader," and al- though the disposition to find a scapegoat whenever things do not move as interested persons desire must always be treated with discouragement, there is evidence in the despatches received at the Colonial office that we require a stronger agent at the Boer capital, and one better qualified to meet the astute and wily President on equal terms. Nor did Sir Jacobus distinguish himself so greatly over the Jameson business as to make it conspicuously certain that a change is not desirable. An uncom- fortable conviction is beginning to spread that Mr. Kruger is laughing in his sleeve at the manner in which he is thwarting Mr. Chamberlain, and is making England look foolish by opposing to her might the dead weight of slow and lumbering obstinacy.

But if a doubt is growing whether Mr. Chamber- lain's South African policy, which appeared so brilliant at first, is likely to develop staying quali- ties, a conviction that Lord Sali,bury has made a terrible mess of our foreign relations is hardly challenged even by his own supporters. In public, of course, they put a good face on it, and still swear by their heaven-inspired diplomatist. But in pri- vate they do not succeed in concealing the suspicion that our difficulties with the United States are largely of his making, and that good luck, rather than his statesmanship, extricated us from the threatened trouble with Germany. Few but the blindest partisans make the slightest attempt to maintain that his diplomacy with Turkey is other than a dismal and ignominious failure, and the fashion in which, as to France, he now blows hot and anon cold is thoroughly disliked by everybody. Nothing could afford more eloquent testimony to the servile discipline of the Tory party than the meekness with which the capitulation to France in Siam has been accepted by our bouncing Imperial- ists. But there is unfeigned disgust at the dis- covery that, the French seem to have taken so ac- curately the measure of Lord Salisbury's foot that instead of the Siam surrender conciliating French susceptibilities as to Egypt it has encouraged further bluster. The advance towards the Soudan may be right or wrong. Lord Salisbury's followers for the most part think it right, but it irks them terribly that their chief does not tell France that our going there is no concern of hers, whether she likes it or not.

Since the notorious theft of his father's body from the magnificent chapel at Dunecht, by the Street of Law Court fame, Lord Crawford and his family have never stayed at Dunecht, which has stood untenanted. His lordship,who resides al most exclusively at Haig Hall, Wigan, has abandoned astronomy,devoting himself to photography and to his splendid library, which has few rivals in this country. The splendid collection of astronomical works, which he presented along with his tele- scope to the Crown, will be housed in a spacious library in the new observatory,which is now one of the best equipped astronomical stations in this country.

The 50,000 or so Sew; and others who witnessed the victory of the Scottish Football team over that of England on Saturday cannot be reproached with a want of appreciation for the prowess of their representatives. The mind reels indeed at the bare contemplation of the copious libations of the "wine of the country" that must have been poured out— and down—in celebration of that glorious victory. Nor would we too curiously inquire at what hour many of that crowd sought their couches after making the echoes of Glasgow ring with the in- spiriting strains of "Scots wha bee." But alas ! the guardians of the peace remained unaffected by the general enthusiasm, and in the course of their noc- turnal perambulations nicked up, as we are in- formed, no fewer than 232 of the flushed patriots and clapped them into lock-ups, and on the Mon- day morning they were brutally cited before the magistrate as plain unvarr.ished "drunks." But still 'twas a glorious victory—and a grand day for the whisky-sellers.

The Marquis of Lvne would fain be an intellec- tual celebrity, it appears; and though he has so far made no very impressive figure in prose or Terse, rumour tells that he still loves to pen trifles in the old way. Perhaps there's a divinity that doth hedge a marquis from criticism. It is even said that his last ambition has been to write an opera ; nay, more, that he has actually written it, and that the stage will have it this season.

A Transatlantic contemporary that amuses its readers from time to time with " horoscopes " thus deals with the Sultan of Turkey :—" This gentleman was born under Sagittarius with that sign in the ascendent, a purple halo around Venus, the dog-star frothing at the mouth and Mars holding up a kicker. lie was tall and slender, with Moslem whiskers, a canvas-back complexion, and a harem gait. Re is very brave, frequently spending hours in his own company. Is quite versatile; loves at first sight, and has a keen sense of humour. Has a shrinking, feminine nature, faints at the sight of blood, and would do good work as a cable-car grip- man. Should cultivate the society of elderly spins- ttrs. Would make a good smoke consumer or a vivisectionist."

When the Education Bill was brought in it was received with a chorus of praise on the Unionist benches. Experience shows,however,that measures which obtain a reception of thisisort on their intro- duction not infrequently suffer -most at their later stages, and I hear that a number of supporters of the Government are already beginning to look ask- ance at some of the main provisions of the bill. They do not at all like the very wide powers with which it is proposed to invest the new educational authority. Supposing the majority of the County Council happen to be Nonconformists, they can, of course, elect a committee favourable to their own views, and, what is more. they can even bring in militant Nonconformists from the outgide to com- plete the arrangement. Of course this cuts both ways. The Liberals take the same objection to the possibility of a committee composed entirely of Churchmen, and they object to the power given to the County Council to limit the number of the com- mittee as much as they please and to co-opt out- siders as destructive of the representative principle embodied in the election of school boards. But the Liberals are opposed to the bill altogether, and it has not been drafted with any idea of pleasing them. It is. however, intended as a great conces- sion to the Church party, and the fact that Church- men are showing an increasing disposition to look with doubt at the constitution of the new authority and its possible action is very significant.

One of the leading Churchmen in the House,who is himself strongly favourable to the main lines of the bill, has already personally expressed the opinion that when the Church party come to con- sider the measure in detail they will find it rp.ces- sary to place a large number of amendments on the paper. As the amendments from the Opposition benches will affect every provision, this does not appear to be very hopeful for the chances of a bin which on the most favourable calculation will not be read a second time until early in May. There appears, by the way, to be some substance in the objection to the measure which was freely taken immediately after Sir J. Garst had mule his state- ment—that it will have the effect of enormously increasing the infusion of party spirit into munici- pal contests. One well-known Lancashire Conser- vative, who is a strong Churchman, puts the matter very clearly. "I have always been opposed," he says, "to fighting municipal elections on party lines, but now that it is to be a question of Church or no Church I shall have no further scruples in the I matter. It will be my duty to stand by my own I side.'

div.head: EXAMINER, SATURDAY APRIL 11, 1896
div.p: THE EXAMINER, SATURDAY APRIL 11, 1896
"WOMEN'S CHAT."

Princess Maud's bridesmaidslevill, in all probability, be her elder sister Princess Victoria, Princess Lugeborg,and Princess Thyra of Denmark, the bride's future sisters-in- law ; Princess Victoria of Schlesweg-Holstein, Princess Beatrix of Coburg, Princess Alice of Albany, Princess Ena of Battenberg, and Princess Victoria, the little daughter of Prince and Princess Henry of Battenberg. The Countess of Leicester is organizing a fund among the women of Norfolk for a wedding gift to be presented to Prineess Maud, but the proposal, so far, has not met with a very enthusiastic reception,owing to agricultural depression. Little Prince Edward of York, and his baby brother make a charming picture when driving in the roads around Sandringham. Prince Edward is possessed of fat pink and white cheeks, and pretty fair hair, and is taught to shake his hand to any passers by who may happen to notice him.—lt seems that these small royal children are as imp ervious to weather as their great grandmother, the Queen,for they daily take the air with a complete disregard of wind or rain. The second drawing room of the season is to be held on the 23rd inst., by the Princess of Wales who with the Prince, will arrive at Marlborough House:from Sand- ringham, on Monday the 20th,where they will stay until Whitsuntide. There are to be two more Drawing Rooms early in May,and according to present arrangements the first will be held by the Queen herself. The fourth Draw- ing Room will be held for Her Majesty by either the Princess of Wales or Princess Christian. Mr. W. S. Gilbert is now engaeed upon a play which was originally intended for Mr. Williard, but the agree- ment, by mutual eonsent of author and manager, has now been cancelled. The piece is of a serious character, and it is very probable that when completed it may find its way into the hands of Mr. and Mrs. Cyril Maude (Miss Winifred Emery) who are anxious to secure a work from the pen of so popular a playwright. Mr. W. H. Smiley Johnstone is now engaged upon the "Life of the late Sir Joseph Barnby." The biography will, to some extent, be anecdotal, and will also give a historical survey of the progress of music in this country during the last half century. and of Sir Joseph Barnhy's life and work as composer and conductor. Apropos of music Paderewski'kprices for playing the piano at a private reception, are to say the least very high. It seems a San Francisco woman wrote to Paderewski's manager quite recently, when the pianist was in that city, asking what Paderewski's fee would be for playing at her "At Home." The reply which rrived in due course stated £5OO for five minutes. The lady thought the charge somewhat excessive and wrote again offering £2OO for five minutes. She did not even receive a reply to her note. The weekly salary r f Mdlle. Yvette Guilbert, of music hall fame, has now reached £6OO. Only a little more than five years ago Mdlle. Y. Guilbert was an almost unknown performer, at a third-rate Parisian music-hall, but it so chanced, fortunately for her, that she intro- duced a new kind of song, and a new way of singing, which took the French public by storm, and in an amaz- ingly short time she became a celebrity in her own peculiar line. She has often private engagements, for which she is paid from £5O to £l5O a night. Miss Lnie Fuller gets £3OO, and Mr. Albert Chavalier about £l2O a week. Town has been a little dull lately, as everyone is tak- ing a holiday preparatory to renewed exertion in the coming season. However, befere the world vanished I obtained many glimpses of new modes from complacent friends and unsuspecting strangers. One thing which struck me forcibly was the fact that it seems just now to he the sole aim and object of the dressmaker's life to build our gowns that no one shall be able to discover how we manage to get into them, and it would really be impossible to don several gowns I have lately inspected in anything under a quarter of an hour, so complicated and numerous are the fastenings thereof. Braid and braiding are more ea evidence than ever,and it is to be hoped we shall stop short of encircling our tightly-fitting coats with row upon row of braid above and below the waist, as was the fashion some time since. On a perfect figure this particular style might be harm- less, but I have never seen it on a perfect figure,and the manner in which these rows of braid manage to empha- sise and accentuate imperfections is really distressing. Any trifling discrepancy between right shoulder and left, between left hip and right, is brought into unpleas- ant promenence by this senseless and unbecoming form of trimming. I remember once walking behind a very tall woman with a tremendous stride,who had possessed herself of one of these coats. She happened to be one , of those very numerous persons who have got into the ' habit of taking a longer step with one foot than with the other, and the inequality of gait made the rows of braid -writhe in a wriggling manner that was truly remarkable, and which had the effect of causing my sense of the ridiculous to come uppermost in a highly inconvenient way. Very beautiful are many of the new waistcoats pre- pared for wear with open coats. Some are elaborately embroidered in many coloured silks, others in white kid or leather are adored with a tracing in jet or steel. At the neck a dainty jabot of fine lace, fitted to a folded stock of soft muslin is to he worn with these very dressy waistcoats. Speaking of jabots reminds me that if we do not indulge in this particular form of neck decoration, to be correct we must go to the other extreme and don severe, turn down collars and cuffs of plain linen. "How Women Walk" has recently been the subject of discussion in a Parisian journal. According to this authority the palm must be awarded to Frenchwomen. The Britishwoman, it states, does not walk, she travels. Her limbs appear to he moved by the engine of a steamer, and her feet have the proportions of an Atlan- -.

tic liner ! Concerning the gait of women of other coun- tries this interesting journal goes on to state that the ' German is heavy, one feels the earth tremble beneath her tread. the Spanish woman "prances," the American re- sembles the pendulum of a clock, the Italian "skips," the Russian "skates," the Dutch woman "rolls," and the Belgian "tramps" about. Now although these re- marks are ungallant arid uncomplimentary, to cur own nation•particularly, we cannot but own that there is a certain amount of truth in them. Numbers of women do not seem to care how they walk so long as they cover the distance they wish to traverse. somehow. But if they could only see themselves as they appear to the casual onleoker, lima very differently would they com- port themselves! How often a pretty face and figure are spoilt by a stoop of the shoulders, and a wrifzglinT. hustling walk! Corsican women are models of queenly grace, and the reason is plain. They have a curious custom of carrying burdens, waterpots, etc., on their beads. I noticed a Corsicin woman going en board a steamer at Marseilles not long ago, carrying her bat y in her arms and her por`manteau on her head. As nearly all the water in Corsica is carried from wells by women

in waterpote, the women acquire from youth the prac- tice of carrying burdens on their heads. An frur's practice of this exercise a day, with for instance a book or pillow on our head, would do wonders in the way of making us into types of grace and ease, when before we were the exact opposite. Smoking civarettes made of tea is the very latest craz amnng women of America. Now tea has been given a bad na:ne as a drink of late,hut in the form of smote it seems to deserve all the hard things laid of alcohol by teetotalers. Tea cigarette smoking is utterly ruinous to the nerves, and srineone with a passion for statistics has caleulated that twenty of these cigarettes a day are equal to about forty cups of tea as regards the quantity consumed, or to about two hundred cups, as regards the effects. A Pretty stiff dose this. The tea cigarettes are on sale in New York at several first class sto-es of cigar dealers who have a women's trade, and this has come about simply because the women ask for them. There is no doubt that it would have been better for women, if, in their craze for something new they had contented themselves with smoking Turkish tobacco in- stead of looking for substitutes which are more harmful In fact, if not in name. It is a matter for regret that omelettes—the com- monest dish abroad—are so seldom seen on British tables. There seems to he a deeply-rooted idea that only a really first-class cook can manage to serve them up, but this is absurd. Here is a simple and dainty re- cipe which the most uninitiated could not fail to under- stand and carry out. Take two eggs for each person, stir together, whites and all, in a cup. Be sure not to beat them. Flavour with a little chopped parsley.pepner and salt, and a pinch of onion if liked. Turn the in- gredients, which have only been mixed together, not beaten into a saucepan. Take a fork, stir gently, until solid enough to turn over. Then serve. It takes just threc minutes with a good fire.—" Madge."

div.head: All rights reserved. THINGS A WOMAN WANTS
div.p: All rights reserved. THINGS A WOMAN WANTS
TO KNOW.

I WONDER if you have seen the charming muslin and cotton crepes that have been intro- duced for this season's wear ? I have been perfectly revelling in them for the last two days. Yesterday morning I went to buy some at a shop where a very large consignment had just arrived. The assistant was exceedingly good and turned over a number for my edifica- tion, and I came home possessed of three or four lengths of muslin, which will be speedily transformed into the smartest blouses.

One I thought particularly pretty; it had a white ground with narrow stripes of black about three-quarters of an inch apart, and an indistinct and somewhat blurred pattern scattered over it. The colourings were so dull as to look almost faded, but the tout ensemble was highly pleasing. Having secured my material, the next thing was to find a really pretty pattern for a blouse, and as I am nothing if not original, I sat down
My Blouse. No. 2039. Paper Pattern, 6id. To be had from PATTERN DEPARTVVNT, 18, HENRIETTA STREET, LONDON, W.C.

immediately with pen and paper before me, determined to sketch one for myself. lam n a bit of a critic in these matters, and so I made at least ten or twelve sketches before I evolved one to entirely pease me. However, I suc- ceeded at last, and here it is. You will notice that the blouse is made on a tight-fitting lining, the upper part of the yoke being covered with a coarse lace. The material for the front is in three parts; the centre being gathered fully into the neckband, and the side fronts are gathered and set into the shoulder-seams. These are brought down into a V at the front, the centre fulness forming the intervening part. I dare say you have alrePdy noticed that, although full sleeves are still worn, the fulness gets higher and higher up the arm with each week that passes. The portion of the sleeve from the elbow to wrist is perfectly plain and tight- fitting—the tighter the better—and the puff itself only extends about half-way to the elbow.
Another blouse I intend making up after the design which I gave you two or three weeks ago, and which no doubt you will remember. (No. 1854.)

And now I want to give you a sketch of a charming design for a child's pinafore. It is made with a pointed yoke back and front, the yoke being edged with insertion and frill of lace. The material for this pinafore should be either nainsook or line jaconette; the skirt with the frill should reach to the bottom of the dress, and two widths of material will be found sufficient. I would advise that this pinafore be made to button neatly on the shoulder, or, of course, if peeferred, it could be fastened down the centre of the back. Two tucks orna- ment the lower edge of the skirt.
A Simple Pinafore. (Age 6to 8 years.) No. 2)43. Paper Pattern, 61d. To be had from PATTERN DEPARTMENT, 18, IfErtexErma STREET, LONDON, W.C.

At the present time, wherever one goes, little else is heard than talk about the latest idea in bicycles. A week or two ago I was able to give you a wrinkle as to the cleaning of the handle- bars and other plated parts ; to-day I have another which will, I think, be equally useful. Formerly it mattered little whether bicycles were well kept or not, but since ladies have taken to the wheel, trimness in every respect is essential.. Do not content yourselves now with only polishing the bright parts of the machine; give the japanned portions a tlea,ningi too, now ' and again with beeswax and turpentine, pre- pared,as if for furniture polish. it. should he applied in the ordinary way, and afterward:- polished. The labour entailed is not great, and the result is.so good that the time bestowed on it is time well spent. Last week I gave you a recipe for sunburn, and since then another recipe has been sent to me by a correspondent, which, she assures me. is very efficacious and at the same time most soothing to the skin when it is sore. I give it you here: , , Place some Fuller's earth in a saucer, and mix it smoothly with cold, soft water into a liquid paste; apply this to the sunburnt skin, rub it well in, and leave it for a few minutes, afterwards washing it off with tepid water, when all traces of tan will be removed. I feel sure this will be useful to you now when cycling, boating tennis, and all kinds of active games. are in full swing. • The fashion of Japanese screens has been in for some time; many of these are made of paper, and though exceedingly pretty, are very fragile, and I find that even with the greatest care holes get poked in them occasionally. What can be done with these screens, the frames of which are still good, but the covering shorn of its beauty? Let me tell you what I have done with mine. I choose a good, but light quality. Turkey- red twill, and with this covered the frame of the screen both back and front, straining the twill tightly, and keeping it perfectly straight. Afterwards I nailed a very thin flat galloon round the edges to bide the tin-tacks with which I had nailed on the twill, and the whole effect is charming. I have used my screen both in my sitting-room and in the hall, and I find it is always admired. When nailing on the gimp use upholsterers' gimp-pins; they are smaller and much sharper than the ordinary tin-tacks.

div.head: LEGAL DECISION.
div.p: A LEGAL DECISION.
IMPORTANT TOTCHEMISTS AND
OTHERS.

On the 13th ult., the court of Chancery grant( d an important injunction at the suit of the Dr. Williams' Medicine Company, against a firm of Chemists .at Cardiff, who had sold, under the title of "Pink Pills for Pale People" (without name), a substitute for the well- known advertised remedy Dr. WilliLms' Pink Pills for Pale People. Counsel on both sides having been heard, It was erdered by the Court that the defendants be restrained from supplying under that name, or any abbreviated title, pills other than those manufactured by the Dr. Williams' Medicine Co., and from passing off such pills as Dr. Williams' Pink Pills for Pale People ; render account and pay over to the Company the entire profits on pills previously sold ; and pay the plaintiffs' costs, to which order the defendants submitted. The importance of this ruling is considerable, and it will have far-reaching consequences. The Solicitor to the Dr. Williams' Medicine Company (Mr. C. Urquhart Fisher, 45, Holborn Viaduct, London, E.G.). invites communications, in confidence, from persons who have seen substitutes for Dr. Williams' Pink Pills for Pale People offered for sale, and will take proceedings against the sellers.

div.head: HIDDEN HAND;
div.p: THE HIDDEN HAND;
CAPITOLA THE MADCAP. BY MRS. E. D. E. N. SOUTHWORTH.
CHAPTER MI.

THE ORPHAN'S TRIAL. "We met ere yet the world had come To wither up the springs of youth, Amid the holy joys of home, And in the first warm blush of youth: We parted as they never part Whose tears are doomed to be forgot; Oh, by what agony of heart, Forget me not !—forget me not !" —ANoNntors.
At nine o'clock the next morning Traverse went to the library to keep his tryst with Colonel Le Noir.

Seated in the doctor's leathern chair, with his head thrown back, his nose erect, and his white jewelled hand caressing his bearded chin, the colonel awaited the young man's communication. With a slight bow, Traverse took a chair and drew it up to the table, seating himself, and after a little hesitation, commenced, and in a modest and self-respectful manner announced that he was charged with the last verbal instructions from the doctor to the executor of his will.
Colonel Le Noir left off caressing his chin for an instant, and with a waive of his dainty hand, silently intimated that the young man should pro- ceed.

Traverse then began and delivered the dying directions of the late doctor, to the effect that his daughter Clara Day should not be removed rom her paternal mansion, but that she should be suffered to rel am n there, retaining as a matronly companion, her old friend Mrs. Marah Rocke. " Umm ! umm ! very ingenious, upon my word," commented the colonel, still caressing his chin.

"I have now delivered my whole message, sir, and have only to add that I hope, for Miss Day's sake, there vi I be no difficulty thrown in the way of the execution of her father's last wishes, which are also, sir, very decidedly her own," said Tra- verse.

" Umm—doubtless they are—and also yours and your worthy mother's." " Sir, Miss Day's wi 1 in this matter is certainly mine. Apart from the con-ideration of her plea- sure, my wishes need not he consulted. As soon as 1. have seen Miss Day made comfortade, I leave for the far west," said Traverse, with much dignity. " Umm—and leave mamma here to guard the golden prize until your return, eh ?" sneered the colonel.
"Sir, I do not—wish to understand you," said Traverse with a flushed brow.

"Possibly not, my excellent young friend," said the colonel, ironically; then rising from his chair and elevating his voce he cried—" But I, sir, understand ?don and your mother and your p, etty scheme perfectly ! Very ingenious invention these 'last verbal instructions.' Very pretty plan to entrap on heiress; but it shall not avail you, ad- venturers that you are !—This afternoon, Sauter, the confidential attorney of my late frother-in-law, will be here with the will, which sl;a11 be read in the presence of the assembled household. If these last verbal directions arp to be found duplicated in the wi//, very good they shall be obeyed sot, they shall be discredited." During this speech, Traverse stood with kindling eyes and blazing cheeks, scarcely able to master his indignation; yet, to his credit be it spoken, he did 'rule his own spirit' and reply with dignity and calmness.

" Colonel Le Noir, my testimony in regard to the last wishes of Dr. Day can, if necessary, be supported uy other evidence—though I do not be- lieve that any man who did not himself act in habitual disregard of truth, would wantonly quea- tion the veracity of another."

"SIR I—this to me 1" exclaimed Le Noir, growing white with rage, and making a step towards the young man. "Yes, Colonel Le Noir, that to you! and this in addition :—you have presumed to charge my mother (in connection with myself) with being an adventuress! with forming d ishonourable 'schemes,' and in so charging her, Colonel Le Noir, you utter a falsehood." " Smilax 1" cried Le Noir, striding towards Traverse and raising his hand over his head—with a fearful oath—" retract your words, or--" Traverse calmly drew himself up, folded his arms, and replied coolly : "I am no brawler, Colonel Le Noir; the pistol and the bowie-knife are as strange to my hands as abusive epithets and profane language are to my lips; nevertheless, instead of retracting my words, I repebt and reit rate them. If you charge my mother with conspiracy, you utter a falsehood. As her son, I am in duty bound to say as much. " VILLAIN- 1" gasped Le Noir, shaking his fist and choking with rage ; "VILLAIN you shall repent this in every vein of your body 1' -Then seizing his hat, he strode from the room. "Boaster 1" said Traverse to himself, as he also left the library by another door. Clara was waiting for him in the little parlour below. "Well, well, dear Traverse !" said she, as he entered. "You have had the explanation with my gaardian, and—he makes no objection to carry- ing out the last directions of my father, and our own wishes ?—he is willing to leave me here ?" •` My dear girl, Colonel Le Noir defers all de- cision until the reading of the will, which is to take place this afternoon," said Tiaverse, unwilling to add to her distress by recounting the discrrace- ful scene that had just taken place in the library. "Oh ! these delays ! these deiays ! Heaven give me patience! Yet Ido not know why I should be so uneasy! It is only a form! Of course he will regard my father's wishes." "I do not see well how he can avoid doing so, especially- as Doctor Williams is another witness to them, and I shall request the doctor's attendance here this afternoon. Dear Clara keep up your spirits! A few hours, now, and all will be well," said Traverse, as he drew on his gloves and took his hat to go on his morning round of calls. An early dinner was ordered, for the purpose of giving ample time in the afternoon for the reading of the will. Owing to the kindly forbearance of each member of this little family, their meeting with their guest at the table was not so awkward as it might have been rendered. Mrs. Rocke had concealed the insults that had been offered her. Traverse had said nothing of the aftronts put upon him. So that each, having only their own private injuries to resent, felt free in forbearing. Nothing but this sort of prudence on the part of individuals ren- dered their meeting around one board possible. While they we e still at the table, the attorney, Mr. Sauter, with Doctors Williams and Dawson, arrived, and was shown into the library. And very soon after the dessert was put upon the table, the family left it, and, accompanied by Colonel Le Noir, adjourned to the library. After the usual salutations, they arranged themselves along each side of an extension table, at the head of which the attorney placed himself. In the midst of a profound silence the will was opened and cad. it was dated three years before. The bulk of his estate, after the paying of a few legacies, was left to his esteemed brother-in-law, Gabriel Le Noir, in trust for his only daughter, Clara Day, until the latter should attain the age of twenty-one, at which period she was to come into possession of the property. Then followed the distribution of the legacies. Among the rest the sum of a thousand dollars left to his young friend, Traverse Rocke, and another thousand to his esteemed nsighbour, Marah Rocke. Gabriel Le Noir was appointed sole executor of the will, trustee of the property, and guardian of the heiress. At the conclusion of the reading Mr. Sauter folded the document atal laid it upon the table. Colonel Le Noir arose and said: "The will of the late Dr. Day has been read in your presence. I presume you all heard it, and that there can be no mistake as to its purport. All that remains now is to act upon it. I shad claim the usual privilege of twelve months before ad- ministering upon the estate or paying the legacies. In the meantime, I shall assume the charge of my ward's person, and convey her to my own residence, known as the Hidden House Mrs. Rocke," lie said, turning towards the latter, "your presence and that of your young charge is no longer required here. Be so good as to prepare Miss Day's travel- ing trunks, as we set out from this place to-morrow morning." Mrs. Rocke started, looked wistfully in the face of the speaker. and seeing that he was in determined earnest, turned her appealing glances toward Tra- verse and Doctor Williams. As for Clara, her face previously blanched with grief, was now flushed with indignation. in her sudden distress and perplexity, she knew not at once what to do. Whether to utter a protest or continue silent—whether to leave the room or re- main. Her embarrassment was relieved' by Tra- verse, who. stooping, whispered to her

• "Be calm, love all shall be well. Doctor Wil- liams is about to speak." -And at that moment indeed Doctor Williams arose and said: "I have, Colonel Le Noir, to endorse a dying message from Doctor Day, entrusted to my young friend here to be delivered to you, to the effect that it was his last desire and request that his daughter, Miss Clara Day, should be permitted to reside during the term of her minority in this her patri- monial pome, under the care of her present matronly friend, Mrs. Marah Rocke. Doctor Rocke and myself are here to bear testimony to these, the last wishes of the departed—which wishes, I believe, also express the desires of the heiress." "Oh, yes ! yes !" said Clara, earnestly. "I do very much desire to remain in my own home among my own familiar friends. My dear father only consulted my comfort and happiness when he left these instructions." "There an be therefore no..reason why Miss Day should be disturbed in her present home," said Traverse.

Colonel Le Noir smiled grimly, saying: "I am sorry, Doctor Williams, to differ with you, or to distress Miss Day! But if, as she says, her lamented father consulted her pleasure in those last instructions, he certainly consulted nothing elBe—not the proprieties of conventionalism, the opinion of the world, nor the future welfare of his daughter. Therefore, as a man of Doctor Day's high positien and character, in his sane moments, never could have made such a singular arrange- ment, I am forced to the conclusion that he could not, at the time of giving those instructions, have b -ten in his right mind. Consequently, I cannot venture to act upon any verbal instructions,' however well attested, but shall be guided in every respect by the will, executed while yet the testator was in sound body and mind." "Doctor Rocke and myself are both physicians competent to certify that, at the time of leaving these directions' our respected friend was perfectly sound in mind at least," said Doctor Williams.

• "That, sir, I repeat, I contest. And acting upon the authority of the will, I shall proceed to take charge of my ward as well as of her estate. And as I think this house, under all the circum- stances, a very improper place for her to remain, I shall convey her without delay to my own home. Mrs. Rocke, I believe I requested you to see to the packing of Miss Day's trunks." "Oh. heaven, shall this wrong be permitted," ejaculated Marah. "Mrs. Rocke, I will not go unless absolutely forced to do so by a decree of the court! I shall get Doctor Williams to make an appeal for me to the Orphan's Court," said Clara, by way of en- couraging her friend. "My dear Miss Day. that, I hope, will not be required. Colonel Le Noir acts under a misappre- hension of the circumstances. We must enter into more explanations with him. In the meantime, my dear young lady, it is better that you should obey him, for the present, at least, so far as retiring from the room," said Doctor Williams. _

Clara immediately arose, and requesting Mrs. Rocke to accompany her, withdrew from the library. Doctor Williams then said: "I advised the retirement of the young lady, having a communication to make, the hearing of i which in a mixed company, might cost her an n. nocent blush. But first I would ask you, Colonel Le Noir—what are those circumstances to which you allude which render Miss Day's residence here, in her patrimonial mansion with her old and faith- ful friends, so improper L" inquired Doctor Wil- liams, courteously. "The growing intimacy, sir, between herself and a very objectionable party this young man Rocke 1" replied Colonel Le Noir. " Ah 1 and is that all ?"- . "it is enough, sir 1" said Colonel Le Noir, loftily. "Then, suppose I should inform you, sir, that this young man, Doctor Rocke, was brought up and educated at Doctor Day's cost, and under his own immediate eye ?" "Then, sir, you would only inform me that an eccentric gentleman of fortune had done—what eccentric gentledien of fortune will sometimes do— educated a pauper." At this opprobrious epithet, Traverse, with flushed face, started to his feet. "Sit down, my boy, sit down; leave me to deal with this man,' said Doctor Williams, forcing Traverse back into his seat. Then, turning to Colonel Le Noir, he said : " But, suppose, sir, that such was the estimation in which Doctor Day held the moral and intellec- tual worth of his young protegee, that he actually gave him his daughter 1" " I cannot suppose an impossibility, Doctor Williams," replied Colonel Le Noir, haughtily. "Then, sir, I have the pleasure of startling you a little by a prodigy, that you denominate an im- possibility I Clara Day and Traverse Rocke were betrothed with full knowledge *and, cordial appro- bation of the young lady's father I" " Impossible ! preposterous I I shall counten- ance no suco ridiculous absurdity I" said Colonel 1 Le Noir, growing red in the fade. "Miss Day, Doctor Rocke, Mrs. Rocke, and, myself are witnesses to that fact." "The young lady and the young man are parties immediately concerned—they cannot be received as witnesses' in their own case; Mrs. Rocke is too I much in their interest for her evidence to be taken you, sir, I consider the dupe of these cunning con- spirators—mother and son," replied Colonel Le Noir, firmly, • "Tat," said Doctor Williams, almost out of patience "I do not depend upon the words of Miss Day and her friends, althougn I hold their veracity to be above question; I had Doctor Day's dying words to the same eflect. And he mentioned the existing betrothal as the very reason why Clara should remain here in the care of her future mother- 'in-law." "Then, sir, that the doctor should have spoken thus, is only another and a stronger reason for be- lieving him to have been deranged in his last moments! You need give yourself no further trouble! I shall act upon the authority of this instrument which I hold in my hand," replied Colonel Le Noir, haughtily. "Then, as the depository of the dying man's last wishes, and as the next friend of his injured daughter, I shall make an appeal to the Orphan's Court," said Doctor Williams, coldly. "You can do as you please about that; but in the meanwhile, acting upon the authority of the will, I shalt to-morrow morning set out with my ward for my own home." "There may be time to arrest that journey," Said Doctor Williams, arising and taking his hat to go. In the passage he met Mrs. Rocke. "Dear Doctor Williams," said Mrs. Roche, earnestly, "pray come up to poor Clara's room, and speak to her, if you can possibly- say anything to comfort her; she is weeping herself into a fit of illness at the bare thought of being, so soon after her dreadful bereavement, torn away from her home and friends." " Tut ! tut I no use in weeping! all will yet be right !" "Youi have persuaded that man to permit her to remain, here, then ? ' said Marah gladly. "Persuaded him! no, nnr even undertaken to do so 1 I never saw him before to day, yet I would venture to say, from what I have now seen of him, that he never was persuaded by any agent except his own passions and interests, to any act whatever. No, I have endeavoured to show him that we have law as well as justice on our side, and even now I am afraid I shall have to take the case before the Orphan's Court before I can convince him. He purposes removing Clara to-morrow morning. I will endeavour to see the Judge of the Orphan's Court to-night, to take out a habeas co" pv..s order- ing Le Noir to bring his ward into court, and serve it on him as he passes t hrough Staunton on his way home."
"But Is there no way of preventing him from taking Clara away from the house to-morrow morn-

jug?" "No good way. No, Madam, it is best that all things should be done decently and in order. I advise you, as I shall also advise my young friends, Traverse and Clara, not to injure their own cause by unwise impatience or opposition, We should go before the Orphan's Cour4 witu the very best aspect." "Come, then, and talk to Clara. She has tha most painful antipathy to the man who claims the custody of her person, as well as the most distress- ing reluctance to leaving her dear home and friends; and all this, in addition to her recent ,heavy afflic- tion, almost overwhelms the poor child," said Mrs. Roeke, weeping. "I will go at once and do what I can to soothe her," said Doctor Williams, following Mrs. Rocke, who led him np'to Cla: a's room.. They found her prostrate upon her bed, crushed with grief. "Come, come, my dear girl, this is too bad! It is not like the usual noble fortitude of our Clara," said the old man, kindly taking her hand. "Oh, Doctor, f9rgive—forgive me! but my mirage must have .been_ very small, for I fear it is

To a.reporter of the "Orkney Herald," who visited him, Mr. John Clouston, mason, late bell-man and town crier, of Alfred-street, Stromness, narrated an extracn- dinary affair. He said :—" During the spring of 1895 I had a severe attack of sickness whicL incapacitated me from all work. My symptoms are not -easily described. For many years I have been troubled with severe bilious attacks, and while suffering from one of these turns I had a stroke, followed by utter prostration, which ren- dered me unable to work, or even. walk any distance. Severe pains in the limbs and arms,and indeed all over my body, would. make me start like a person awakened from a night-mare; 6.t other 'times my limbs became powerless, like a person suffering from paralysis, and when the pain abated for a little I was almost helpless. While sitting by my own fire I used to feel a cold shiver that no amount of clothing . would dispel. The pain and suffering continued and increased in severity for three months. About this time I saw in the newspaper reports of similar cases that had been cured by Dr. Williams' Pink Pills for Pale People, and I . resolved to give them a trial. After taking the first box the pains gradually got easier. I commenced with one Pill after each meal, and after a time increased the dose to two. The alarming sym- toms above described gradually wore away, and when I had finished the last box I felt hale and well, and in my usuarstate.of• health—in fact better than I have been for many years. I have never been troubled with my health since ; even my old trouble, biliousness, has gone. I cannot but believe that Dr. William's' Pink Pills were the means of saving my life. I have Hoorn- mended them to my neighbours. & near neighbour of mine, who has been in delicate health for years, is now using them, and althongh she has only had them for a short time,she is deriving great benefit. They are unlike other medicine ; they are easy to take, and quickly build up the system. This case confirms the remarkable 'cures affected by Dr. Williams' Pink Pills, not only in cases of paralysis and rheumatism, but in all the many disorders which follow influenza and rheumatic fever, or arise from an impoverished state of the blood and nerves, such as anaemia, pale and sallow complexion, general muscular weakness, loss of appetite, shortness of breath', pains in back, nervous headache, early decay,all forms of female weakness, hysteria, lecomotor ataxy, sciatica, palpita- tions.low vita.lity,and wasting strength from any cause. These Pills are genuine only with the full name, Dr.Wil- liams' Pink Pills for Pale People,and are sold by chemists and by Dr. Williams' Medicine Company, 46, Holborn- viaduct London, E.C.,at 25.9d.a box, or six for 139.9 d. They are unrivalled as a tonic and strengthening medi- cine for both sexes.
ROBBERY IN WARRINGTON STREETS.
" SIX MONTHS HARD LABOUR"

At Warrington Borough Police Court on Monday morn- ing, Mr. F. Monks, in the chair, a rough looking young fellow named John Broderick, of Pillings Court, was charged with stealing from the person of Patrick Walsh the sum of £5 53. 91 in rnoney.—The Chief Constable said the prisoner was charged with larceny from the per- son, but the original charge preferred agains- him was for the more serious offence of robbery with violence. In order that the case might be dealt with that rnorning.he had altered it to the less serious charge. The prosecu- tor, Peter Walsh was a farm labourer and worked f3r Mr. Massey, tarmer, Martinscroft. Being an army re- serve man, he came into Warrington for the purpose of drawing his reserve pay of £4 its. ld. on Saturday. He drew the money at the Warrington Post Office,and after. wards went into the Old Crow public house. There he met Catherine Murphy, a woman he had known prey- , iously, and she invited him up to her house in Greens Court off Dial-street. 'there appeared to have been go- ing on a sort of jollification or party at this house, an important feature of which seemed to have been an ex- tensive consumption of beer. Walsh sent for a gallon and a number of persons sat drinking it until about 1 30 in the morning. While Walsh was there the prisoner Broderick and a young girl came into the house and par- took of the refreshment. Broderick who had become very friendly with Walsh invited him to stay the remainder of the night at his mother's house in Pilling's Court. Walsh assented and shertly after one o'clock the two men set off together. While in the house,Walsh noticed that Broderick acted very strangely, and wanted to fumble about his (Walsh's) pockets. Broderick knew that Walsh, being an army reserve man, had drawn a sum of money, and he fumbled about Walsh's pockets to such an extent that shortly after two o'clock Walsh said he bad had enough of that and went out of the house. The prisoner seemed loth to lose his prize and said he would go with him and show him the way. After turning out of Dial-at. into Fennel-st., Broderick made a sudden assault. He thrust his hands into Walsh's trousers pockets, threw him to the ground, and turned the pocl,ets inside out, taking the contents, £5 sa. 9d. Walsh was thrown to the ground with such violence that his eye-brow was cut. He cried out" Murder "and "Police." P.C. Turner who had heard money jingling and a scuffle, rushed to the assistance of Walsh just in time to see a man making away into Victoria-st. Walsh was picked upand gave an accurate description of the prisoner. Inspector Taylor made an inspection of the ground where Walsh was found lying and altogether £2 2s. Bd. was founi scattered about where the scuffle had taken place. Inspector Taylor and police officers proceeded to the house of Broderick/s mother where they found him in bed. He was brought to the police station and placed between two other men, and Walsh unhesitatingly identified the prisoner as the man who attacked and robbed him. A great quantity of blood was found on Walsh's head and face.and when Broderick was apprehended his clothing was found spotted with blood. He (the Chief Constable) did not think the pri- soner would deny the charge. There was only is. 11d. found upon Broderick but he had had ample opportu- nity of getting rid of it before he was apprehended.— On being charred with the offence, the prisoner pleaded guilty.—D.B. Monaghan gave evidence as to the charac- ter of the prisoner. He had been an inmate of a reforma- tory in consequence of stealing,and since his release had been several times convicted of theft. This was his tenth'appearance. He was a man that did not work and would not do so, and beloneed to a gang something similar to the Manchester scuttlers.—Prisoner stated that he was drunk at the time. Be was committed to prison for six months' hard labour.

Further particulars are given in teleerams from Bulu- wayo and Pietersburg of the revolt of the Matahele. There has been some rather severe fighting near Hutu- wa.yo. A recident of that place save that up to the present, taking the whole" disturbed" ares,, abou t 80 white people have been killed.

div.head: EXAMINER, SATURDAY, APRIL 11, 1896.
div.p: THE EXAMINER, SATURDAY, APRIL 11, 1896.

Dr. Montague, the Canadian Minister of Agriculture, has ended his visit to England and is now on his way back to Canada. He made good Use of his visit to im- press upon Mr. Chamberlain, whom he met on several occasions, the great desire Canadian Ministers have for all the co-operation the British Government can give in directing the attention of suitable British emigrants to the abundant fertility of Canadian lands. " Get popu- lation, and all else shall be added unto you," is Mr. Chamberlain's very wise maxim for the Colonies. "Then help us to get them," is Dr. Montague's rejoinder. He dined with Mr. Chamberlain before leaving London, and had a long interview with Mr. Long on the subject of the Cattle Exclusion Bill. His protests :on the latter question were, it is feared, unavailing.

It is probable that the tenaciousness to life of that many times slain chief Osman Digna has given colour to the rumour from the Cape that Lobengula is not only alive but is to lead an army-3r impi—against Bulu- way°. The report, however, may assuredly be dismissed as baseless. It is true that the actual place of Lo Ben's burial is not known, but the most circumstantial ac- counts of his death came to hand from native sources, and a favourite Induna told how he thrust an assegai into the dead body of hi a royal master, in accordance with time-honoured custom.

A good deal of comment has been aroused in legal circles by the announcement that the General Council of the Bar has declared against barristers practising in courts of which their fathers or near relatives are judges. It is chiefly in county courts that this rule will apply. But it will operate to some extent also in the Chancery Division.

On Tuesday night a man, a native of Berne, fell into the famous bear pit, and was found on Wednesday morning torn to pieces by bears. No one witnessed the occurrence,but it is presumed that the unfortunate man, who, after attending the weekly market here, had spent the evenkg in drinking at various taverns, wished on the way ilome to look at the bears, and that in leaning over the parapet he lost his balanca and fell into the pit. It was noticed that the bears hid been making con- siderable noise since ten o'clock at night,and on Wednes - day morning the fury of the beasts against their prey was still such that they could only ba induced to leave the mangled remains by streams of water being brought to bear upon them from pipes worked at high pressure. previ.us efforts to part them by torches having proved unavailing.

div.head: NOTES AND NEWS.
div.p: NOTES AND NEWS.

The young Empress of Russia evidently finds the Russian climate agrees with her, for a correspondent, who had an audience with her last week, writes that she has quite lost the fragile appearance that distinguished her when she first married. It is de rigneur to be dressed entirely in white when the Empress commands an inter- view, and in black if it is the Dowager Empress.

Of all the sovereigns of the world, the Shah of Persia is said to possess the largest treasure in jewels and wsld ornaments, it being valued at twelve million pounds.' This is prooably exceeded by the Pope's wealth in similar • valuables.

Nansen's wife comes from a noted family. Michael Sara, her father, was distinguished as a Norwegian naturalist. Ber mother is the sister of the poet Wet- haven. At present Mme. N mien is almost as keenly. interested in the concert room as in the North Pole, for she is Norway's foremost concert singer.

Mr. T. J. Macnamara, the editor of the" Schoal- master," who has come so prominently to the front over the Eitication question,is the son of a Crimean veteran, and was born in Canada. '. In his youth—necessarily a time of stir and movement—he learned " Gil Bias "and "Don Quixote" off by heart. He became a Board School teacher in 1871, when the family settled in Bris- tol. Mr. Macnam.lra. is n.w the president-elect of the National Union of Teachers. Be lives in Dulwich,where his study Is a monutoental Education Question in itself, so full is it of scholastic pamphlets and documents that betoken the specialist. He thinks the teaching market is utterly glutted, and the future of the young male teacher exceedingly unpromising.

In the Paris maternity ho=pitals weakling babies are kept like chicks in incubators until they are strong enough to hear the rough winds of the world. Our Consul at St. lago de Casa, Mr. F. W. Ramsden, tells of a new method of fighting a dreadful disease by the exact opposite of these Paris incubators: This is a refrigerat- ing box invented by Dr. Garcia for the treament of yel- low fever. It is a sort of a very large coffin with a pent-roof made double,and a glass window in the side. It is brought in pieces into the patient's room, :crewed together, -be is placed in it, and' the double roof is filled with ice. The temperature is kept a few degrees above freezing,,and is graduated by the use of the ice. The period in the box is limited to three days, but the patient,it is stated, is usually cured in a day and a half to two days, the theory being, we suppose, that the bacilli of the disease cannot reproduce tnemselves except at a high tunmerature. A friend of Mr. Rarnsden who was attacked by yellow fever and tried the box, told him that soon alter being put in it his headache de- creased, the pains in the bask be,same less severe, his great thirst ceased, and in a Finn time he experienced a feeling of perfect comfort and rest. It is to be hoped that some English hospital will make trial of the plan for the treatment of fever and influenza here.

General Neal Dovi, the well-known Prohibitionist,who I recently celebrated his ninety-second birthday, is re- I ported to be in a remarkably vigorous condition. His , mental powers have not yet felt the touch of age, and during the late municipal campaign in Boston he wrote a series of articles in which he assailed those to whom he was opposed with all his cld vigour. He keeps up his correspondence with temperance workers all over the world, and writes much for publication.

German merchants are unquestianably enterprising, but their methods are not always courteous. The Lon- don representatives of a well-known German manufac- turing firm have recently sent out to their customers an inquisitorial circular, which is the perfection of inso- lence. After coolly complaining that exact information as to their castomers' standing cannot be obtained by prying elsewhere, an answer is requested to the follow- ing queries : Established in what year? Name of proprietor or partners? What goods do you trade in chiefly? Who are your banks? Have you any property outside your business capital? Your trade references? Prussian m4nners are a byword in Germany, and the above specimen will hardly increase the estimation in which they are held in England.

A ludicrous case,arising out of an incident in a French ralway train, has come before the Paris Correctional Court. An Englishman named London accused a French lady, Madame Larose, of having taken his boots during a journey to Paris. The lady's version of the matter was that she entered with her daughter a first-elms carriage, and saw the plaintiff snugly esconced in a corner. When the train stetted be pulled off his boots, drew his travelling cap over his eyes,and stretched himself at full length along the seat. During the night, which was very warm, Madame Larose, objecting to the boots,tied them together and, their owner being still asleep, she dangled the article 3 outside the door of the carriage, attaching them to the handle. At the station where the train stopped a railway porter cut down the Briton's boots and put them in a goods van. The consequence of this was that Mr. London had, on arriving at a his destination, to leave the carriage in his socks and search high and low for his lost footgear, which he eventually found. He summoned the defendant on account of the inconvenience caused to him by her free and easy mode of dealing with his property. "Has the plaintiff got hisiboots now ?" asked the magistrate • and the reply was affirmatively given in dumb show, the Englishman showing one of his feet to demonstrate that he had re- covered his property. "Then what do es he want to come here for ?" sternly observed the dispenser of law. "His boots were not stolen, and he ought not to have taken them off in a railway carriage. The case is dismissed."

A proposal for another international sporting contest comes from America. Thiß time the challenge has to do with whist. The sixth American Whist Con- gress is to be held at Brooklyn in June, and the corres- ponding secretary of the American Whist Leagnq writes that "there is a universal desire on the part of the whist players of America to have an international match during the time of the Congress, and when the American players are congregated from all sections of the country. Be therefore suggests that England should send a team of four or more players to compete with the best the United States can produce.

The " Telegraph " Paris correspondent writes :—At what age can an unmarried woman be described as an old maid ? This vexed question has just been officially settled here in what many people may regard as rather an ungallant manner,thonah it should be explained that the line had to be drawn between young and old of the fair sex, with ng interval between the two definitions. A worthy citivn had bequeathed a sum of money to be devoted to annual presentations to a certain number of young unmarried people of both sexes who had sup- ported their parents in their declining years, the object beitg to enable them to settle themselves in life. No special aae was mentioned, and the Prefect of the Seine had to solve the pro- blem to the best of his judgment. Id. Poubelle has accordingly issued a decree setting forth that bachelors and spinsters are to be considered as young until they have attained the age of 30. This, of course, is not an illiberal allowance,but then comes the converse proposi- tion,and there is no alternative for the unmarried women but to be classified as " vielles filles " as soon as they have attained the age mentioned.
