No woman at all is allowed to serve liquor, and two waitresses in a Dutch beer saloon were arrested on Sunday for serving tomers with beer. In private clubs it is forbidden that drink shall be served to members on Sundays, either with or without meals. A person is even forbidden to offerliquor in his own home to visitors, and a police officer is empowered to invade a private residence if he suspects that others than the actual members of the family are drinking wine at dinner. The room where the liquors are kept at hotels must he open to the street and a ooliceman stands in front, where he can watch that no person other toan the proprietor or his assistant is allowed to enter the room, and then only for the pur- pose of getting a bottle to serve to an actual resident or guest in the hotel. A test case was made on Saturday of a man conducting a large boarding-house for labou,- ere who breakfast at four o'clock each morning. It was decided that he should not be allowed to serve the meal at that hour on Monday mornings, and that the labour- ers must either go to work hungry or delay starting until later.

A story reaches New York from San Francisco to the effect that George Gard, late chief of the Southern Pacific Railway Detective Service, claims to have dit,- covered a conspiracy to kidnap Mr. Cornelius Vanderbilt and a party of his friends while travelling last week on the railway, but that owing to the precautions taken the plot failed. Gard says :—" Shortly before Mr. Vander- bilt and his party reached El Pamo,in Texas,l received a letter detailing the plans of the gang to kidnap Mr. Vanderbilt. According to the letter, the conspirators, including my informant, had arranged to stop the Van- derbilt special train at some point in the San Joaquin 'Valley, on the western slope of the Sierra Nevadas, in Southern Calif.rnia., and had decided that if they did not find a sufficiently large sum of money among the party Mr. Vanderbilt should be held to ransom. Gard says that NO:en the railway company heard of the details it was arranged that a pilot engine should be sent ahead of the special train,and that the latter should be stopped at Bakerville at the entrance of the valley and detained there all night, passing through the valley in the day- time ou Tuesday last. This arrangement probably upset the plans of the conspirators." Gard, it is said, is con- sidered a trustworthy man,and his statement is generally accepted as correct.

div.head: EXTRAORDINARY BIGAMY CASE.
div.p: EXTRAORDINARY BIGAMY CASE.
A VISIT TO WARRINGTON.

Robert James Venable Smith, wheelwright, 38 years of age, was again before the justices at the Manchester Paiice Court on Tuesday on the charge of bigamy. Ac- cording to the evidence in possession of the police the prisoner has had an extraordinary career, having in different parts of the kingdom undergone the marriage ceremony no less than five times,ail the women victim ised been alive at the present time. He commenced by marrying his first wife, Carrie Naomi Roberts, at Mill- brook, Bedfordshire, in February, 1884. He lived with her five or six years.and then deserted her and the child. He turned up in Manchester, and in October, 1889, married a domestic servant named Rose Oyawshaw, at St. Phillip's Church, Hulme. They had lived together only seven weeks when the prisoner went away, but re- turned in abont six months' time. He stayed another five weeks,and then finally decamped. He was always more or less out of work and was supplied with clothes and tools, by Miss Crawshaw, who had saved some money. which, fortunately for her, the prisoner did not draw upon to any considerable extent. Liverpool was the scene of his next matrimonial escapade, the victim being Annie Mercer, another servant, with whom he went through the marriage ceremony, in 1892. He told her that he had not been married ' before,- and that his name was Herbert Vincent James. They lived about three months in Liverpool, and then went to Leeds. At the latter place he asked her to keep him by going on the streets, and when she refused he sent her back to Liverpool. The following year he married Alice Dales at Heckmondwike. The couple went to Birmingham, and whilst there he made the acquaintance of another woman named Elizabeth Carr. Losing no time, he had the banns published, and after getting hold of what pro- perty Dales was possessed of he took tier to Warrington. Ho saw her settled there and returning to Birmingham ' married Carr last year. At the time of his arrest by De- tective Williams he was living with yet another woman in Manchester, but had not got so far as the marriage ceremony. When formally charged with the offences he admitted his guilt, and said he had mad: a fool of him- self. It may be added that following upon his marriage with Dales the prispner enlisted in the Royal Engineers, but only had a very brief career in the army, being drummed out for misconduct. The prisoner, who said that he was separated from his first wife by arrange- meet, was committed for trial at the next Manchester Assizes, at which all the women he has wronged have been bound ever to give evidence.

div.head: LAND OF GENNES.IRETH.
div.p: THE LAND OF GENNES.IRETH.

Imbosovned in its graceful bills Gennes'reth's valley lies: A fertile land of brooks and rills, Olerarched with sunny skies. The sounds of busy life no more Relieve its solitude ; And only runs mark the shore Where teeming cities stood. But all its scenes, around, above, And all its loneliness ; Are fragrant with the wondrous love Of Him who came to bless. In this fair land the Son of God In mortal flesh was found ; These now deserted paths be trod, And made them holy ground. Here in the calm of eventide The poor around him drew; And while His power their needs supplied, They felt His mercy too. This sea once knew His gentle tread, Once bore His sleeping form : It's winds and waves in silence fled, When be rebuked the storm. These lonely hills His temple were, The stars His altar-light : And tears that marked His vigil there Mixed with the dews of night. But men despised His wondrous grace, Denied His power to save : And gave to Him no dwelEng place, No rest but in the grave. Yet still He called from shore and sea, From vale and mountain crest : " Come weary sinners unto Me," "And I will give you rest." And, gra:.ious now as He was then, Be loves the humble poor; And gives His rest to weary men Who trust His promise sure. J. H. W. CLINDINNING.

div.head: BEFORE AND AFTER INFLUENZA.
div.p: BEFORE AND AFTER INFLUENZA.

Everybody who has had the influenza knows the ex- treme weakness that follows it. Be does not need to be reminded of the necessity for building up the system in this weakened state. But if we all wait until we are in this extreme of weakness before taking steps to ever- come it, some of us will surely never come out of it. It is not every system that can stand being reduced to emaciation; and the best advice that can be eiven to all is to!fortify the system, so that it will be less subject to attacks of illness. You cannot get away from the truth that a well-nourished body is less liable to disease than a poorly-nourished one. Tlere is a letter that explains a point or two :

"I had a very bad attack of Influenza in the winter of 1892, which left me very weak and low-spirited. I could not get un courage to do anything; I had lost a good deal of flesh and did not seem to regain my strength. I tried various remedies and they were of no avail. I thought more than once that my doom was sealed, but seeing one of your advertisements about Scott's Emulsion, I thought I would give it a trial. I soon found that it was everything that you claim for it,Scott's Emulsion built me up wonderfully,and proved to be just what I needed to give me strength, I think it is a wonderful remedy.—Yours very truly, (signed). E. BANNISTER, 36 Mitchell-street,Newtown, October 21st, 1895."

I confidentlF believe Mr. Bannister would never have thought his" doom was seated "if he had tried Scott's EITUISiOri earlier. This is the trouble with hundreds of thousands of sufferers. They wait too long before they begin with the right treatment. Scott's Emulsion is a perfectly natural remedy for weak, emaciated, or wast- ing conditions. It increases vitality, makes healthy flesh, enriches the tlood and brings the whole body up to its normal condition. It is nourishment for babies and children who do not thrive, and life itself to the consumptives. It represents the principle of vitality so necessary to all who are thin and i ale and threatened with disease.
Scott's Emulsion cannot be duplicated. It is peculiar to itself, and may be distinguished by trade-mark of a man carrying a big f.sh on his back on the wrapper. (8)

div.head: NOTES ON GAMES AND
div.p: NOTES ON GAMES AND
ATHLETICS.
RUGBY FOOTBALL.

The Warrington team has been very busy this Easter, playing four matches within five days. It cannot be said that the wirepullers have covered themselves with glory in the four engagements,in fact,there seems to be some- thing very erratic in their form. In the first place,they go down before Runcorn, and on the following day they suffer a total eclipse at Leeds. On Bank Holiday they shine in their true form once more,and on Tuesday night they are truly brilliant when facing the burly Wiganers. Two disastrous defeats and two splendid victories—such has been the experiene,e of the Warrington team this Eastertide. To account for this see-saw-like experience is not an easy task.

Runcorn's defeat of Warrington by twelve points to nil was not altogether undeserved owing to the wretched manner in which several of•the home team fumbled when goad openings presented themselves. The score certainly does not represent the afternoon's play, for Warrington pressed quite as much—if not more—than their opponents. But Runcorn snapped up any oppor- tunities for scoring which were given,and as Warrington failed to do the same, they had the mortification of see- ing the wearers of the " myrtle green" record a secpnd couple of points in the competition at their expense.

The result of the following day's play at Leeds caused still greater surprise. When that leviathan score of three goals (one dropped) and four tries (26 points) to Warrington's solitary try was read,there were some eyes at Warrington almost as large as saucers. The team which journeyed to Leeds was not what may be des- cribed as a strong one, but it was never expected that they would be so severely thrashed. The home team was entirely at an advantage in not having played the pre- vious day and being thus fresh for their work, but still Warrington should have played a better defensive game. The result has seriously affected Warrington's average, and ak it was the last visit of the team to Yorkshire this season it is a pity that they did not leave a better re- cord behind them.

These two reverses seemed to have had a salutary effect upon the Warrington team, for on Monday they played with a determination to win which was irreAst- able. Stockport, wearing the laurels of victory over the crack Manningham team, received such a rebuff, on the Wilderspool enclosure which they will have cause to re- member. From start to finish there was only one team "in it "and that wasn't Stockport. Burton's re-appear- ance in the home team was heartily welcomed, and he seemed to infuse new life into the homesters. Ihe two half-backs were in fine form. and Higginbottom bids fair to become as popular as his co-partner—" Smack" Bate. An interesting feature of Barber's play was his success as goal kicker, scoring two really fine goals. The reselt was a well-earned victory for the home team by fourteen poigts to three, and helped to atone for Satur- day's repulse.

It was a case of Greek meeting Greek on Tuesday evening when Warrington's old rivals—Wigan presented. themselves in their cherry and white on the Wilderspoil ground. Wigan come with a far better record than could be stated of their opponents. In the Lancashire section of the competition they occupied the premier place, and in the combination they were twelve points ahead of Warrington.Then again,only the day previous, they had beeen the Leeds club which Warrington have a slight remembrance of, and consequently there were very few optismistic enough to predict a victory for the home team. However, as is often the case in football, the unexpected happened, and after a stubbornly con- tested game Warrington retired victorious to the chag- rin of the 1,500 Wiganers present. Cross was responsible for the try scored by Warrington, although he was in- debted to Lawless for the cross-kick which enabled him to score. Barber in his new role as goal-kicker was again a success, and his kick won the match. Higgin- bottom played a sterling game throughout, and the threequarter line gave a splendid display in passing. The only weak point in the home team was the fullback— Evans being somewhat too slow. Many would like to see tSurton given a trial in this position.

This victory has improved Warrington's position won- derfully in the competition, and it is to be hoped that they will maintain it. There are now but four matches to play before the close of the season, viz.: Wakefield Trinity, Widnes, Broughton Rangers and Halifax. As was predicted in this column a week ago, the Wakefield Trinity club will journey to Warrington to-day in conse- quence of the suspension of their ground. If the home team play with anything like the determination which characterised Tuesday's match, they should again come out victorious.

The team selected to represent Warrington to-day will be as follows :—Full back, J. W. Evans ; three-quarters, Broady, Burton, O'Brien, Barber ; half backs, Higtin- bottom and Clarke; forwards, Hill, Nevins, Taylor,Fair- burst, Saunders, Berry, Burrows and Thornton.

div.head: CYCLING.
div.p: CYCLING.

As in former years the Easter tour of the Warrington Cycling Club was to North Wales. On Friday a good number in spite of the wet weather travelled to Llan- gollen where a good time was snent. On the Saturday the number was augmented to 30, and whilst part of the club visited the famous scenes in the district, another party set over the mountains to Glynn and spent the day in trout fishing. On Sunday same of the members jour- neyed on to Llandudno, others to Cerrig-y-Drindn whilst the remainder drove round by Berwyn and Glandwddy, and had a gay time. On Monday a farewell visit was paid to the chief places of interest and after dinner the whole crowd, some by wheel and some by traie, set off for Warringtnn which was reached in good time, after a most pleasant and enjoyable Easter tour.

div.head: OUR LOCAL CHURCHES-WARRINGTON.
div.p: OUR LOCAL CHURCHES-WARRINGTON.
WYCLIFFE P.S. A. SOCIETY.

In consequence of the Easter holidays the attendance on Sunday at the meeting of this society was not so numerous as usual. AL J. Porritt officiated as chairman, and in his address said that Eastertide was always a time of rejoicing to the Christian, for it spoke tc him of a risen and living Christ. Some people asserted that Christianity was played out, but he (the Chairman) did not believe it. Christ was more popular to•day than ever.—The speaker was Mr. Wilson of Manchester. who spoke of the value of eiving testimony for Christ in whatever circnmstances they were plared.—The Rev. J. Yonge stated that the membership for the present year already stood at 850. He asked the members to make the P.S.A. a still greater force in the town for good. Messrs. A. Lang and Thomas Hawthorn also assisted in the service, and Miss Pemberton sang a solo which was much appreciated.

JAPAN ES E COM PETITION. (By Mn. H. WHITETAIL) (Continued.) As to the things that build up a nation, Japan undoubtedly teas them, or nearly so. A commercial and industrial greatness go hand-in-hand with a bountiful supply of nature's gifts, coal and the common metals, iron and copper. With the dis- position and ability to utilize these, the secret of a nation's greatness is not far to seek, Japan is blessed in the possession of coal measures of enor- mous magnitude,so placed that they may be worked at the lowest cost. She has also a moderate supply of iron of fair quality, and has neighbours with enormous lodes ready to supply her whenever a de- mand shall be made upon them. Her copper mines have been worked for centuries, and show, no signs of giving out, and Japan will make the best of these treasures. Her minerals, and her ability to use them, is now the great question. We know not what the future has in store for us; electricity is making great strides. In the meantime coal is of the first importance. In 1877, Mr. Lyman, the geolegist in charge of a government survey, in his report said, " One of the principal results of the geological survey of Zezzois the recognition of the fact that on this island there are perhaps 150,000 millone of tons of workable coal, or two thirds as much as the coal of the same thickness in the celebrated coal fields of Great Britain. The amount of coal on Zezzo would put the island in position to furnish the present annual production of Great Britain for nearly 1,000 years," This: is further corroborated by Rein who sags, "There are thicker seams in Japan proper (than in Zezzo) that have not yet been opened." The coal fields of Japan are not being worked for domestic consumption solely. A large export trade has grown up which is displacing British coal in all Asiatic Countries. The exports which'were valued at about £400,000 in 1885 had increased to £1,300,000 in 1894, and according to a correspond- ent of the" London Times" English coal has been driven out of every country east of Singapore, and Japanese coal is now used as far west as Colombo and Calcutta. As showing the important bearing the gold and silver question has upon commerce the 'following from the same correspondent is interest- ing, showing largely the reason for this displaze- ment :—"The silver price of Cardiff coal, notwith- standing the fall of its gold price, has increased from 10dols. to 15dols to 16dols. silver per ton, while, with the excellent plant laid down in Japan to work the native mines and the construction of railss aye to convey their output to the chief indus- trial centers, the price of Japanese coal has fallen to 3dols. silver per ton, or for the purposes of competition with gold countries to little more than 6 shillings gold per ton. The depreciation of silver might, in fact, be said to operate as a system of protection in favour of the industries of silver countries as against those of gold countries." In 1889 the production of iron was small, and not near sufficient to meet the home demand, more re- cently Japanese and European engineers have ex- pressed the opinion that iron in abundance will be obtained,meanwhile they are looking to Corea and Formosa where there is an abundance. They are skilful workers of iron,which their armourersitrans- fer into famous weapons of steel. They produce swords by which one can eut through iron nails without nicking the blades in the slightest. They are not alone expert in the fashioning of weapons. In the decoration of iron they have produced re- sults which surpass those reached by any other people. Inlaid work has been directly applied to cast iron. It is frequently met with on tea kettles, vases,&c.,&c. Copper also they have in abundance. Government statistics show the yearly average during the years 1877-81 was 8 900 tons. Japan has other metallic resources than those mentioned, and has achieved some distinction in the fashioning of modern machinery. The "Times " correspondent, whom I have quoted, closes his report of the Riot° exhibition with the following :—" Not only are .all these things made in Japan just as perfectly as in America or England or Germany,but the machinery for making them is also constructed in Japan. Steam engines, presses, cutting, turning, weaving, printing and other machines are all made in Japan. There are also ample supplies of raw material.such as coal and iron and woods of all kinds, so that this island empire is in a state to compete with the rest of the world." It has been the rule with observers, and writers on Japan to cultivate the impression that the peo- ple would develop along lines which would make them continually increasing customers of the 'Western world, and that tea and silk only would leave her shores in payment for her imports. It is time to get rid of this idea, a rude awakening is close at hand. The Japanese have been ready lenough to accept the best the Occident could offer them, but it will be an error to assume that after once learning their testa% they w)1 refuse to profit by it. Respecting their shipping the American Consul wrote in April 1895 :—" The enterprising Japanese have Japanete shins manned by sailors ready to accept wages which the American and European sailor would refuse with scorn, will sail into our ports bringing manufactured article's the product of three to ten cents, a day labour. They have within a few years established docks and machine shops for-the building of medium sized warships, and each subsequent year has witnessed fewer orders going to foreign markets for naval supplies. Japan is a breeder of sailors who are ready to work for very scant wages. wages so low that the ships manned by them can afford to underbid every competitor in the freight. carrying business. A writer in the December " Contempor- ary Review " says "Turning to the East, it is prac- tically certain that we shall have to face, in the near future, a very serious or even a ruinous CMl- mereial competition. The Japanese are already building their own war vessels of a large size. In five years' time they confidently hope to underbid Great Britain and all the world in the construction of steam vessels, and a most, competent authority, Dr. Elgar, who has examined the question during a prolonged stay in Japan, seems to think theis ex- pectations are well founded." in the Manchester" Guardian "of Feb. 11, 1896, I see an article which entirely confirms the position I have taken inStheee letters. Under the caption of "The exportation of Textile machinery," the writer says " The rapidly increasing exports of tex- tile machinery from this country have recently excited some disquietude in the minds of numerous Persons interested in the British cotton industry. In 1893 the shipments amounted to £5.255,877, in 1894 to £5,478.816, and in 1895 to £6,163,047. There can be no doubt that much the greater part of the machinery comprised in the general term " textile " is for use in one branch or snwher of the cotton in- dustry outside the United Kingdom, and the in- ference is quite justified that much, if not most of it,will in fact be employed in competition with the cotton mills and the printing.bleaching and dyeing works of this country. It is set up in countries which practice Protection, such as those of the Continent or the United States,or those which enjoy a special advantage as producers from their mone- tary system such as India. China and Japan." In slosing this series of 'letters I should like to notice first, that it woul ' be utterly futile to at- tempt to place any check upon the exporting of machinery. That will continue RO long as a cus- tomer can be found ; next, as to coal, the export of which, and its getting is a source of wealth to shipper and owner, and of a questionable "living wage " to the miner, I think it likely that England is trying to get rid, as fast, as she can, of one of the real secrets of her greatness, and that a day of re- pentence will come. Touching Protection it is quite clear to me that the day that Cobden thought was close at hand, is receding further and further into the dim future. Not during the next five decades will America be a free trade country. Not during the next ten decades will free trade be adopted as the only panacea for indus- trial Europe's troubles. I almost think the time has come when discriminating powers should be given to a government, not selfishly par- tizan to determine what shall, and what, shall not come into the country. This and state ownership of land with country or municipal ownership of the nation's resources would make the people aunit, and break up the system that makes one men rieh, and ten men poor. And now to cloee, several refer- ences have been made in the foregoing to the money question. It it, a question I have never been able to understand, but I can eee plainly that there are men of light, and leading" who think that, the ex- change values existing between the various nations does not work beneficially all round, and, if I may AO presume, I would recommend Trades' Councils to look around among their fellow townsmen and in- vite those who could be found, able and willing to give a few popular talks upon this, apparently, question of emergency, and be ruled accordingly as to future legislation.

SERIOUS ACCIDENT ON THE SNOWDON RAILWAY.

The line to the summit of Snowdon was opened on Mon- day, and the result was most disastrous. The firat train made the as:•ent in safety,but on the return journey the gear which connected the Ongine with the centre "rack "rail failed,and the engine began to move down the hill at a rapid rate. The accounts of what followed vary considerably. According to one correspondent the brakes on the passenger carriages were applied so sud- denly that the coupling with the engine was snapped. Another states that there were no couplings, the car- riages simply obeying the law of gravitatiou,and the re- tarding power being exerted by the engine. Whatever the cause, the result was that the engine dashed on in front. The driver and fireman leaped off and escaped, but the engine left the rails at a sharp curve, and now lies at the bottom of the Pass of Llanberis. The disaster did no end here. The engine in its fall struck down a telegraph post and disarranged the " block" system. The bell rang in the summit station,and the second train started down the line,ru ning into the first and smash- ing an empty carriage. One of the persons who sprang from the train had his leg broken, and others were cut and bruised. Altogether, a more disastrous day for the fortunes of the Mountain Railway could hardly have been imagined.

div.head: WA.RRINGTON.
div.p: WA.RRINGTON.
THE LITE Mn. JOSEPH DAVIES, J.P.

Mrs. Davies, widow of the late Mr. Joseph Davies, J.P., has had erected in the Parish Church in memory of her husland, some new dark oak choir stall fronts. They are an exact reproduction of the old oak fronts of the clergy stalls that had been erected before the restoration, the work hav- ing been very ably carried out under the superin- tendence of Mr. Thomas Davies, builder, Butter- market-qt. The choir stalls—two in number—ars about 151 t. in length, and they are certainly, an im- provement to the interior of the building. On a small brass plate at the end of one of the stalls is the following inscription'in blue and red letters : "in memory of Joseph- Davies, of the . Old Warps, Warrington, who died 22nd March ,1895 These choir stalls were placed here by his widow. Easter,lB96.' Ou the wall above the pulpit steps is a much larger solid brass memorial tablet, which has the follow- ing inscription also in blue and red letters :—" In memory of Joseph Davies, of the Old warps, War- rington ; born 4th November, 1826; died 22nd March, 1896 He laboured with zeal fqr many years in the public cause of his native town, and when warden of this church raised funds to build this tower and spire. His works do follow him." The incriptionin each case is surmounted by a red cross.
LOYAL ORDER OF ANCIENT SHEPHERDS, WARRINGTON DISTRICT. -

On Saturday the quarterly meeting of the above district was held at the Ironworkers' Home Lodges Bowling Green Inn, Bank Quay. The mewing was presided over by the Dtitrict Chief (Bro. T.C.Duck- worth), who was supported by the Deputy (Bro. William Eckersley), Treasurer (Bro. James Parr), District Secretary (Bro. P. Edgar), Trustees (Bros. Potter and Bennion), and 20 other delegates from the lodges forming such district. After the roll had been called, the district secretary read the state- ment of accounts for the past quarter. and .having been verified by the auditors (Messrs. Kirkham and Massey) as being correct and highly satisfactory it was passed. • More new members,viz., 32, as against 25 the previous quarter,were forthcoming,and even- tually passed, special mention being made as to the efforts of the Shepherds by Night Lodge, Lymm. The present membership of the district stands, in- cluding the new members passed, at 889, being an. increase of 18. P.P.C.S. Bro. William Gleave, of the Morning Star Lodge, was unanimously elected to represent the district at the forthcoming A.M.C. of the Order at Newcastle-an-Tyne in Whit-week. After other busine‘s had been transacted, a short statement as to the quinquennial returns was made by the di-trict secretary. He stated that he was highly pleased at the efficient manner in which the work had been performed by the.secretaries of the lodges, pointing out that it was no light task they had to petform, and that it required time ' and thought, and that he desired to put on record his appreciation of the efforts the lodge officials had made to prepare and complete the returns in the time fixed by the Board. After remarks from Bros, Weir, kialey,Kirkham, and ett!ers, an agreeable and plettita nt meeting terminated by the Chief thanisin I the delegates for their attendance.

A BOOK FOR MARRIED WOMEN

The information contained in this book ought to be known by every married woman, aud it will not harm the unmarried to read. The book is canversiently divided Into 12 chapters. The first chapter treats of the changes at puberty,or when a girl becomes a woman. The second chapter treats of marriage from a doctor's standpoint; points out the best age for marriage, and wno should have children and who not, and furnishes useful in- formation that one can ordinarily get only from an In. doctor. The third ch4pter treats of the marriage of blood relations; and condemns such marriages as a rule. Chapter four treats of the signs of pregnancy. The filth chapter tells how a woman should live during the pregnant state. The sixt'a chapter treats ot mishaps and how to avoid them. The seventh chapter treats cf maternal impressions and shows that birthmarks are not due tolongings on the part of the mother, Is-A rather to her poor health. The eighth chapter teaches how to have easy confinements. Certain people believe that women should bring forth in pain and trouble, but the hygienic physician says that confinements can be made comparatively easy if certain rules are obeyed; these rules are given. The ninth chapter treats of the proper management of confinement until the baby is born. The tenth chapter tells how to treat the mother till she is up and about again. The eleventh chapter treats of sterility ; gives the main causes of it, how these .may bo overcome and children result. The last chapter treats of the "change," a most important article for all women over forty. The book is full of useful information and no book is written which goes so thoroughly into matters relating to married women. Some may think too much Is told ; such can scarcely be the ca3e, for knowledge is power and the means of attaining happiness. The bcok can be had from Dr. T. R. ALLINSOI4, 25 Box, 4, Spanish-place Manchester-square, London, W., in return for a Postal order or is. id.

the awards. There are lawyers, farmers, clerks postmen, dustmen, school-boys, journalists, car- penters, tailors and masons. Natives of India have received the coveted honour—JOT RAN for risking his life in rescuing a woman and two children from drowning in a well near Delhi, and FATCH DIN for attempting,to rescue NADI BAKSH from a mountain torrent. The Stanhope Gold Medal is the chief prize of the Society, and there must have been a good deal of consideration before its destination was finally decided upon. It was, however, awarded to Mr. E. A. HATTON, one of the crew of the Dunbar Castle. This gal- lant seaman, on the third of March last year jumped into the sea to rescue the carpenter who had been washed overboard. The vessel was go- ing at a good speed at the time and the sea was infested with sharks. HATTON, we are told, had almost reached the drowning man when the latter threw up his arras and disappeared. There are many other deeds recorded in the Society's re- port almost or quite as perilous as this,yet no one will deny that HATTON is amply entitled to the gold medal.

The "drawing of lots" is surely a very primitive and unsatisfactory method of deciding an election. Yet that is the way a tie in the election of parish councillors for Stockton Heath was settled, and the plan rise, we believe, been adopted at some other places besides. It has been said that the drawing of lots is not a-prescribed way of deciding which of two candidates equally favoured with votes by the electors is to be declared elected and which is to re- main out in the cold, but returning officers will no doubt have considered that point for themselves. It is certainly not an improvement upon the " cast- ing vote."

The news that the London and North-Western Railway Company intend to oppose for the third time tbe Borough Extension Bill—this time in the House of Lords—will cause a considerable amount of surprise, and no doubt arouse feelings of indigna- tion amongst the ratepayers. The Rail way Com- pany's persistence in opposing the Bill has already cos:. the town sortie thousands of pounds, and they now propose to compel the Corporation to make a further call upon the pockets of the ratepayers in order to getthe;Bill through the House of Lords. The object of the Railway Company is to get a reduction in rating which no other payer of rates either claims or receives. It will be remembered that the Select Committee of the !louse of Commons quickly dis- posed of the objections to the extension of the borough raised by the London and North Western,and so far as we know there is nothing to show that the opposers of the Extension Bill are likely to be any more successful before the House of Lords. But this great railway company has a long purse and it appears to be very determined to make Warrington pay smartly for its Extension Bill. There is, per- haps, a little consolation to be derived from the fact that the Company as a large ratepayer will have to pay its share of the costs.

THE ISSUING OF DEFAULT SUMMONSES.— INTERESTING CASE. Before His Honour Judge Wynne Ffoulkes at Warrington County Court, on Thursday morning, a case dealing with the issuing of default summonea was heard. James Turton, grocer, Haydock, sued Peter Hughes of Raydock for Is. Ild, for goods supplier!. Mr. A. Browne, solicitor, appeared for the defendant, and objected to the form of the summons, the plaintiff having issued a de- fault summons, and his affidavit having stated that the defendant was a grocer whereas he was a miner, and his wife carried on a small business as a chip-potatoe dealer. The goods sued for, Mr. Browne contended, were not sold in the way of trade, and therefore the amount being under £s,a default summons ought not to have been issued. His Honour said from the rules it was quite clear that that was 80, provided the facts as stated were correct. The plaintiff must provs that his affidavit was correct.—On being called the plaintiff was cross-examined by Mr. Browne, and he admitted that the defendant was a miner work- ing three days a week, and also that it was in a eata.ye with a small window where he alleged the (I,4endrait c3rried on business. There was no name ovvr the door, and the defendant's wife always at- tended to the business.—His Honour said it was extremely doubtful whether the affidavit. was cor- net or not, and as it. lay with the plaintiff to make out his case, he was bound to rule that Mr. Browne's contentien was correct, and adjourn the summons until the 7 h May for tile purpose of an ordinary stituranni,ling taken out.—Mr. Browne made an offer to the plaintiff to cerr4ent to a verdict of ..C2 18s. 4d., the amount admitted by the defendant, provided he would take the money by instalments. The plaintiff refused, and an ordinary summons will now have to be taken out.

div.p: WESTON POINT. '

SUDDEN DEATH IN A BoAT.—On Saturday morning John Fradley, an infant son of John Fradley, a boatman of Stoke-on-Trent, was found dead. 'The child when taken to bed the night previous by the parents who slept in the cabin of their boat, was apparently in a normal condition of health, but the next morning the m ther on awakening found the child very ill and it expired within a few minutes.

VESTRY MERTING.—On Tuesday eveniner the parishion- ers held their meeting in the schoolroom. The Vicar (the 8.,v. D. S. Bowen) filled the chair. The accounts were presented by Mr. John Jeffs and showed an adverse balance of 134. 74. Votes of thanks were passed to the eflicials and to the choir for their services during the past year. The Chairman nominated as his warden Mr. Rosenberg. On the proposition of Mr.Cookson,seconded by Mr. T. Grounds, Mr. Jphn Jeffs was elected people's warden, Messrs. S. Bercitford and J. Hayes were chosen sidesmen, and Messrs. Cookson and T. Grounds were appointed lay representatives. INQUEST ON & CHILD.—On Wednesday morning. Mr. J. E. Worsliev, held an inquiry at the Weaver Hotel on the body of john Fradley, aged six weeks, son of John and Eliza Fradley, ttroadheath, Stoke -on-Trent. The parents were living on the narrow boat. Havelock, lying in the deck at Weston Point. On Friday night they went to bed about eleven o'clock with the child which from its birth had been a healthy baby. On awakening about five o'clock next morning, Mrs. Fradley found the child apparently dead.—Dr. McDougall. div.head: FRODSHAM.
div.p: FRODSHAM.

THE EIOLIDAYS AT FRODSHAM.—This popular resort Was also visited by hundreds of visitors from Liverpool and Winchester and Warrington, though the place was by no means aO thronged as in previous years. Tha strong point about Frodsham is the Overton fills, and the pleasure grounds there, were well patronized,— dancing to an excellent band being the great attrac- tion. NARROW ESCAPR FROM DROWNINCI.—Late on Friday evening Mrs. Ankers and Miss Edwards, of Runcorn, narrowly escaped being drowned in the river Weaver. It seems they were walking to Frodsbam from Runcorn and had reached the bridge at Rock Savage when in the darkness they missed their way and fell into the water. Luckily the splash was heard by the gatekeeper, who with the assistance of several willing hands succeeded in rescuing the women from their dangerous position. They were taken to the house of Mrs. Thomas, where they received every attention and were able to proceed home apparently none the worse for their unwontal im- mersion.

PARISH CHURCH SCHOOLS.

An entertainment was held in the Parish church school on Thursday night. There was a good attendance. The programme was in the capable hands of Mr. Walter Cheshire and Mr. Aubrey Cneshire, "the juvenile Gros- smith." The proceeds were in aid of the Prize Fund.
RUNCORN POOR RATH.

Messrs. James Handley and P. Speakman have affixed their signatures to a new poor rate of is. 21. in the £, which should realise £2,739 Os. 41 This was the same as the corresponding period last year. The poor rate for the first half-year was 14. 21. in the £. WESLEYAN DAY SCHOOLS, RUNCORN.

As will be seen from our advertising columns a re- union of the old scholars of the Wesleyan Day Schools will be held on Monday next in the Brunswick School, Runcorn. The opportunity will be taken as a fitting one to make a presentation to Mr. John Simpson in recogni- tion of his services in connection with the schools. Mr. S. Taylor, J.P.. C.C.. will preride. HEATH TENNIS CLUB, RUNCORN. _

The last dance of the season in connection with the Heath Tennis Club, Runcorn, was h4id on Wednesday night in the Brunner Guild Hall. There was a good at- tendance,and dancing:was kept up to music rendered by Mr. W. Gro inds. Dr.Annett officiated as M.C. During an interval in a long amd enjoyable programme Mr. A. Grounds contributed two songs.
MILITARY CONCEIRT-S AT RUNCORN.

On Wednesday two military concerts were given by the Band of Her Majesty's Life Guards in the Public Hall, Runcorn. The concerts which were not over well attended were of exceptional merit. In addition to capital selections by the band, Madame Eugenie Morgan gave several vocal selections, and Mr. Dudley Causton, the popular society humourist, gave two of his ini nit- able sketches. div.head: BOATMAN MISSING AT-RUNCORN.
div.p: A BOATMAN MISSING AT-RUNCORN.

Considerable anxiety is being felt by the friends of John Hough who has been missing since April Ist. He a:as last seen after 11 p.m. on that date goine towards Old Quay Swing Bridge in the direction of his flat which was Icing at the River Wall near Runcorn Bridge. It is thought by his friends that he has fallen either in the Ship Canal or the River Mersey. and the likely places have been dragged during the week hut with no result. The mater is in the hands of the police who have offered a reward and published a description of the missing n- in.

the holidays at Runcorn have been accompanied with fairly favourable weather though nn to Mondir leaden clouds were conspicious by their gloomy presence, and the sun's rays by their absence. The thoeatening weather was displaced on Monday and made way for bright and inviting sunshine and many inhabitants of Runcorn en- couraged, by the pleasant change left the town for local Pleasure resorts. THURSDAY.—Before Messrs. E.lmison and S.Taylor. TILL ROBBERIES—THE RESULT` OF FAST COMPANY AND GAIABLING.—John Austin (aged 16),0f Bold-at., Runcorn, was charged with stealing £3 133.. the monies of his em- ployer, Walter Collier, from a shop in Egerton- at., betweed the Ist February and 4th April.—Walter Collier, provision dealer,Church-at., said that defendant had been in his service 2i years, and resided in Bold- st.with his parents. They had check tills at the branch establishments and one at Egerton-st. which had not balanced for some time. He acccrdingly instructed the manager to ascertain how it was, and owing to the sus- picious movements of the prisoner on Saturday he (wit nen) charged him with stealing, and prisoner admitted taking several sums amounting' to £3 13s. Prisoner,who had btien betting, acknowledged taking more than speci- fied in the charge, out of the LEL He wished the Bench to pass an exemplary sentence on prisoner, be- cause he had bad two •r three cases during the last six months and they had been treated leniently without any effect. —Sergeant Lee said that about 1 a.m. on Senday last Mr. Collier brought the prisoner down to the police station and said he had suspicions about him. He searched the lad and found in a leather pocket on his braces £2 103. in gold. Prisoner did ndt deny the offence and on being charged acknowledged tha, for between one and two years he had been taking 15s. per week. Prisoner had been keep- ine test company. On the 2nd April he took 34., on the 28,-„h March 10s., 21st March 54..' 25th March 34., 24th March 24. Prisoner admitted that he had been betting and said that he had 51. on Runcorn at Warrington and won 10s.—Prisoner's mother said she did not know any- thing ti, . money. Her son had been well looked after and never inore thau 31. had been found in his pocket since he had been working with Mr. Collier. She was not aware that her son had been betting.—Prisoner pleaded goi;tv a.nd had nothing to say.—The chairman characterized the boy as an extraordinary one, who was not s-irry for what he had d-me. He would be sent to gaol for 21 days with hard labour and the bench hoped that it would be a warning to him.—An order was made for the money found on the prisoner to be returned to Mr. Cellier who promked to pay the mother the lad's wages for :he last week.

div.head: RUNCORN URBAN DISTRICT COUNCIL
div.p: RUNCORN URBAN DISTRICT COUNCIL

The last meeting of the Runcorn District Council waq held in the Town Hall oa Thursday morning when there were present—Mr. E. Imison (chairman), the Rev. Dr. Gastaldi, Messrs. P. Speakman, J.P., C.C., F. Wiswall,H. J. Once, J. Jones, T. Dean, Id. Sweetman, D. Bisbrown, .1. W. Lightburn, G. Hewitt, J. Pritchard, R. H. Pos- nett, and Collier, F. zi. Lake (law clerk), E. Marshall (secretary), and J. Wilding (surveyor).
MEDICAL OFFICER'S REPORT.

Dr. McDougall in his report stated that the number of deaths registered auring the past month totalled 23, one of which was an inquest case. Of the remaining 22 two were due to kidney disease,three to phthisis.two to pneu- monia, two senile decay, and one each to debility, rheu- matic fever, pleurisy, premature birth, bronchitis, dentition, heart disease, and septic perilomtes. The 23 deaths showed an average death rate for the 12 months of 14.19 and exclusive of inquest cases 14 21. There were registered during the month 22 births. Thirty- four deaths were registered in the corresponding month of last year.
High-way and Building Committee's minutes were passed on the motion of Mr. Bisbrown, seconded by Mi. Speakman.
THE HEALTH COMMITTER'S MINUTES.

Mr. Wiswall moved the adoption, and in reference to the Port Sanitary order said that he did not agree with the proposal,and considered that it was hard on Runcorn that such places as Widnes and Warrington should be left out as they were. He thought they should send on their petition and he believed they would be able to make out a good case.—Mr. Dean seconded the adoption of the minutes which were carried. The follow- ing is the petition which the committee in its minutes has decided to send forward : The memorial argued that in equity all. the riparian auth- orities ought to be joined in the authority and contribute. It was pointed out that in the draft order of 1893 for the constitution of the Port Sanitary Authority for the customs port of Runcorn the boroughs of Warrington and Widnes were joined to the Urban and Rural Authorities of Runcorn, snowing that at the time the Local Govern- ment Board were of opinion that those two towns ought to contribute to the expense of protecting the district from cholera and other infectious diseases. In the draft order it was proposed that the borough of Widnes should contribute almost equal proportions with Runcorn, whereas under the Manchester Port Order, 1898, the Runcorn Urban District Council is to contribute 1-20th of the whole cost and Widnes absolutely nothing. Though the shipping at Widnes is almost entirely coast- wise the cargoes mainly consist of goods transhipped from foreign vessels at Liverpool and elsewhere and brought to Widnes in smaller vessels for manufacture. ['here is a large traffic between the docks at Weston Point and Runcorn and the Widnes dock in the carriage of salt, Ikc., to Widnes for manufacture. Hence tne docks at Widnes are brought into constant contact with vethels from foreign ports and the sailors therefrom. The number of vessels using Widnes docks was in 1890- 91 about throe fifths of the number coining to Runcorn. As to Warriugton, the borough boundaries were now being extended so that the Ship Canal will become the boundary on one side while the population will be over 50,000. Extensive docks and wharves are about to be constructed in connection with canal and estuary at Partiugton. In the district of 'dam and Altrincham are large coal tips, coaling basin,with 20 acres of quay area. and Si acres of quay area and half a mile of quay length* The trade here has considerably increased and is likely, to do so. The excuse for excluding these districts ap- pears to be the allegatioa that the trade is entirely ex- port, but this is net correct, for where you have a large coal export you almost always have a large timber im- port for colliery proprietors. This trade has already I developed considerably on the canal. Even if the trade of Partingtou was entirely export the vessels are mostly foreigners recently discharged at Manchester or else- where. At Ellesmere Port there are extensive docks, lay-bys, graving docks, and repairing slips for vessels. It is the transhipment port of the Shropshire Union Canal and the London and North-Western Railway Co. This place having specially favourable rates for tolls and dues and considerable exemption under the Manchester Ship Canal Act, 1885, is rapidly increasiag in import- ance as a most seriousirival to Runcorn docks.Whi:e the before named places are increasing the tendency at Run- corn is to decrease. See Lewis' report where he states that with the completion of the Ship Oanal the shipping has to some extent further shifted and probably that of Runcorn may become less than previously. This ten- dency is deliberately encouraged by the conduct of the Manchester Ship Canal in allowing vessels to go to Man. cheater, Salford, and Stretford, free of dues, while ves- sels coming half that distance to Runcorn are charged full dues, also by the greater facilities for lowering and dealing with Manchester bound vessels as compared with those for Runcorn. The Urbaa District of Run- corn is small in area,population,and rateable value, and owing to the almost closing of the three Alkali manu- factoriea in the district,the population is now some 2,000 less than at the time of the last census, and the ratepar- ing capacity considerably reduced. The docks are ust;cl namely for the transhipping' of materials to and from the potteries. Little, if any, is brought to the district for manufacture or consumption within. Hence the benefit derived from shipping is small compared with the number of vessels, and consists mainly in the lablur required to supplement that of the crews in discharging carr.o. The Manchester Port Order,lB9B, is most unjust to the memoralists in that it throws unlit a small and decreasing district a burden far in excess of that placed on districts which are rapidly increasing and are obtain- ing the principsl benefits to be derived from tie order. The present injustice is shown by the compari- son of the amount in the £ on the rate the proposed scheme would inflict. If the same annual expenditure was taken at probably too low an estimate of :21,600, and the same is divided as men- tioned on the proposed oreler,the Runcorn Urban District Council would have to levy a rate of nearly ?2-1. in tho L, while the city of Manchester would only require at the rate of 1i of a id. in the £ for its share, and the borough ct Salford about 1-5 of id. in the L. But unjust 4s this is now it will yearly become more so as the traffic is attracted to the Manchester end, and the benefits of Runcorn diminished. The memorialists, therefore, submitted that the order should be amended on the ground that it was inequitable, as rn-iny districts whieli ought to contribute are omittod, and that the amount of contributions asked from Runcorn Urban Dis- trict Council is far in excess of their just proportion as compared with the other riparian autoorities. The Water Committee's ainmuteA were passed on the motion of Mr. Pritchard, Feconded by Mr..l,nes,and the Markets Committ?,e's minutes were adopted on the mo- tion oi Mr. Grice, seconded by Dr. Gastaldi.
FINANCE COMMITTEE.-INCREASED RATES.

Supplementary rates were presented by the Finance Committee, which also recommended that a general dis- trict rate at the rate of 24. 1111. in the £ for the year ending 31st March, 1897 be made ; and that is. 5?1,1. he collected in the first six months and is. 50 in the second six months. ' Mr. Lighthurn moved the adoption of the Finance Core- mittee's minutes both in connection with the ordinary recommendation and the supplementary ones. It was a very unpleasant duty for him to move the supplemen- tary one which recommended a rate of 2s. 11d, in the £. He mieht say that the committee had gone through item aftei item of the expenditure with a view to curtailing the amount. Some people might .remark " Well we could do with less, instead of having a 2a. 111, rate Jet us have a 2s. 6d. rate and make it do," hut he could assure them that it could not be reduced to less than 24. 11d. He might say the reason for the increase might be truly said to rise from the great number of unoccu- pied houees. He could say that lithe ratepayers had been with the committee when they considered the esti- mates they would have seen that the committee did all they could to keep the rates down.—Mr. Pritchard in seconding regretted that they found it necessary to recommend an increased rate of 21. in the E.—Dr. Gastaldi thought that it was an inopportune time to in- crease the rates In Runcorn at the present time. He thought that a 2s. 9d. rate was sufficient. If ' they raised it to 2s. Ild, they would nrevent a great many people from coming in Runcorn. He moved that the rate for the year should only be 2s. 9d. in the L.—Mr. Sweetman, in seconding, said he saw in the estimates an item for the reconstruction of footpaths. They wanted doing very badly, but there were things which might have been Igt out of the esti- mates which were put in. There were the salaries of officers which he thought might have been reduced.— Mr. Collier said he could not understand any gentleman proposing an amendment after what they heard at the committee meeting at which most of the Council, in- eluding Dr. Gastaldi, were preent. It seemed to him ' a sort of mania tn oppose improvements when money was concerned. It was a shame that two members should get ma there, and talk, so to speak, "to the gal- ' lery," and put thena is a ridiculous light, when every member knew they had done their duty as they ought to do it.—Mr. Bishrown stated that if they had c-arried out the esemates there would have been a rate of 34. 911. in the E—Mr. Speaktnan said that as a general thing it was not the usual course to oppose the recommendations of a committee when they found that committee consisted of the whole Council. He thought that the Council was doing its best, and he had pleasure in supporting the proposal.made by .he Chairman of the Finance Commit- tee.—Mr. Grice thought that the amendment would have been well left cut that morning. They were all aware of the depressed condition of things in the town, and ,ct hen they considered that there were 700 houses empty in the ton they might be thankful that there was not a larger increase on the rate. When houses were empty the empty property did not pay the rate, and Ph - rate had to come- from the property occupied. After a short discussion, Dr. Gistaldi's amendment was nut and re- ceived the votes of its proposer and s-c ,nder. The ori- ginal resolution was afterwards put and easily carried.
A SUGGESTION FROM MR. JONES.-TRE STATE OF THE TOWN.

Mr. Jones said he had been asked to bring a matter before the Council which he knew very well would not come within its duties. It was pointed out to him some time ago that it might have some good effect if a public meeting on the condition of trade in Runcorn were held, with special invitations to gentlemen of means and busi- ness men who have some interest in the town. There were scores of workingmen out of employment and they were told that 700 houses in the town were empty and things were no doubt in a very deplorable condition. Worst of all there was no ray of light in the darkness around them. He thought it was time they endeavoured to do something.—Mr. Speakman thought that perhaps more good might be done by holding a private meeting. He did not think they could discuss the matter with pro- fit to themselves and the public at a public meeting.— Mr. Lightburn quite agreed with the particulars of Mr. Jones' suggestion. If they had a private meeting they might formulate something which they could present to a public meeting.—Mr. Pritchard in supporting Mr. Jones' idea deplored the absence of a Chamber of Corn merce in the town,which would, he thought, help trade interests in Runcorn.—tifter further remarks the Chair- man said that it would not be in order for them to pass a resolution. He understood Mr. Jones wished to have an expression of opinion. Personally he would like to associate himself with everything that had been said.— Mr. Jones said he had to tender his thanks to them for the mancer in which his suggestion had been received, and he hoped they would be able to move in the matter and hold the meeting.—The matter then dropped and the business of the Council was brought to a Germina- tion.
Monday, proved a sorry outing to the Yerkshire men who went home beaten by three tries to nil. It will, therefore, be seen that in the holiday matches Runcorn managed to secure a triple event-

Returning once more to where I started from (the meeting of the Rundorn Rural District Council) it will not be out of place to make some reference to the proposed Port Sanitary Authority. It is now most plainly seen that this proposed Authority will pinch Runcorn more than any other district, while at the same time our town will get the least benefit from it. There are many places equally interested, which should be made to pay an equal share of the expenses of the Authority. It, iR to be hoped that the memorial sent up by the Council will have some, effect particularly with the redistribution of the area over which the Authority is to have power.

div.head: OVERSEERS APPOINTMENTS.
div.p: OVERSEERS APPOINTMENTS.

The Chairman informed the Gnincil that he had re- ceived a communication from the Local Government Bcard conferring upon the Council power to appoint and revoke the appointment of the assistant overseers. It did not affect the holder of the office hut when the time came to appoint his successor they would have power to revoke the appointment cf it turned out unsatisfactory.

div.p: THE EXIMINER,
SATURDAY, APRIL 110, 1896.

IT cannot be said that the pros- The Education pects of the new Education Bill have improved since it was laid before the House of Commons last week. The Bill is not, so far as. can be seen, accepted by any sect or party as a thoroughly satisfactory measure, though it is, of course, condemned for different reasons by different critics. The more extreme champions of the voluntary system are dis- appointed by what they consider the inadequacy of the new grants in aid of their schools,and some of them are disposed to look with suspicion upon what may be described as the rudiments of public control that are to be found in the proposed new educational authorities. On the other hand,there can be no question that one of the main objects of the Bill is to strike a blow at the direct public con- trol of education which is at the present time exercised through School Boards, and this feature of the Bill is condemned by Liberals all through the country. Mr. T. E. ELLIS, the chief Liberal whip, in a vigorous speech to a Welsh audience, denounced Sir JOHN GUEST'S proposals as "unsound from stem to stern." He pointed out the splendid work which has been done by School Boards in raisiug the level of education, and then deplored the fact that it was now proposed to put a summary end to that process. "The two great instruments of pro- gress in popular education are," says Mr. Elam, " the strong impulse of a directly ;an d specially elected local authority on the one hand, and the strong hand of a highly organised, well- staffed, and wisely directed State department. This Bill maims and distorts and blunts these two instruments." Mr. ELLis declares that the Liberals in Parliament will fight the Bill, line by line, "to modify if not eliminate its retrograde and vicious provisions, and will protest with every emphasis in their power against the clerical at- tempt to mutilate the best features- of a national system of education on which the country relied for its commercial progress and its social strength and safety." There are reasons for believiryi that Liberals will not be left entirely without aid in their opposition to at least some portions ef the Bill. The " Birmingham Daily Post "which is the most representative of the Liberal Unionist organs in the Press offers the strongest objecti on to the provision which gives the new Educational Committees the power of stopping the development of the School Board system. As it points out this is a power which will be used in some dis- tricts to starve and dwarf the Board schools in order to protect the voluntary schools. Tile " Post " may not in this instance be the direct mouthpiece of Mr CIIAMBERLAIN as it has been on .other occasions, but it is hard to believe that at least some members of the Liberal Union- ist party will not show that they have not sacri- fice-1 all their principles to the most reactionary Toryism. Apart from political utterances, the most remarkable condemnation of the Bill has been pronounced by the National Union of Teachers. This Union has during the present week held its animal convention at Brighton, and, as was inevit- able under the circumstances, it has given the new Bill a great deal of consideration. The executive of the Union proposed to approve of the setting up of the new education authorities by County and County Borough Councils, but the rank and and file of the teachers utterly refused to endorse this recommendation. An amendment was pro- posed affirming that educational authorities should be directly elected by the parochial electors. In the debate which followed the supporters of the amendment were in overwhelming strength, and in the end they carried their point by 14,479 votes to 9,255. This is undoubtedly the most striking pronouncement that has vet beon made:on the edu- cation policy of the Government, and coming from the quarter it does, it must have an immense weight in the country.
THE annual report cf the Royal Brave Deeds. Humane Society is an inspiring

record of brave and self-sacrificing deeds. During last year the society recognised in one way or another the gallant actions of eight hundred different persons. Its awards were dis- tributed in almost every part of the Empire. Thirteen medals or parchments were, for instance, sent to India and forty-one to the colonies. Twenty of the Society's awards were made to officers and men of the Naval Service, six to coastguards kind naval reserve men, forty-eight to officers and men of the land forces, and thirty-two to members of the police forces. Many ladies distinguished themselves by the performance of heroic deeds. A Miss M. L. .EvaNs who is one of the recipients of the fourteen silver medals was awarded this honour for a triple rescue 'at Southampton. She was standing on klythe Pier when a boat containing two woman and a man capsized close at hand. Miss ENTAbis at once sprang into the water with all her clothes on and actually succeeded in bring- ing the drowning people within reach of the land- ing steps. Almost every trade or profession seems to be represented amongst the recipients of

div.head: RUNCORN SCHOOL BOARD.
div.p: RUNCORN SCHOOL BOARD.

The monthly meeting of this Board was held on Thursday evening in the Town Hall, Runcorn. There were present Mr. J. Pritchard (chairman), the Rev. Dr. Gastaldi, Mr. S. Taylor, J.P., C.C., Mr. E. Imison, J.P., Mr. T. Norman, J.P., and Mr. J. MOFS (clerk).
MANAOEMENT COMMITTEE MINUTES.

The School Management Committee recommended the payment of account amounting to £283 70., including the salaries of teachers. The consideration of the draft scheme of salaries was resumed, and several alterations having been made the further consideration was di- ferred. At a subsequent meeting it was recommended that the salary of Mr. J. C. Cragg, assistant master at Victoria Road Boys' School, be advanced to £B5 per annum ; that the salary of Miss E. Crowther, assistant mistress at Granville-st. Girls' School, be increased to £42 103. per annum; and the salary of Miss Jessie Ash. brook, assistant mistress at Granville-at. Girls' School,be advanced to £42 10 per annum, each increase to com- mence from May Ist. The consideration of other appli- cations for advances of salary were deferred.—The minutes were confirmed.

div.head: SCHOOL ATTENDANCE COMMITTEE.
div.p: SCHOOL ATTENDANCE COMMITTEE.

The minutes of this committee showed that 65 parents had been summoned before the committee out of which 58 appeared and it was decided to take proceedings against 10 parents. The visitors' repart for the month showed that for the month ending March 28rh, the number of scholars' onf the rolls was 3,411 against 3,443 with the corresponding period last year. Five years ago the number of scholars was about the same as at present, from which it might be inferred that the ordinary annual in-rease which by this time would have amounted to 350 or 400 scholars had been con- trasted by the corresponding decrease, caused by the re- moval of families from Runcorn. There was an improved attendance at the schools durine the month, the percen- tage being 83.6 and against 82.6 in March 1895. The average attendance was 2,851 against 2,845 for the same period last year.—Rev. Dr.Gastaldi la moving the adop- tion of the minutes said that something would have to be done with the refractory children who were continually playing truant. It. demanded real consideration from the Board.—Mr. Taylor seconded the resolution which was carried.

div.head: TUE PRECEPT REDUCED BY HALF.
div.p: TUE PRECEPT REDUCED BY HALF.

The Chairman proposed that a precept be issued on the Council for a sum of £350. He was glad to say that the amount was small in comparison with £7OO in the corresponding period last year and £7OO in September. The Board had then to provide finances for the main- tenance: of the Wesleyan schools, but the end of the school year was now approaching and the Government grants were now coming in to meet the expenditure on those and the other schools. He might say that the Wes- leyan schools had been handed over to the Board in a good financial condition. The Government grant paid to the Board amounted to £520136.6d.,and the undischarged liabilities were £252 6s. id., leaving a balance of MO 17s. 51. in their hands from the late school managers, and that sum had gone in the reduction of the demand upon the ratepayers for the coming year.—Mr. Norman In seconding, was glad that the Chairman had mentioned the facts about the Wesleyan Schools, for at the time they wete taken over the public were of cpinion that they had taken over a rotten concern. He could speak freely for he was not a manager, and he might say that the managers of the school for many years had pursued a most economical system, and when the time e4me to hand the schools over, their desire was to hand them to the Board in a good financial condition.— Dr. Gastaldi thought that the ratepayers would be satis- fied with the state of affairs.—The resolution was then es rri..d

div.head: ANTIQUATED STANDING • DOERS.
div.p: ANTIQUATED STANDING • DOERS.

Mr. Norman drew attention to the standing orders be- ing antiquated. He thought improvements could be made which would lead to the business being more efficiently conducted. He proposed that the Chairman Mr.lmison and Mr. Taylur be a committee to revise the standing orders.—Rev. Dr. Gastaldi seconded, and it was carried. This concluded the business.

div.head: W ESTON.
div.p: W ESTON.

FasEnat. or MRS. CLARK.—On Monday afternoon the remains of Mrs. Ann Clark. aged 71 years, wife of Captain Clark, of Westdale, were interred in the Run- corn Cerneters. 'The deceased who died on Good Friday, was well known in Weston. The Rev. W. N. Stap es was the officiating clergyman. There were a large num- ber of ity,urrierg arid f riends present, includin.,. Captain Clark, Mars. F. %V. Clark, R. R. Clark, L. Rosenberg, Marshall W. Harris. E. Rosenberg, L. Rosenberg, jon., Richa-t1 guSS, R. Morris, and F. W. .Fitton. Amongst the contributors of the many beautiful wreaths which covered the coffin were: Captain Clark, Mr. and Mrs. B. R. Clark, Mrs. Whitfield. Mr. and Mrs. Rosen- berg, Mr. and Mrs. fiarris,Vlr. H. Pretty (Landon),Mrs. Grounds, Mr. and Mrs. H. Grounds, Catherine, the ten- ants, and Mr. R. Morris. The undertaker was Mr. R. Morris, fligh-st., who carried out the duties.

ACCIMINT.—Tilornas Price, of Weston, in the employ of 111e3sta. Yarwood Bros., net with an accident on Wednesday about seven o'clock at night. He was in charge of a pony and luggage cart and was passing the yard close to the station when the animal shied And he was thrown out under the wheel,which passed over the lower part of his body. Fortunately he did not appear to he much injured.

Nzw Poott RAT.—Messrs. S. B. Chadwick and E. Imison have affixed thdr signatures to the new poor rate for the ownship of Weston at in the £ which should realize £626 34. Hid. The rate is the same as tne last half year's, but 21. less than in the correspond- ing period twelve months ago.

div.head: THINGS HEARD AND SEEN AT RUNCORN. AY OUR RUNCORN CORRESPONDENT.
div.p: THINGS HEARD AND SEEN AT RUNCORN. AY OUR RUNCORN CORRESPONDENT.

It is generally thought at Runcorn that the town is—speaking from a trade point of view—about as low as it can get, and now the tradespeople gener- ally are waiting " Micawber like r for something to turn up. The last meeting of the District Council was by no means encouraging. The Chairman had a lengthy report to make, and a doleful tale to tell, and wound up a dolorous effort by moving an in- crease of 2,1. in the district rate. Evidently from what was said at the meeting the Finance Commit- tee have done all in their power to keep down rates but with the depression in trade, the Council have to contend with the depreciation in the ratepaying capacity of property which in itself has forced up- on the Committee the necessity of putting up the rates. Much as the ratepayers will grumble, the rate itself will have to he paid.

It remains to be seen whether Mr. Jones' sugges- tion will bear forth fruit. Certainly trade will liven up more quickly if the townspeople help it to do so, and a public meeting or a good private meeting of influential men may lead to some direct improvement. Looking at the natural advantage Runcorn possesses from a commercial point of view one cannot help wondering at the folly of its being dependent almost entirely upon the ctemical trade. There are several trades which would flourish all the better for the many conveniences which they would find at Runcorn, if wealthy manufacturers could only be induced to consider the natural advantages that the town possesses.

The holidays at Runcorn passed away almost un- eventfully. Of course what business there is at Runcorn was at a standstill and thousands took ad- vantage of the many excursions to local pleasuse resorts. Frodsham was undoubtedly the most popular rendezvous.

The Runcorn Football Club during the holidays have had quite a series of victories. Commencing on Good Friday at Warrington where they detested the home team they followed it by administering a smart drubbing to the representatives of the chemi- cal town across the water on the Saturday. HE WANTED TO LIE DOWN AND DIE

"Can you show me somewhere where I can lie down and die ?" was the astounding query which a stranger in Warrington on Thursday last week a.ddrevcd to P C. Hodkkiss. The stranger was very peculiar in his man- ner,and in answer to the officer's questions, he stated that he had been drinking out of a bottle which he pro- duced, labelled" laudanum—poison," and containing a little quantity of that deadly fluid. The officer had a conversation with one of his superiors and they agreed that the best place for the man to lie down would be the police station. Accordingly he *as marched there, and examined by Inspector Taylor (a S. John Ambulance man). He found him suffering fro-n opium poisoning. and promptly administered a strong emetic which cauaed him to empty the contents of his stomach. This was followed by a drink of coffee.and the effects of the draft of laudanum passed off. On being charged with attempt- ing to commit suicide, he replied, "Yes I have done it, Jam tired ot life." The doctor afterwards saw the pri- soner and stated that the Inspector had saved the man's life by his action. The man gave his name as Frederick Prior, of 45, Rye-st.' New Basford, Not4ingham. He lived at Warrington during the construction of the Ship Canal. but left about twelve months ago. The Chief Constable in stating the facts of the case to the magis- trates on Saturday,said it transpired that there had been a quarrel between the man and his wife, and he being of a sensitive temperament had come away, .and being low in spirits had committed that rash act. rut,. Chair- man (Mr. Cha.ndley) reprimanded the prisoner for his foolish act, and he was then discharged. INDECENCY IN THE PARK—EXEMPLARY PENALTY.

On Wednesday morning At the Warrington Borough Court, before Mr. John Fairclough (chairman) Mr. 1 Geddes, and Alderman Wright. Isaiah Dig.tt. a middle aged and respectable looking man residing in G street, was charged with having unlawfully and wilfully disclosed his person in Bank Park, with intent to insult certain females, on the ttrh April ; he *as also charged with using obscene language at the same time and place. —Defendant pleaded guilty to both charges.—The Chief Constable detailed the circumstances of the case, which were of a dieeusting character, and gave the names of the three children, the. eldest of whom was only 11.— Mr. Ashton park-keeper saw sufficient of the occurrence to corroborate. Ile also added that the defendant had been frequenting the park recently and he had suspected him.—The Chief Constable said that Detective Barlow and Roper took the children through the streets in the hope of their identifying the man and they were success- ful and the children picked him out firm a'group of men. This was his first offence of the kind and he had hitherto borne a good charae,ter.— The Chairman of the bench said this kind of conduct must be put a stop to, and no punishment they could give was adequate for such an offence. They would enforee the full penalty however, and send defendant tolgaol for three months' bard labour. —This met both charges.

div.p: MINOR CASES.;
WARRINGTON BOROUGH POLICE COURT.
SATURDAY.—Before Mr. Chandley (chairman). and Mr. T Birchall

THE CHIEF CONSTABLF: AND OBSCENE LANOTTAGE.—MichneI Grant, a respectable looking man. of Warringt n. was Sum- moned for using obscene and prorane languarre in Church-st on Thersday afternoon.—Chief Constable Talho stated that, shortly after three o'clock on Thursday afternoon he wss Naming drawn Church-st. The street was crowded at the time, and he heard the prisoner in altercation with another man. Both were under the influence of drink. The prisoner used some most abominable lenguage, and he (the Chief Con- stable) on meeting a police office- rent him to get the pri- soner's name and edireas. The prisoner would not go away, so in consideration of the scandalous language he had need. he was locked up. He had been in custody ever sine., and perhaps the magistrates would think he had been sufficiently punished.—Mr Birdsall remarkf d that the use of bad Taegu- age in the tewn was very prevalent.—The Chief Constable said it was, and h would do his 'test while in Warrington to stop it.—The prisoner was disehargsd with a caution. DRUNK AND DISORDERLY.—BUIO% Tat lock was fine t ss. and costs for being drunk and disorderly in B wsey st., and Wil- liam Thompson for a like offence in Sank ey-st. was mulcted In a similar penalty. MONDAY.—Before Mr. F. Monks (chairman). Alderman Sut- ton, Mr. T Birchall and Hr. S. Wright. AN UNSUSTAINF.D CHARGE —John McDonough, living at Town Hill, was charged under a warrant at the instance of .his mother with assaulting ind beating her.—The complain- ant made quite a pitiable tale to the megisfrates when the warrant was issat d, but she now made out that it was quite trivial affair. She said defendant had had a drop of drink, and " shove 4 her with his foot. "—The Chief Constable said the woman was committing deliberate perjury. she came before the magistrates on Saturday, and told them that the prisoner had kicked her in a savage manner. The man had a splendid character from the army, having served in the Grenadier Guards, and the police gave him a very good char- acter. The woman was evidently in a passion when she came on Naturday —The Case was dismissed. WILFUL DAMAGE —Martin Dooley. Bakehonse-yard, was charged with not having appeared to a summons for com- mitting wilful damage to the property of Richard Smith in January. 1.895 —Mrs Smith deposed that the damage was made good by the prisoner's wife She would withdraw the case on payment of the costs.—The magistrates ordered the prisoner to pay the cots. ASSAULTING A POLICE OFFICER —Joseph Phillips. 57, Leonard-street, was charged with being drunk and firs- orderly in Winwick-stre t the previous night, and also with assaulting P.C. F. Cooper whilst in the execution of his day. P C. Cooperstated that prisoner was making a disturbance near the Central Station, and witness advised him to go home. He thereupon struck witness a violent blow on the face. They closed together and both fell to the ground. Ira answer to the Chief Constable, witness stated that the chin strap of his helmet was broken.—P.C. Clarke gave corrobo- rative evidence. A fine of 10s. and costs, or in default, four- teen days' imprisonment,was imposed. A BRUTAL Hams atm.—Alfred. France. 21 Oliver .st., was charged at the instance of his wife with assaulting her on the 3rd inst. The complainant stated that on the date men- Coned the prisoner 'lame home the worse fur drinir. He threw his clogs on the table and smashed the crockery, and after- wards struck her on the face. He also assaulted her the week previous. He had given her ss. 61. in wages during the past three weeks. Prisoner was committed to prison for one month bard labour. The complainant as'red for a separa- tion order, bat was told th:.t the magistrates had not power to give her one on the present charge TUESDAY.—Before Mr R. Garnett (chairman). Mr. B. J. -Guest, and Dr. Starkey Smith. AEBEIns OF MAINTENANCE.—James Harrison, New-road, Latchford, was summoned for arrears on his wife's mainten- ance, amounting to £5 us. 61. The money had been due since August 13th Teat. Defendant did not appear. —The magistrates ordered that the money should be paid or in de- fault two months' imps isen men t. WEDNESDAY —Before Mr. John Fairclotigh (chairman), Mr J. Geddes, and All rman Wight

DRUNK AND DISORDERLY. —John Jones from Oldham, was fined ss. and costs for being drunk and disorderly in Butter- market st. on Monday. THEFT FROM A PUBLIC•ROUSE. —James Jones, a man with 25 convictions against him, was chmlerl with stealing on Monday from the " Legh Arms." Mersey-at., two noggin bottles of whisky, the property of Joseph Henry James.-- The Chief Constable said that at five o'clock' in the evening of Monday, defendant and another man were in the bar of the Legh Arms." The landlord went out and defendant seized two bottles of whisky from the bar. A customer named Frank Brown saw him and shouted to the landlord who caught defendant in the doorway. Information was given to the police, and Detective-Sergeant Mouaghin apprehended defendant.—Mr. James, the man Brown, and Motile' in cor- roborated, and defendant was sent to gaol for one month's bard labour.
