WARRINGTON V. WIGAN.

A strong team with a goodirecord represented Wigan ' on Tuesday evening,when their return engagement with Warrington was played. The Wigan team was, accom- panied by about 1,500 of their supporters. Warrington were without the services of Barton and Broady. The weather was fine, and about six thousand spectators lined the enclosure. Warrington won the toss and the visitors kicked off towards ' the pavilion goal. Btrber made a smart return, and a scrimmage took plape at midfield. " Smack " Bate getting possession passed to Fairhurst who kicked into t0u.311 a-, the visitors' twenty- five. Shcirtly afterwards Winstanley wtsforced to touch down. Barber by a long punt eaus'ed the Wigan custod- ian to again save. Nevins made his mark from the drop- out, but Flowers receiving a catch returned smartly,and the effort • was nullified. ' -Wilding and Jag° were next prominent with till kicking, and a rush to the home line I was effectively stopped by fligginhottom. Scrimmages• ensued in dangerous proximity to the home goal, but Lawless intercepting a pass arnongst the Wigan three- quarters raced away, transferring play to mid-field: ' A mull by Winstanley almost let Cross' in, but Flowers saved his side from disaster, and tho game was carried out of - danger by the . visiting forwards. A very good passing movenaent by the. _Warrington -three- quarters . was next noticable, ,but the visitors not to be -denied transferred play by a desperate rush. They sue-. ceisdeci in passing the Warrington fullback, but O'Brien savt!d finely. ,Taking the game to the Wigan line again Warrington experienced hard luck in. not scoring. Suc- cess, however,satne,at length, for Lawless kicked the' ball under the Wigan goal pests, and Croas succeeded in dropping upon it and scoring amidst much enthusiasm. Barker kicked a fine goal from the place. At this point Bate had to retire through injoriei, to his knee, and the visitors now made strenuous efforts to,.eqnaliue. A fini., •oppnrtunity for scoring occurred when the vi4itors were granted a penalty kick, but Webster , made a very poor attempt. Balf time soon afterwards arrived with War._ rington leading ky five poi ;ts. Bate again appeared on ,restartim.t.and a fine dribble by the Warrington forwards carried the ball past theWizao edstodian, and another score seemed, imminent. Wins!•anley.however,n-tanaged to get possession and saved daringly. -Play afterwards raged about half way until Dakin by a dribble trans- ferred play to Wigan territory. The Visiting forwards worked the bail back again and O'Brien- again , saved, stopping- their' .onward career.. The War-

rington defence waS now severely tested, but the players were fully equal .te the exigencies of the occasion. Higginbottban. especially, tackled well. Get- ting the ball away Warrington rushed down the field, and Lawless receiving a pass from Cross was almost over. Another vii tto the home goal wa3 now paid by Wigan, and Dix-m was pushed into touch when within an ace of scoring. After continued prensing, a passing movement amongst the visiting three-quarters ended in Dixon crt,ssing the line. Webster took the place hick but failed, and thus left Warrington leading by two points. Time was now nearly tirj,, and during the re- maining minutes of the match excitement ran high, and Wigan tried hard to score. The home team kept thorn* out, and the game ended in a victory for Warrington. Score, IN'trrington one goal (five points), Wigan one try (t:hree points). The teams were as follows :—Warring- ton.• Evans. ; Lawless, Cross. Barber, arid O'Brien, three-quarters; Bat-e and Ili.-ginbottem, half- backs ; Nevins. Taylor, Fairhurst, 'Lakin, Burrows, Berry, Saund rs, gind Andrews. Wi,gati, Winstanley,full back; Flowers, Wilding, Jago, Dixon, three-quarters ; Walker and Foster. half-backs; IThsworth, Rigby, Yates, Brown, Benson, Webster, Green, and Perkins, forwards. Mr. Smith, of Widnes. was the itnferee.

ner registered the first try in the match. Failing at goal the Runcornians still had much of their own way from a general melee. Taylor again scored for the home team, while shortly afterwards Myers who was the last of a four-handed passing movement in which Butterworth

Robinson and Faulkner,were conspicuons,easily got over. As neither try was converted the scores were Runcorn, three tries, Batley, nil. WARUINGTON " A " V. RUNCORN VlCS.—This match was played on the Warrington ground on Saturday. The home team had all the play and won by 2 goals 5 tries (25 points), p 1 goal (dropped) 4 points.

div.head: WARRINGTON v. LEEDS.
div.p: WARRINGTON v. LEEDS.

The Warrington club had a hard task before them when on Saturday, following the severe exertion of their match with Runcorn on Good Friday. they journeyed to Leeds to play off their return with that town club. The task was all the heavier when it is considered that Leeds had had no match on Good Friday and accordingly they were in the pink of condition and were also well repre- sented in the following team viz.,. Wilkinson ; Walker, G. Efainstock, Walton and H. Hainstock ; Smith and Ridgley ; Grigg, Parfitt,ltiley, Glover, Armstrong,Smith, Thompson, Saveden. The Warrington players were Heesem ; Broady, Barber,Cross, and Lawless ; Bate and Eliggiabottom ; Hill, Swift Nevins, Sudlow, Berry, An- drews, Wilcox and Fairhurst. Counter attraction kept away many hut there were about 1.500 spectators to witness Hill's kick off. Tt did not bode well for Warrington that they had tO face a stiffiehibreeze, hut the opening stages were manifestly in their favour. The visiting ferwards followed the kick off smartly, too smart for H. Flainstock to get in an ex- change, as he fumbled a bit. Heesom shared a similar experience ior G. Flainstock having relieved with a long kick Midgley got at Heesorn and easily ac- counted for him. Warrington nearly had another lesson given them as to the pains and penalties of in- fringing for. Leeds being given penalties in quick succession Walton and Glover made good attempts at goal. Things were being kept merry enough for Warrington but any danger there was was soon averted by Leeds being penalized. It was exchanged and Barber and Bate cleared a way for themselves with Broady at their heels. All were nicely •under weigh and Broads' being put in possession by Bete spurted talfway where he was forced in touch. It was hard lines but it did not long prevent Warrington's progress for Higginbottom secured from the ensuing scrimmage and fed Cross who got clear arid passed to Nevins who failed to accept it as he might have done. This ptored a lost opportunity,for Walton with a big kick found touch at Warrington 25, and Walker with another almost dropped a geal, the hall travelling a trifle wide. Qace in Warrington territory Leeds did not relax although Fligginbottom and Brcady did manage to force them back to halfway. The.defen- sive abilities of Warrington were teeed sorely for some time and, at length gave way, for Smith from a clever pass from 14Iidgel3y got over and Glover made the try a goal. Up to this point, which represented 25 minutes play, Warrington had been having as much of the play as Leeds hut a cliange took place for Walker Scored shortly afterwards and then when pressure was at its highest the ball was kicked over but with no Leeds player near it, and Barber attempting to kick it dead missed and thus gave S. Smith the gift of an uncon- verted try. The interval was close at hand when Ef Hainstock drepped a neat goal. Half-time, Leeds 17 points, Warrington nil. Ibis last ten minutes of the first half had told severely on Warrington, and they took the field again pretty much done up. Leeds early Zeds, tracks for Heesom's charge, Barber kept them at bay for a time,but another round of passing which the Warrington threeqirarters were slew to interrupt enabled J. Flainstock to score. A. word of pealse is due to Broady for the plucky way he tackled en the occasion, first collaring Walton and then Flainstock, the latter practically carrying him over with him: Nothing daunted Warrington came away from the drop out, the place kick having proved a failure, and Lawless made good use of a pass he received from Bar- ber kicking and then following up he reclaimed posses- sion and passed to Bate. It Feemed an easy thing, but Bate did not hold it at first attempt, and when he did he passed to Cross instead of making a dash with it. His pass was neither Very well delivered nor ' accented, and 'When Cross got agoing. instead ' of the clear field Wilkinson had in the mean- time rushed up and tackled him near the line. Another tackle on line fol:owed and it was undoubtedly a slice of hard luck that prevented their scoring. They ( were given a penalty in a good position for scoring'but Hill proved unequal to it and then the play was as , rapidly transferred. Mideley scored. It seemed as if Warrington were to be beaten pointless but their turn name. Barber and Broady eluding opposition raced from half way and the latter scored behind the posts. Even this easy place was not improved upon. Warring- ton tried to add to their genre and came near doing so. Leeds transferred, thanks chiefly to their better passing and stronger kicking and ta the lack of combination amongst the Warrington team. Riley scored and a minute from time Smith added another so that a rather one-sided score, though not quite en one-slded a game, read at the finish—Leeds. 3 goals 4 tries (28 points) ; Warringten, 1 try (3 points). •

div.head: WARRINGTON V. STOCKPORT.
div.p: WARRINGTON V. STOCKPORT.

Fresh from their notable victory over Manningham, the Stockport team journeyed to Warrington on Mon- day. Saville was the chief absentee from the visiting team, he not having recovered from the injuries he re- ceived on Saturday. Bennett, formerly a player in the Warrington St. Mary's team,hut who was recently trans- ferred to the Stockport " A " figured in the Stockport fifteen on the Wilderspoel enclosure. Warrington placed a very strong team in the field, probably the best that has donned the "Primrose and blue" this season. Bur- ton received an ovation on rejoining the team after several weeks', absence. J. W. Evans deposed Fleesom at full back, and Burton took Cross's -place in the three- quarter line, giving that player a rest. The forwards were a strong lot as will be seen from the team list which was as follows : Warringtnn : Full back, J. W. Evans ; threequarters. Broady, Barber, Burtms, Lawless ; half-backs. Bate and Hgeinhnttom ; forwards. Taylor, Nevin, Dakin, Fair- hurst, Saunders, Hill, Andrews, and Burrows. Stockport: Full back, Wc?reley ; threequarters, Rob- inson, Sands Chorlton, Bailey ; half-bAcke, Norris, Ben- nett ; forwards. Turner, Smith, Mills, Lengthorpe, Har- rison, Gerside, Wrigley, and Johnson. Beautifully fine weather prevailed, and when Gerside kicked off with the sun facing the visitors, there would be about five thousand specta- tors present. The preliminary exchanges were in favour of the Stockport team. but a free kick to the homesters enabled them to gain ground, and b 7 short stave+ War- rington carried play into the visitors' twenty five. A nice passing movement initiated by Bate, and taken no by Burten, Barber and Bra-dy was next witnessed. The latter player was knocked into touch when near the line. Warrington continued to press and Burton essayed a drop at goal, but was unsuccessful. A moment later Bate made his mark. Burton took the kick but failed to send the ball over the crossbar. Again and again, the Warrington players placed the Stockport line in jeopardy but the good tackling of the visitors served them in good stead. Robinson brought his side a little welcome relief by intercepting a pass between Bate and Lawless, The game was, however, soon again toeing hotly- contested near the Stoekport line, and receiving a pass from a scrimmage, BArber was within an ace of scorine,Worsley proving the stumbling block. Another free kick to War- rington proved ineffectual, and a fine passing movement amongst the Stockpart halves and three-quarters carried play into the home territory. Broady was next promi- nent with a useful run. After a little give and take play the home team was granted a free kick for off-aide play on the part of their opponents, but Burton's effort was aeain unsuccessful. Sands next made his mark,and the I kick was responded to by Bate. Success attended War- rington'e efforts soon afterwards for Taylor scored near the posts, and Barber kicked a goal. From the kick-out, Warrington again invaded the visitors' quarters. and re- ceiving a free kick in their twenty-five, Barber kicked a ,capital goal amid the cheers of the spectators. En- couraged by this substantial lead the home team played vigorously and showed better combination than their opponents. Some splendid passing movements were witnessed.and one really fine one ended successfully. It commenced with the forwards, and after having passed through sortie half-dozen players' hands, Bate put the ! finishing tcuch on,crnssing the line in grand style. The point was not increased. Re-commencing, the Stock- port team made strong efforts to score, and the whistle for half time soon afterwards sounding, the score stood, Warrington 11 points, Stockport nil. Warrington re-started, and in reply R obinson found touch in his own half. After a scrimmage or two, Robinson relieved his side by a long punt into touch at midfield. A passing movement by the home three-quarters brought the game again int:, the visitors' territory. and Broady had hard lines in not seerine. From a scrimmage, the visitors got possession and Langford was prominent by a good run. A penalty kick also helped the Stockport men who by shert stages worked the ball into the home quarters, and forced the homesters to touch down. Broady kicked out and Sands returned. Give and take play ensued, until at length Burton by a fine effort crossed the lines, scoring under the posts. The point was not allowed owing to some little infringement. Amends were made soon afterwards, for Taylor receiving a pass from Bur- ton, again scored. Tlae visitors were now completely outplayed, and rarely entered the home half. Towards the close, however, owing to a misunderstanding between Evans and Broady, Stockport gained an open- ine, and Norris receiving & pass from Bailey scored. Chorlton took the kick but failed. Nothing further was scored, and the game ended :—Warrington, two goals (one penalty) two tries ; Stockport, one try, or fourteen points to three.

div.head: ASSOCIATION.
div.p: ASSOCIATION.

FRODSHAM T. RIINCOM—This match was played at Frodsham on Wednesday evening in very pleasant weather and before a fair gate. The Ivone captain hav- ing won the toss the visitors ataited the game and the home team soon settled down to play ; the whole cf the forwards passing in splendid style and Webb scored for the home team five minutes from the start. Hardly had the bait been restarted before the same player again beat the visitors' custodian with a splendid shot. The visitors rallied for a time. But could not break the home de- fence Littler and Rogers playing a very safe game. The home team were soon round the visitors' goal and C. Linaker scored number 3 and very soon Selby scored number 4. Half-time arr;ved with the score, Frodsham 4 goals, Runcern nil. C.Linaker restarted the game, the visitors playing a tar better game, were soon round the home goal but could not score. The home team now rushed away and Selby scored number s,the same player adding number 6 and after a very pleasant game the home team retired victors by 6 goals to nil.

div.head: tUGBY FOOTBALL WORKS' COMPETI.
div.p: tUGBY FOOTBALL WORKS' COMPETI.
TION.

This competition for medals.promoted by the commit- tee of the Warriov,ton Football Club has been continued during the week, and swme interesting games have been played. The attendances have been very satisfac- tory.

PENEETII TANNERY T. WHITECROSS (NETTING DEPART- 3IENT).—About three hundred spectators assembled on the Wilderspool ground on the morning of Bank-Holiday to witness this match. The Whitecross men were the first to commence scoring, Mather being the individual to cross the lines. Stung by this reverse, the tanners played with more vigour, and at length; Higham equa- lised, scoring a clever try. On resuming the Penketh men continued to press, and Dumbell gave them a de- cided lead by dropping a goal. The whistle soon after- wards sounded for half time. Of the second half Pen- keth had by far the best of the game, and again crossed their opponents' lines. The try.however,was disallowed and the result was the game was as at half time. via.: —Penketh seven points,Whitecross three. Th4sPenketh men used their feet to more advantage than their op- ponents, and this may be accounted for by the fact that many of the players have been accustomed to the Asso- ciation game. One of their players was somewhat unique in his way as a footballer, being may in posses. ion of one arm,but nevertheless he played a better game han some of his more fortunate compeers. MEssas. MONKS, HALL, AND Co. v. CASTLE RUDDER WORBS.—This match in the competition was played on Wednesday night, when the ironworkers proved the superior by two goals to nil. Their superiority lay in the smartness of the forwards,who were a very good set.

div.head: SHIP CANAL.
div.p: SHIP CANAL.
THE TRAFFIC,

During the past week 85 sea-going vessels have passed over :he Ship Canal, of which 42 have arrived from and 43 sailed to other ports. Foreign traffic has accounted for 14 arrivals and 12 sailings, and from home ports 28 vessels have arrived, whilst 31 have sailed to vlaces within the United Kingdom. Several large consignments of pig-iron have been imported from Ardrossan,Harring- ton and Ulverston and pyrites from Hu6va. General oargoes have arrived at the docks from Rotterdam,Flam- burg, Copenhagen, Gothenburg and New York, as well as from a number of home ports. American cotton has reached Manchester, and the Capenor from Galveston and the Limport and Holt liner is now in the canal with 1,200 bites ot cotton from New York, bringing the total amount of American cotton imported direct to Manches- ter this season up to 80,393 bales. The Swedish Prince arrived early in the week with 2,808 bales of E.Typtian cotton from Alexandria, and with this consignment 57,207 bales of the Egyptian staple have now been landed ,at Salford since the opening of the season. The Anchor , liner Nubia and the Clan liner Clan Macrae have sailed Iwith large shipments of piece goods, machinery, and galvanised iron for Bombay, and the support which has been extended to these vessels shows distinctly that the port of Manchester has obtained a strong hold of this branch of the Eastern export trade. The traffic returns for March show an increase upon those of February, and with the resumption of the summer trade and the estab- lishment of the new regular services it is expected that there will be a considerable increase in the returns dur- lin the next three or four months. MANCHESTER CORPORATION AND THE SHIP CANAL.

A heavy price (says the "Daily Chronicle ") continues to be exacted from Manchester for the maintenance of its Ship Canal. Next month the Corporation levies a rate of 1.. 21. in the pound to pay the interest on the £5,000,000 which the town invested in the undertaking. To meet the instalmont due to the sinking fund during the year another rate of 6.1. in the pound will be re- quired. This expenditure would be viewed with equa- nimity if the end were in sight, but the future is full of uncertainties. While the traffic and the revenue in- crease, the business done is anremunerative, and seems likely to remain so under the present rates. And while the keen railway competition lasts the rates cannot be reduced. Not only has the interest on the debt to he met but it is probable that before long new capital expendi- ture will have to he incurred. Originally the Corporation wrs only asked for £700,000. The demand rose to £2,500,000 and then to £3,000,000 and to £5,000,000. Manchester was at first jealous of its canal, and did not desire the proffered co•operation of Salford and Oldham. Now it would welcome financial assistance from its neighbours.

div.head: WARRINGTON v. RUNCORN.
div.p: WARRINGTON v. RUNCORN.

Great interest was centred in this match which took place on Good Friday on the Wilderapool CausewaY.The "gate "may be. described as a record one. The grand- stands, the enclosure, and the ground were all densely packed, and 'many people were scarcely able to get a view of the game at all. It will be remembered that on the first engagement between the teams this season, Runcorn won by two tries to nil. At the time of the kick off yesterday the weather was beautifully fine, but when half time was reached,rain fell heavily; and some- what marred the game. Runcorn were without the ser- vices of Warder, and the only alteration in the home team was the substitution of Wilcox for Nevins. The teams were composed as follows :—Warrington: Heesom, full back ; Broady, Cross, Barber,and Lawless, three quarters; Bate and Higginbottom, half hacks; Wilcox, Fairhurst, Dakin, Swift, Hill, Andrews, Saunders, and Berry, forwards. Runcorn: Hough- ton, full hack ; West, Robinson. Butterworth, and ' Myers, three quarters : J. Faulkner, Nickson, half backs ; W. Faulkner' Farmer, Langley, Moores, Hughes, Reece, Walker, and another, forwards. W. Faolkner started for Runcorn and Lawless replied, Faulkner making his mark. Some exciting work oc- curred on the goal line, and Hughes made a mark in splendid position. W. Faulkner kicked a capital goal amid the cheers of the Runcorn spectators. On restart- ing Warrington invaded the visitors territory and Law- less went off with a rush but was tackled by West, and losing the ball Barber picked up but failed to get away. Hill now made a good attempt to lower the goal from a "penalty," and vane tall kicking took place between Heesom and Houghton, the advantage remaining with the former. Runcorn could not drive them out until J. Faulkner started a passing movement that ended in Myers finding touch in the home quarters, and after some rather scrambling play, J. Faulkner scored a try at the corner. W. Faulkner failed to increase the point. Play remained for a time in the home half despite a splen- did effort by Cross. Toe home forwards now worked well and gave their halves possession several times,Law- less failing to hold the ball after a nice bout of passing, when he practically had the line at his mercy. Runcorn now drove Warrington back,and Heesom made his mark on the line. Barber intercepted a pass from Myers, and after a short sprint passed to Lawless,who again mulled. A moment later Barber aroused much enthusiasm by clever work, Butterworth stopping his onward course. The home team gave several pretty exhibitions of passing, which the effective tackling of the visitors rendered harmless, while Lawless failed in two attempts to drop a goal. Myers relieved the pressure and by short stages Runcorn reached the Warrington_ quarter line. _After some

_ scrambling play in which Warrington had theadvantagei West was compelled to touch down. The home three quarters then brightened up and several capital ethibi- Lions of passing occurred, but the defence war too strong to be penetrated. Several fair chances were however, lost by wild passing and bad judgment and half-time arrived with the score, Runcorn one goal, one try (seven points), Warrington nothing. Hill restarted for Warrington in a heavy shower and Houghton found touch beyond the hall way flag. Cross and Higg,inbottom caused Runcorn to be on ths defen- sive. The visitors' forwards wheeled several packs and Farmer dribbled well into the home quarters, where Myers narrowly escaped dropping a goal. The home backs started several passing movements but they seemed unable to hold the now gzeasy ball. While the visitors more sensibly played a forward game, Houghton made a mull in his own quarters, and offside play caused a scrimmage to be formed on Runcorn line, J. Faulkner kicking to Hee- som, who was collared before he cmild reply, and after a series of scrimmages Nickson made a dash for the line,but Heesom blocked the way. Long kicking caused Houghton to kick dead, and after a lot of uninteresting play in v hich neither side could claim an advantage, Heesom touched down at the other end. For five minutes Warrington were hardly pressed, and Myers picking up smartly dashed over the line behind the posts. and Farmer kicked a goal. Just on time Broady' made a good run, hut the Runcorn forwards dashed away from the resulting scrimmage, and the whistle blew for time, the score standing—Runcorn tws goals (one from a mark), one try ; Warrington, nil.

div.head: RUNCORN v. WIDNES.
div.p: RUNCORN v. WIDNES.

The representatives of these neighbouring towns fought off their fixture on the Widnes ground on Good Friday. After four minutes play J. Faulkner " crossed over" for Runcora but Farmer failed to place a goal. The game was fought with great determination, and Nixon of Runcorn, and Drum- mond of Widnes, left the field injured. At half time the score was Runcorn one try, Widnes nil. In the second staft,e play was very good, and some fine passing was seen. Runcorn continued to have much the beg of the game, and Messrs. Faulkner and Butterworth By their contributions of a try each placed the result of the game, when time was called, in favour of Runcorn by three tries to nil.

div.head: LOCAL VESTRY MEETINGS.
div.p: LOCAL VESTRY MEETINGS.
ST. JAMES', WARRINGTON.

The annual vestry meeting in connection with St. James' Church. Wilderspool-road, was held on Monday at noon. The Vicar (Rev. F. Slater) presided, and amongst those present were the Rev. J. W. B. Sproule (curate), Captain Hutchinson, Messrs. C. S. Burgess, J. Warburton, T. Jackson; W. Eckersley, W. H. Stansfield, A. Thernley, and J. H. Green.—Mr. Burgess presented the financial statement, which showed that the expen- dituie amounting to £197 18,. 10d. had exceeded the income by £ll ss. 3d. The income included general offertory £74 1... special offertories £35 4s. 50.. general expenses £l3 14s. 4d. He regretted that the offertories were £l3 or £l4 less than the previous year. The ex- penses were a little less, but the balance due was un- fortunately £3 more. They had not received quite so ' -ouch money from outside sources, the total amount be- ing about Mali against £3O. He, however, thought the position of the cherch.was somewhat better, and the new wardens might look forward in the expectation of being in a better. position when they met the Vestry the following year. The accounts had been signed by the churchwardens, and had been audited by Mr. James Jackson.—On the proposition of Captain Hutchinson, seconded by Mr. Stanfield, the accounts were passed.— The Vicar said he was glad to lam'able to ask Mr. Burgess to be Vicar's wardorf for another year. He had been afraid that Mr. Burgess was going to leave the town, but he the (Vicar) hoped it would net come to that.—Mr. Burgess, on being elected, said it seemed ut- terly useless for him to keep telling the Vestry that he thought it would be very much better if a new Vicar's warden were appointed. He believed he had held the office of Vicar's warden longer than any other person in office in Warrington. He did not think he could do otherwise than accept office after that fresh mark of their confiience. The coming year would probably be a very arduous one for the wardens. They intended to apply for faculty to take down the gallery, to alter the West end, to put in new windows and build new ves- tries. He aid not think it would be done in one year, bet it would tax the energies of the wardens to do all the work that was necessary. He believed the Vicar would not be satisfied until the work bad been completed. —Mr. Eekereley moved, and Mr. Jackson seconded that Mr. J. H. Warburton be the people's warden. This was unanimously agreed to.—The sidesmen were appointed as follows :—Mes.irs. 'Venn. T. Jackson, B. Cotton, J. Millwood, Stansfield, W. Eckersley, J. Astley and Cap- tain Hutchinson.—Messrs. Burgess and H. Houghton were appointed lay representatives on the ruri-deaconal conference, and the meeting terminated with votes of thanks to the wardens for their past services, and to the Vicar.

div.head: ST. ANN'S CHURCH
div.p: ST. ANN'S CHURCH

The Rev. J. Davies presided at the vestry meeting on Tuesday. There were also present—the Rev. P. J. Byrne, Messrs. Unswrth (deputy vestry clerk), W. H. .Rigbey, F. Taylor, G. Gleave, Chalmers, Houghton, Bretherton, E. Winter, Bunch, Warner and others. The Chairman intimated that he had again chosen Mr. Bunch as his warden.—On the motion of Mr. &leave seconded by Mr. Chalmers; Mr. F. Taylor 'was re-Ap- pointed people's -rrarclen,a vote of thanks being unanim- ously passed to him.—lc was decided to increase the number of sidesmen from six to eight, the following, I gentlemen being elected :—Messrs. A. Owen, M. R. War- ner, S. Nayllr, G. Gleave, J. Baird. W. Pollard, S. Daniels,E. Winter. and F. Taylor, the last-named gentle- man to represent the Sunday School.—Messr .J. Baird and E. Winter were selected as delegates.—Votes ot thanks were accorded the churchwardens, side,smen, , organist,and choristers for their services during the past year, and also to Mr. IThsworth for attending that meet- ing.—Mr. F.Taylor submitted an abstract of the church- wardens' accounts for the past year, showing the total offertories to be £lB9lls. lid., an increase of about £l4 on the preceding year. (Hear, hear.) The balance in hand was £3 4s. 7cl.—The Rev. J. Davies commented favourably upon the finances of the church. The ac- counts were adopted. • •

div.head: ST. PAUL'S.
div.p: ST. PAUL'S.

Vestry meeting held on Monday morning, the Vicar (the Rev. H. V. Pigot) in the chair. There were also present—the Rev. R. Brierley (curate). Captain Chorley, and Messrs. W. D. Jeans (vestry clerk),William Chantry Jahn Craddock, Joseph Lawless, John Hayes, T. W. Chantry, A. J. Jolley; D.' Fanshaw, J. Lawton, John Hough, Bebbmgton. J. Hankinson, J. H. Smethurst, Cooper,and Bate.—The accounts were presented by Mr. Chantry (people's warden), from which it appeared that there was a balance in favour of the wardens at the be- ginning of the year of £l2 9s. 71. The receipts for the past twelve months had been £144 84. 7d., and the ex- penditure £l4O 19s. 10d., leaving a balance of £.3 83. 81 in favour of the parish. The annual tea party realised £2B, se. 4d., and the Sunday evening collections £B5 13s. Bd.—On the motion of Mr. Jolley, seconded ty Mr. Lawless, the accounts were adopted.—The Vicar said that for the last two years his churchwarden had been Mr. James Smethurst. He was sorry to say he would not take office again. He (the Vicar) appointed Mr. William Chantry as his warden for . the ensuing year.— On the motion of Mr. Jaliey,seconded by Mr. Hankies'-n:4 Mr. Craddock was appointed people's warden.—Mr. Chantry appointed Mr. William Lawless as his sidesman, and Mr. Craddock selecte I Mr. Hayes. The following additional sidestnen were appointed :—Dr. Adams. Dr. Nuttall,and Messrs. T. W. Chantry, Joseph Lawless, A. J. Jolley, J. H. Smethurst, R. J. Chorley, Hankinson, H. Greenough, and H. Toit.—lt was decided to continue the Sunday evening collections for church expenses,and Messrs. D. W. Finney and William Richardson were re- elected the lay representatives.—The Vicar proposed a vote of thanks to Mr. Jeans for his services as vestry clerk.—The motion was seconded and heartily agreed to and a similar compliment was paid to Messrs. Smethurst and Chantry for their services during the past twelve months.—Mr. Jolley proposed a vote of thanks to the Vicar and Mrs. Pigot for their services during the past 12 months. There had, on one or two occasions, been some elements of friction in the parish which had caused uneasiness and pain to their respected Vicar; but things had now resumed their usual ioutine. (Hear, hear.) Whatever might happen they would loyally support their Vicar. (Hear, hear.)—Mr. Joseph Lawless seconded the motion.—The motion was agreed to.—The Chairman expressed his thanks for their sympathy and help.

div.head: HOLY TRINITY.
div.p: HOLY TRINITY.

The annual meeting of the parishioners was held on Tuesday night in the vestry. the Rev. E. C. E. Carleton, vicar,occupying the chair. There were also present—the Rev. H. R. Wild, Messrs. W. J. Forshaw (representing Mr. George White, vestry clerk), T. Welsby (vicar's warden), W. J. Hotion, (peoyles' warden), W. H. Harrison, J. Hesketh, R. Byerley, Naylor, E. Booth, J. H. Halton, W. Walker, J. Dunbabbin, J. Harding, P. Randall and R. W. Rowson.—The balance sheet of the wardens showed a balance at the beginning of the year of £1.3 103. id. The total receipts were £289 2s. 7d. After meeting expenses there was a balance of 15s. 4d. standing to the credit of the wardens. —Mr. Rowson presented the balance sheet of the Whle- dall Charity, which bare a balance in hand of 7s. lid.— The balance sheets were both passed.—The Vicar said be thought they all knew his views on the subject of the appointment of wardens. The offices should circulate, and this could only be done by having a change of officers at intervals of two or three years. It weuld be understood, therefore, that if he did not re-appoint Mr. Welsby personal circumstances were entirely out of the question. He had now much pleasure in nominating Mr. R. Byerlev to serve as his warden for the ensuing year.—Mr. Byerlev accepted the post, after which the vestry appointed Mr. W. J. Forshaw as their warden.— Mr. Webby was then appointed by Mr. Byerley as his sidesman, and Mr. W. J. Hatton was chosen by Mr. Forshaw as his sidesman.—The vestry appGinted the fol- lowing gentlemen as the remaining sidesmen :—Messrs. Dunbabbin, Rowson, Booth, Rose, Halton, Harding, Gerard and McGregor.—Messrs. Rowson and Dobson were appointed lay delegates._ Mr. G. F. F. White was

appointed vestry clerk, and Messrs. W. H. Harrison and Walsby were selected as auditors.—Votes of thanks were accorded the retiring churchwardens, the members of the choir, and the Vicar for presiding. ST. PETER'S CHURCH.

The annual vestry meeting was held on Monday morning. The Rev. B. Percival (vicar) was in the chair, and there were also present—the Rev. J. A. Cooil (curate), Mears. Ralph Norman (people's warden). A. Lomax. Joseph Taylor. T. Pearson.R. Sumner,J. Hands, James Taylor, W. McCollom, P. Green, R. Knight, P. Edgar (representing Mr. S. D.Buckton, vestry clerk),lV. Stanley, Kaye, Cowdell, R. Poole, and W. Taylor.— Mr. Ralph Norman submitted the balance sheet for the past year. It showed that at the end of last year there had been a credit balance of £8 94. 6d. This, together wito other items brought the total income up to £l2O 6s. 103/4d. The expenditure amounted to £l2O Os. 7-0., leaving a small balance in hand.—On the motion of Mr. McCollom, seconded by Mr. Green, the balance sheet was adopted.—TheNVicar warmly congratulated the church wardens upon the financial success of the past year, and expressed the opinion that the church was advancing. ' Before proceeding to the appointment of , churchwardens, he would like to state how deeply grateful he felt to the parishioners generally for their kindness towards him,and,the hearty way in Which they had worked and supported him'during the twelve months just ended. He was sorry, however. that they were about to have a change; Mr. Norman could not see his way to remain in the position of people's warden any longer. Mr. Roberts had, he was pleased to inform them yielded to his pressure, and had consented to re- tain the position of vicar's warden for another year. He was pleased to move that a hearty vote of thanks be ac- corded them.—Mr. Joseph Taylor seconded, and the proposition was carried.—Mr. Norman acknowledged the compliment,—On the motion of Mr. Edgar, seconded by Mr. Lomax,Mr. BAmford,Winwick-street, was chosen people's warden.—Mr. Green intimated that it was his intention to retire.—The following gentlemen were elected sidesmen : Messrs. Stanley, Kaye, Taylor, Cow- den, Barnton, Dagna.ll, Horne, and McCollom.—Mr. Edgar proposed that Mr. Braily be elected to represent the Sunday School.—The motion was carried.—Mr.Kaye was appointed lay representative, on the proposition of Mr. Edgar, seconded by Mr. Pearson.—The 'Vicar said that tenders had been received for the renovation of the Vicarage, and Mrs. Beamont had most kindly promised

WARRINGTON BOTtOUGH EXTENSION BILL.
FURTHER OPPOSITION BY THE LONDON A.ND NORTH WESTERN RAILWAY COMPANY.

Greatly to the suprise of many in Warrington and district, the London and North Western Rail- way Company have decided to petition against the Warrington Borough Extension Bill in the House of Lords. It thus appears that the Railway Com- pany are determined to oppose the Bill to the bitter end. This decision of the Company will put the ratepayers of Warrington to still further ex- pense. The recent opposition to the Bill in the House of Commons was solely confined to the Rail- way Company, and now hundreds of pounds more must be wasted in legal expenses in piloting the Bill through the House of Lords. Indignation has been expressed in the town at the Company's action, which is more surprising considering the poor case they made out when before the Select Committee of the House of Commons. The Com- mittee quickly disposed of the Company's objection which were confined practically to rating.

div.head: GOOD FRIDAY AT WARRING--
div.p: GOOD FRIDAY AT WARRING--
TON.

A good number of Warrington people took ad- vantage of the cheap excurions to seaside resorts and other places on Good Friday. Some ot those who possessed cycles also took their departure for fresh fields and pastures new, although the rain which fell during the night rendered the roads not very suitable for this increasingly-popular pastime The weather, during the morning rather dull,' brightened somewhat at noon, but in the afternoon, there were heavy showers of rain. Ser- vices were held at the various churches, and in some cases,were well-attended. In the afternoon,the chief attraction in the town was the football match, at which over eight thousand spectators were present. Several meetings were held at night, re- ports of which will be found appended. WESLEYAN FOREIGN MISSIONARY ANNIVERSARY.

The annual missionary festival in connection with the Warrington Wesleyan circuit was held on Good Friday in Bold-street Wesleyan Chapel, A morning service was held at eleven o'clock, and lasted one hour. It was conducted by the Rev. Arthur Triggs, for some years missionary in Ceylon and appointed as deputation from the Wesleyan Ceylon, House. He took for his text for the annual missionary ser- mon, ii. Corinthians, Sc., 14 and 15 verses. " For the love of Christ constraineth us,' Sic. He said there were two subjects in their thong ht that morning they were met to commemorate the death of their Saviour, Jesus Christ, and at the same time to think of the work of foreign missions. The two thoughts were intimately connected. But for the death of Jesus Christ, there would have been no missions either at home or abroad. Foreign missions were the completion—the outgrowth, of what- He did for men on the cross. The iev. gentleman urged them to consecrate themselves afresh in Christ's service, and help to spread the gospel throughout the world. —A collection on behalf of the Wesleyan Foreign Missions was afterwards taken.—There was a fair atendance at the evening meeting which was pre- sided over by Mr.E.Brown,of Ly sam, the oldest local preacher in the circuit. He delivered a brief address. —The Rev. G. D. Mason read the annual report which showed that the total income of their Foreign Missionary Society during the year had been £125,806 12s. Bd., and the total expenditure £127,457 us. 2d. The total debt on the society at the beginning of the year was £30,478 15s. 101., which had now been more than liquidated. Towards that special effort for liquidating the debt,Warring- ton circuit contributed £BB is. 2d. in connection with the Day of Intercession. The ordinary in- came of the society had received from the Warring- ton circuit during the year £260 118.2d.,heing prob- ably the largest amount collected in the circuit, in its history. (Applause.)—lnteresting addresses dealing with missionary work were delivered by the Revs. Arthur Triggs and Owen Watkins (super- intendent of the circuit,and for many years mission- ary in South Africa). The former gentleman gave a graphic story of missionary labour and success in Ceylon, and the title of the Rev. Owen Watkin's address was " Boers, Blacks, and British." In the course of his address he gave a history of the Trans- vaal, and, speaking of the Outlanders grievance.:, he contended that they were perfectly just in their demands, and were only asking for the restoration of the rights taken from them in 1881. He knew Dr.: Jameson personally. Ile was not an impetuous man at all but very cautions in his action, and he belived he did not dash into the Transvaal without fearing that there was just cause for it. A vote of thanks closed the proceedings. AMALGAMATED SOOLETY OF RAILWAY SERVANTS. - -

With the commendable object of raising funds for the orphanage in connection with the Amalgamated Society of Railway Servants, the Warrington branch of this organisation promoted a tea and concert which took place in Brick-street schoolroomon Good Friday evening. The amount raised for the orphanage lest year in War- rington was about £6 10s., but this sum will be materi- ally increased this year. About 150 persons sat down to tea,at tables presided over by Mesdames Birchall, Jenks, Rigby, Bradbury, Toft, J. Taylor, Ellison, and Miss Bramhall. Excellent arrangements had been made by a committee consisting of Mr. J. Taylor (hon. secretary of the Warrington branch), Messrs. Adams, Ellison, and J. Toft. The concert, which was provided after tea, was of a most:enjoyable character. The chair was occupied by Councillor H. Roberts, J.P.Soniri were well rendered by Miss Lily Birchail,Miss Mason, Miss Blackhurst, and Mr. 8. Hassall. The instrumental selections included piano- forte duet, Misses A. and H. Hill ; pianoforte solo, Miss Annie Hill ; concertina solo, Mr. William • Whittaker ; clarionet solos, Mr. Hipkiss' ; and violin solos by Master Bennett. Mr. Joseph Critchley was the accompanist.

About 180 members of the congregation and friends were present and enjoyed the tea provided and prepared by the following ladies :—Mesdames Andrews. Webster, Davidson, Adams, Cliffe, J. Adams, Pearson, Carter, Dumbell, Albinson, Wilkinson, J. Fairhurst. Dutton and the Misses Lightfoot. Hunt, Wells, Hayes, Fairhurst, Grounds, Boardman and Bates. After tea a meeting was held over which the pastOr—Rev. C. Andrews—presided, being supported by the Rev. J. Younge, Rev. J. S. Hughes, Rev. J. S. Summers and Mr. W. S. Wilkineon (secretary). From a statement made by the last-named gentleman, the chapel, congregation and Sunday school are in a flourishing condition. During the past year five persons bad come forward for baptism and had joined the church and in the year they had had a clear increase In the membership of six. In the Suuday school there were 145 members with about 15 teachers, and out of the number who had joined the church several of them had been and were members of the Sunday school. The Christian Endeavour Siciety was also holding its meet- ings regularly and doing good wnrk. During the even- ing addresses were given by the Chairman, Rev. J. Younge, Rev. J. S. Hughes and Rev. J. S. Summers, and a musical programme was gone through by the members of the choir aid by a few friends.

div.head: DOUBLE MURDER IN LONDON.
div.p: DOUBLE MURDER IN LONDON.

" A revolting fcrime was perpetrated in Whitechapel, London, on Saturday. Owing to the inability of a young relative to gain admission to the house of a Mr. J. Levi, the aid of a police constable was obtained. The door of the house was foiced open, and the dead 'sods? of Mr. Levi was found in one of the lower rooms. He had been killed with a knife. In an upstairs room the searchers discovered the body of a woman named Gale, who had acted as housekeeper for Mr. Levi. Her throat had been cut, and her head had also been badly injured by blows. In the ceiling of the room a hole was seen, and it was at once surmised that the murderer had been Interrupted inhis work of robbing the house and had sought to escape through the roof. Armed with a poker, a police clambered through the hole and on to the roof, followed by a civilian named Wragg. They saw a big burly fellow hiding behind the chimney, but as they tried to seize him he sprang over the parapet into the roadway below—a distance of over forty feet. He alighted on a little girl named Hyatns, and strange to say, escaped with a fractured shoulder and other minor injuries, while the little girl got off with some severe in- juries. The man, who was unconscious when picked up. was taken to the London Hospital, where he was detained.

The recent turn of afflirs in the diplomatic world at Constantinople to the, disadvantage of Great Britain has embarrassed the ffforts of the British benevolent agencies in their operations for thefrelief of the distressed Armenians. The gravity of the situation is such that the Duke of Argyll, despite his delicate health, presided on Wednesday at a special meeting of the Relief Cpmmittee, and a long and serious conference was held. I hear that the Committee contemplate appealing to Russia. It is suggested amongst other measures that a deputa- tion should be sent to the coronation of the Czar, mid that the Imperial clemency should be asked on behalf of the Armenians. Om names of the Bishop of Hereford and Canon Mac Coll being ment.oned as probable delegates. Meanwhile the authorities of the Russian Church are being sounded as to the possibility of enlisting the sympathies of the Holy Synod on behalf of the starving Armenians.

GOOD TEMPLAR GRAND LODGE OF
ENGLAND.

The twenty-seventh annual session of the Good Templar Grand Lodge of England and United Services was opened for the week on Easter Monday, at South- port,by Councillor Joseph Malins, Grand Chief Templar. The sessions were attended by about 500 representatives and officers—some from every English county, and from the Naval and Military Districts. The total adult and junior membership in England on November let was 102,320, in over 1,400 adult lodges and 700 junior temples—a total of over 2,000 branches, the Navy hav- ing over sixty lodges,and the army about fifty—besides a much larger number in the army in India. The session was heralded on Saturday by a juvenile procession and demonstration,nresided over by the G. Supt. of Juvenile "Templars, Councillor Vorley, of Leicefeer. On Easter Sunday the Rev. C. J. Reskelly, G and Chaplain (Gloucester), led a morning prayer meeting. and in the afternoon preached the annual sermon, the Derby-road Church Choir and String Band and the Maelor Welsh Choir rendering sacred pieces. Special Temperance sermons were preached in many places of worship, and at night a Gospel Temperance meeting was held, when the Rev. .1. Cbater presided, and addresses were given by Bro. G. If ayler, G. Goun (Newcastle-on-Tyne), Bro. J. B. Collings, P.G.Co. (Birmingham). Mrs. McKinnon, R.W.G. Vice-Templar (Dundee, and Mrs. M. Parker, 'P.G.V.T. (founder of the British Women's Temperance Association). On Monday morning the "Good Temp- lar Watchword" Company (who publish the offi- cial organ) met and declared a 6 per cent. dividend. On Monday afternnen the annnal see- sion was opened by the. G.C.T., Councillor Matins. The report of Bro. Councillor J. S. Voley, G.S showed the junior membership was close upon 50,000— an increase of 3,634. The North Stafford District had won the challenge shield for the largest juvenile increase. A national juvenile celebration was held in the Town Hall at Leicester, and a national competition had been ,held for prizes, when 184 juvenile members sent in essays on malt liquors and tobacco. The Hon. G. Sec., Bro. W. Sutherland (London), reported the adult sub- scribing membership to be 52,684, making with the juniors over 100,000. The North Yorkshire district showed the largest percentage of increase, but it could not then compete for the adult shield, which went to the next largest—the Military district (under Captain Overton) —which showed a gain of over 500. The Grand Treasurer's (Bro. F. R. Harris, of Cambridge), financial statements showed that in respect of printing and sales, under the management of Bro. J. B. Collings, the receipts had been £6,083 (showing a profit of £806) *. £371 teed been received in aid of the Mission Vans ; £1,183 SS Grand Lodge tax, subrcript,ons, and fees ; and £1,082 for extinguishing the Orphanage debt (which. had been done) and towards clearing the debt on the office buildings. Adding to this the sum of £1,333 received in respect of the official organs—the" Used Templars' Watchword" and the " Juvenile Templar "—the total receipts at this offiees were £10,202. This sum does not include any of the ordinary income of the Good Templar and Temper:lnce Orphanage at Sunbury-on-Thames,nor the subscriptions rnaintainine the county and local branches of the Order, which would amount to a sum at least cq to the above. The members chosen last year to proceed to Boston, U.S.A., to represent the Grand Ledge, at the session of the International Supreme Ledge, reported that Europe, Asia, Africa, and America, were repre- sented ther,at and that the Order had about 12,000 branches in over one hundred different countries.

EARLESTOWN &ND NEWTON.
RESIGNATION OF A HAYDOCK COLLIERY OFFCIAL.
We understand that Mr. W. S. Barrett,the general manager of Messrs. R. Evans and Co., Haydock, has resigned the position he has held for about two years past. DRUNKENNESS.

At the Town Hall, Newton, on Saturday, before Messrs. r. J. Gillespie and R. Stone, James MacDonald was fined 2s. 6d. and costs for being drunk at Newton. Napthalie Waterworth. John Pollitt and Peter Monaghan were each tined 2,3. Od. and costs for being drunk at Croft on Good Friday. For being drunk on licensed premises, on March 14th, James Dowd was sent to prison for 14 days. GOOD TEMPLA.R9.

The weekly session of the Hope of Earlestown lodge of Good Templars was held in the Ca-opera- tive Hall, Earlestown, on Monday evening. Owing to the holidays, and to the fact that many of the members were attending the demonstrations at Southport, there was only a moderate attendance. Two candidates were initiated to membership. After the transaction of other ordinary business, a social evening was spent, games of various kinds being indulged in.

div.head: -SERIOUS ILLNESS OF COUNCILLOR SMITH
div.p: -SERIOUS ILLNESS OF COUNCILLOR SMITH

We regret very much to say that Councillor James Smith, who was lately elected for Crow-lane Ward, has been seriously ill. He has not been well for some time, and last week he visited Harrogate. Whilst there he had a sharp attack of pneumonia, which became so serious that his family were hastily summoned. We are pleased to state, however, tha', he is now out of danger, and in a fair way to recovery.

GOOD TEMPLARY (EBENEZER LODGE). The Earlestown Ebenezer Lodge held its weekly session on Tuesday evening in the Co-operative Hall, Bro. A. Morris, C.T., presided over a good attendance of members. The Secretary read the digest of No. 1 Convention, also a letter from Ash- ton Excelsior Lodge respecting their forthcoming visit on April 21st and a committee was appointed to make arrangements. Four candidates were ad- mitted to membership after which the programme of the evening was given, the Secretary being re- sponsible. Solos and recitations were given by Bros. Taylor and Hopkins. Sisters Hopkins and Whitt y, after which the meeting closed.

div.head: NEWTON DIVISION BOWLING ASSOCIA.TION
div.p: NEWTON DIVISION BOWLING ASSOCIA.TION

The annual general meeting of the Newton Divi- sion Bowling association was held at the Pied Bull Hotel, Newton, on Tuesday evening. Mr. John Jackson presided, and there was a good attendance of representatives from Haydock, Earlesto wn,New- ton C.C., Newton Nursery, North Ashton, Ashton Recs., and Golborne. The business included the election of officers, which resulted as foflows : President, Hon. T. W. Legh, 1.P., treasurer, Mr. J. Jackson.; secretary, Mr. J. Millinwton. The fixtures for the ensuing season were drawn up and pre- sented to the meeting. It was decided to issue in- vitatiens to Burtonwood, Park Lane,and Garswood Hall, in order to get them to join the association again, seeing that the conditions have been made the same as they were at the time these clubs re- tired from the association, that is that the fixtures be played by eight members at home and eight away on the same day. The meeting adjourned until Monday evening next at 8 30 when the balance sheet will be presented.
EASTER HOLIDAYS AT EARLESTOWN AND NEWTON.

The holidays at these places passed over very quietly, and without incident. On Friday and Saturday the weatlier was not at all promising, but Monday showed a decided improvement. The only attraction in the town was a football match on each of the days named. On Friday, Earlestown met Skerton,and with the attraction of the Viaduct Brass Band there was a large crowd of people pre- sent. On Saturday Horwich visited the Earlestown ground, when there was again a good' gate, and on Monday they met Prescot. The result has certainly been very satisfactory for the coffers of the Earles- town club, and as they succeeded in winning two out of the three matches their position as cham- pions of the Lancashire Alliance is assured. A large number of people taking advantage of the quarter fare privilege left the town for various places, a good number spending the week-end at Blackpool. The Viaduct Works and .Nlessrs. Vicars' resumed work on Tuesday morning; but the Vulcan Foun- dry and Messrs. Sloe's works did not recommence until Wednesday. _

div.head: SONS OF TEMPERANCE,
div.p: SONS OF TEMPERANCE,

The usual fortnightly meeting at the Cadets of Temperance was held on Wednesday evening in the Co-operative Hall, Earlestown. The meeting had unusual interest to the juvenile portion owing to the result of the local and district competition for drawing, writing, an needlework. The meeting was open for the admission of parents and friends. Sister L. Barrett presided. Bro. Judson announced the result of the competition. div.p: EARLESTOWN CRICKET CLUB.

div.head: IMPERIAL PARLIAMENT. THURSDAY.
div.p: IMPERIAL PARLIAMENT. THURSDAY.

The House of Commons met again on Thursday after the Easter recess. Mr. CARVELL WILLIAMS asked what parts of the Church Catechism were considered by the Education Department as not being distinctive of any particular denomination,and suited therefore for use in Board schools. Sir J. GORST said the Committee of Council were of opinion that the Creed, the Lord's Prayer,acd the Ten Commaedments were not distinctive of any particular religious denomination. Mr. CHAMBERLAIN, answering Sir E. A. Bartlett, said he had no information to give with regard to President Kruger's proposed visit; and as to the alleged murder of an English officer or tronper by Boers at Blauwberg, in the Transvaal.on the 4th of Janu Irv, while he had no doubt the incident had' been greatly exaggerated, he was still endeavouring to obtain information. Mr. CURZON informed Sir E. Bartlett that the Govern- ment had not entered into any engagement with a foreign Power that the Eeyptian forces would not advance into the Soudan beyond Dengela. The House then went into Committee of Supply on the Civil Srvice Estimatee. A number of small defects in the administration of the Post-office were pointed out he various speakers. Mr. Hanburv, in reoly,eaid he untler- stood thet several of the erieva.nces of which posts', ser- vants formerly cotnolained had been redressed, and he also understood that .there wag now no comnlaint made by postal servants with regard to their political rights. He was fully impressed with the value of those Fervantq, and he thought every possible concession ought to be made to them to enable them to exercise their political rights. Mr. DALZIEL moved a reduction of the vote by £2,000 as a protest against the Postmister General being in the House of Lords. The amendment was negatived by 111 votes to 39

div.head: EXAMINER SATURDAY. APRIL 11, 1896.
div.p: THE EXAMINER SATURDAY. APRIL 11, 1896.

day morning the 14th March, he had a brief interview with Mr. McCorquociale, his brother Mr. A. C.' being present part of the time, the accounts of which be had reduced to writing. Mr. AlcCorquodale told him that his brothers and sisters wished to perpetuate their father's memory by carrying a stage further the re- building of the church, according to the plans and de- signs supplied by Mr. Brierley, architect, when the first instalment of the Work now completed was begun four years ago. They were prepared to guarantee him (the Vicar) penionally,a saim,which they did not wish him to make public for family reasons, but sufficient to cover the estimated cost of rebuilding the four bays of the nave with their north and south aisles, including the heating, lighting and ventilating thereof. Mr.Brierley's estimate for this was £1,500, to which they added a cew hundreds to include the architect's commission, and a margin for contingencies. As the sum he named, was the extreme limit of their guarantee, Mr. McCorquodale said it would be necessary to have a stringent contract drawn up between the family and the vicar, the archi- tect and contractors that that sum should uot be ex- ceeded. He requested him (the vicar) to place himself at once in communication with Mr. Brierley, whom they had already consulted on this matter, and to take all the necessary steps to carry out their wishes. He had had much correspondence with Mr.Brierley with regard to the plans and details,and he had judged it expedient to ap- ply for a faculty for the completion of the church, in case this generous offer to rebuild the nave should lead to anyone making a proposal to continue the work, see- ing that in the architects opinion it was of the greatest importance that the tower should be built concurrently with the nave, up to the ridge of its roof because this would conduce to ultimate economy and the stability of the whole. He therefore asked the vestry to consent to an application being made by the Vicar and church- wardens to the Consistory Court of the Diocese for authority to take down the existing nave, gallery, Sc 3., in order to complete as ir:ion as possible the re,buildieF,r of St. Peter's Church,and to proceed with the erection of a new nave at the cost of the sons and daughters of the late Mr. McCorquodale as a memorial of hiia. (Ap- plause.)—Captain Royse proposed that the veqry con- sent to the application being made by the Vicar and churchwardens to the Consistory Court of the Diocese as stated by the Vicar.—Dr. H. Watkins seconded, and the motion was unanimously carried.—Mr. R. Stuart pro- posed that the pal ishioners of St. Peter's represented by this annual vestry gratefully acknowledge the proffered gift of the late Colonel McCorquodale's sons and daugh- ters as an appropriate offering to God and a fitting memorial of their father."—Mr. Crouchley seconded,and the motion was adopted. The Vicar announced that he had that evening re- ceiver] from Lord Newton an intimation that he would give £5O towards the reduction of the debt of about £l4O on the church. The Vicar said that some provision would have to be made for divine worship during the time they would be turned out of the church whilst the alterations were in progress.—Mr. Stuart suggested that they should make arrangements for temporary worship in the Town Hall, and he made a proposition to this effect.—Mr. A. Blythen seCimded, and this was agreed to. WARGRA.VE CHURCH.

The annual vestry meeting was held in the vestry on Tuesday evening. The Rev. J. Carson (rector) presided. The accounts were presented by Mr. W. Norman,rector's warden, showing that the receints from all sources in- eliding a balance in hand of £8 93. 51., amounted to £2lB 8. 2d. The special offertnries amounted to £53 133. 51., and the ordinary to £lO3 4s, the total balance at the disposal of the churchwardens amounting to £2O 12s. 61.—Mr. Daselden thought the accounts were very satisfactory, and proposed that they be passed.—Mr. W. Thompson seconded, and it was carried.—The Rector announced that Mr. W. Norman would again act as his warden, and he had justified the choice made 12 months ago.—Mr. C. B. F. Borron was re-appointed people's warden. The retiring sidesmen were re-elected as fol- lows :—Measrs. W. Thompson, jun., J. Moss, A. Purnell, H. Sweetlove, T. Haseldeia, J. G. Starkie, J. Wright, T. Cave, T. Molyneux, and J. Burrows.—The salaried officers of the church were re-appointed subject to cer- tain conditions. It was decided to increase the salary of the organ blower from £2 12s. per annum to £4.—On the motioa of Mr. Haaelden, seconded by Mr. Sweetlnve, it was resolved that the gratuity to the choir be £l5, with the best thanks of the meeting for their services. Messrs. T. Molyneux. and W. Thompson were appointed the representatives of the parish at the ruri-decanal con- ference.—Mr. Norman laid on the table for inspection the accounts of the Dean Charity trust. A voluntary rate of twopence in the pound was laid. The Rector proposed a vote of thanks to the churchwaz dens for their admirable services during the past year. Votes of thanks to Messrs. Sweetlove and Purnell, auditors, and to the Chairman were accorded, and the meeting ter- minated.

div.head: VESTRY MEETINGS.
div.p: VESTRY MEETINGS.
FRODSHANI.

On Monday morning the annual vestry meeting was held in Overton (2,hureh,the chair being occupied by the Rev. a. B. Blogg (vicar). Amongst those present were the 12,-2v. E. Simms, Messrs. C. E. Linaker, R. Bate,John Ashton, H. Tdey, H. G. Linaker, B. Rigbey,J. T. Riley, T. D. Timmins, R. Foulkes, and others.

The usual notice convening the meeting having been read,Mr. R. Foulkes said he wished to enter his publlc and also his private protest against the meeting being held on Easter Monday morning inside the church when they had a good schoolroom close at hand. Many other places held their meetings later in the day and gave people an opportunity of attending who could not attend in the middle of the day. This was one reasom why they were held at Frodsham at that hour, and further to prevent any discussion on church matters, ritual,or doctrine by awing the speakers the majority of whom seemed afraid to speak their convictions ru what is looked upon as a sacred building.

div.head: TIM ACCOUNTS.
div.p: TIM ACCOUNTS.

The axclunts presented by the churchwardens showed that the Parish Church offertories had realised £224 103. 1.d., the sundry receipts ss. 9d., which with dona- tions amounted to £23 23. 91, totalled £247 183. 83.. In the expenditure for the year there was included an ad- verse balance last year of £5 153. 911., paid salaries &c. £7455., pensions £4, insurance premium £7,special col- lections for charities £69 183., sundry payments £45 53. 91, alms distributed £lo.and maintenance of divine worship £3B 7s. 91, total £255 is. Linaker moved the adoption of the accounts, and Mr. Riley se- conded the motion which was carried.—Mr. Linaker read the financial statement of the Iron Church showing that the donations amounted to £53 33. 9d., and that through the liberality of the members of the church the officials were able to start the year with a clear sheet. The accounts were adopted. The accounts of the fol- lowing charities were also produced :—Frodsham and Stockham,endowed schools,organ trust,Upton's bequest, and Harrison's charity.

div.head: APPOINTMENT OF OFFICIALS.
div.p: APPOINTMENT OF OFFICIALS.
The Chairman appointed Mr. C. E. Linaker as his warden for the ensuing year, and Mr. R. Bate was elected people's warden on the motion of Mr. C. E. Linairer.

div.head: OTHRIZ BUSINESS.
div.p: OTHRIZ BUSINESS.

Mr. Heywood proposed a vote thanking the ladies of the congregation and others for decorating the church with fl ,were. He considered that if they looked round the building there was no one who could find fault with what was done.—Mr. Hutchinson seconded the motion. —Mr.Foulkes protested against the use of flowers. They tended to aensunus wnrship, and were an attraction to the eye. They were more or less to fill up incomplete and ineffizient evangelical services.—The motion was carried.
The Chairman proposed a vote of thanks to the adult members at Overton and tho iron churches.—Mr. Bate seconded the recolution, which was pissed. MR. FOULKES' ANNUAL 6' PROTESTS!'

Mr. Foulkes, on "other business " being reached, made an attempt to speak but without effect, but on Mr. Reynolds proposing and Mr. H. G. Linaker second- ing a vote of thanks to the Chairman, Mr. Foulkes said he entered his protest against the method by which Non- conformists were proselytized during confirmation cup- ade, making them premise directly or indirectly never afterwards to enter a Nonconformist chapel.—Mr. Linaker asked the Chairman to put the resolution before the meeting.—Mr. Foulkes charged those present with wanting to break up the meeting. That was a scheme to do so. He attempted to continue his address,but was met with repeated cries of " Order, order."—The Chair- man said one thing had been forgotten, and Mr. Riley wished to introduce it.—Mr. Riley said he had great pleasure in proposing that the thanks of the vestry be given to the churchwardens and sidesmen for their valu- able services during the past year.—Mr. Lewis seconded the proposition, which was carried.—Mr. Reynolds then proceeded to put the motion regarding the vote of thanks to the Chairman, and Mr. Foulkes said he promised ta support it, on condition that they listened to him. He then tried to proceed to read a written document, stat- ieg that the very evening last month when the VOar was trying to prove an impossibility, namely, that the rite of confirmation—(" Order, order ")—as administered in the Church of England was Scriptural, a Nonconformist minister in the parish was preaching against it,paintedly referring to the Vicar of Frodsham. (Cries of " Order, order.") Mr. Foulkes said he was quite in order, and he knew why they kept interrupting him. He asked them to allow him to read his paper, and being met with further cries he said he would hand the document to the reporters present.—The Chairman, after order being re- stored, said he claimed a right to speak,and he intended to do so. He thought it *as high time that annual farce came to an end. He had the greatest reverence for the house of God, and Mr. Foulkes had expressed something to that effect that morning. He (th 2 Chair- man) thought it was not seemly for thiem to havN such a farce year after year. He did not know what other people might think about the action and views of Mr. Foulkes, but all he:could say was that his religion ae thus displayed, was not what commended itself to him.—Mr. Foulkes : You are not my confessor. —The Chairman, contirmting, said the conduct seemed tn create bitterness and malice. The milk of human kindness was turned sour, and therefore he for one did not agree with it in that sacred place. Mr. Foulkes made persistent and most ridiculous statements. and he thought it high time as Vicar of the parish to enter his protest against his proceeding. Be thanked them for their vote of thanks,and declared the meeting at a close. TRINITY CHURCH, RUNCORN.

The annual vestry meeting was held in the vestry of Trinity Church, on Tuesday night. The Rev. Dr. Pres. ton presided, and amongst a good attendance we noticed the Rev. A. Bartran, Messrs. Barton. Fletcher, a Bur- rows. Kilcross, W. Hankinson, Hazlehurst, Prince,West- brook, .1. ilorsefield, Broughton and C. Timmins. The Chairman spoke in term of praise of the services rendered to the church during the past twelve months by Mr. C. Timmins, and again nominated him as Vicar's warden.—Mr. Kilcross proposed the re-election of Mr. Hankinson as people's warden, and Mr. Prince seconded the resolution which was carried.

Mr. Timmins said that in the matter of finances they were on the debit side this year, and this was owing to their allowing their zeal to overrun their discretion. They started last year with a credit balance of 21,and taking the accounts up to the 20,11 March this year they had a debit balance of £27 16s. 31 Since then the collections had amountel to £4 51. 31., so that there was really a balance of £23 91. 9d., beyond which not a single penny was owing to anyone else. He had written to the bank to say that he would be responsible for the overdraft, and this guarantee had been accepted by them. The following officers were re-anpointed :—Sidesmen, Messrs. Kilcross, Flazlehurst, E. Turner, Fletcher, West- brook, Garnett, and S. Annett, with the addition of Mr. Samuel Pearson in the place of his father Mr. Thomas Pearson. Lay representatives : Messrs. Hankinson and J. florsefield. Church Council : Messrs. Coleburn, Cue- elegiaam, J. Pritchard, W. Fisher, with the addition of Messes. Westbrook. Garrett, and Gibson. Mariners churchwnrden : Mr. Woods. Mill Brow warden-in- charge : Mr. Cunningham. Auditors: Messrs. Salkeld and Westbrook.

Mr. Salkeld proposed a vote of thanks to the choir- master—Mr Lancaster—and the choir,and thought that the musical service at the church had been ereatly im- proved. Mr. Meadowcroft seconded the motion which was carriei. A vote of thanks was alga accorded the lady helpers for church decorating. Mr. Lancaster was re-appointed choir master. Mr. Arthur Savage organist, and Mr. Broughton apparitor.

div.head: Sr. JOHN'S CHURCH, EARLESTOWN.
div.p: Sr. JOHN'S CHURCH, EARLESTOWN.

The annual vestry meeting was held in the vestry on Monday afternoon. The Rev. T. R. Matthews presided, and there were present the Rev. E. W. W. Kaye, Messrs. Foden, Pimblett, Pilling, Latimer, Jones, Bowes, Wild, Waring, Eaton, Martindale and others.—The accounts which commenced with an adverse balance of £4l 10s. 611., and ended with an adverse balance of £l3 is. 011., were adopted.—Mr. T. A. Pimblett was re-ap- pointed Vicar's warden, and Mr. Paden, parishioners w.rden. The following were appointed sidesmen : Messrs. Leyland, Eiton, Rvlance. Andrews. and Ander- ton. The accounts of the Dean Charity trust fund were nresented. A voluntary rate of 21. in the £ was laid. On the motion of Mr. Jones, it was decided to form a Building lommittee to take into consideration the com- pletion of the church, and the composition of the com- mittee was left with the vicar and wardens. A letter was read from Mr. Whitley, architect, relative to the ex- tension of the church. An appllcatioa from the organist. Mrs. Lotimer, for an increase of salary, was left over. A vote of thanks was accorded the organist and choir for their services.

div.head: TOWNSHIP MEETING AT HAYDOCK.
div.p: TOWNSHIP MEETING AT HAYDOCK.
THE PAYMENT OF GUARDIANS.

Last week at the annual township meeting of Hay- dock, a resolution was passed to the effect that in con- sequence of no accounts of expenses, or report, having been received from the Haydock guardians, the inciden- tal rate be reduced to a farthing in the pound, and that the guardians be not allowed any expenses for attend- ing the Board meetings at Warrington or relief corn- mittee meetings at Earlestewn. To protest against this the guardians called a township meeting, which was held in the Colliery Schools, Haydock. on Thursday night. Dr. Dowling presided, and besides the guardians concerned. Rev. Father Moore, Rev. J. H. Riddette, and Mr. J. Billinge. there was a very large attendance of ratepayers.—The Rev. Father Moore and Mr. Billinee. and Rev. J. H. Riddett,e each gave a resum4 of the work they were engaged in on the Board, the latter stating that the meeting had simply been called to en- able the three poor law guardians to give an account of their stewardship. He had heard the word indignation, hut he did not think that was the proper time or place for it to find vent. When he looked round and saw such a large meeting of ratepayers interested in the ad- ministration of the poor law, which they owed to that little family party calling itself the township meeting, and which reminded him of the nine tailors of Tooley-at, styling themselves "we are the people of England," he thought they owed the best thanks to the gentlemen con- cerned for the opportunity they had unintentionally given them of hearing such lucid and informing state- ments about poor law work to which they had listened that evening. He suggested that meeting because he considered the township meeting a trumpery little hole and corner meeting having the audacity to claim to represent practically 7,000 peaple, and to pass a mania- ' tinn. He was not offering any opinion unon the resolu- tion, but in consequence of it, the Guardians would be In the position next year of the negro orator.who passed his hat round, and found there was nothing in it. tint I exclaimed "thank God I got my hat back." (Laughter.) I They should do their duty whether they paid their expenses or not. They got for going to Warrineton the munificent sum of 41. and for wine to Earlestown the isum of Is. 61. In Mr. Bradshaw's election address 1 appears the words " remember,. increased rates, means increased rents," but he should say as matter of course." reduced rates meant reduced rents." (flear.haar.) Councillor J Forshaw said he was not at the township meeting, but when he heard of it he was snr- prised that there were such mean and shabby men in Tiavdoe.k, but they could all Flee through it. He moved "That this meeting of ratsnayers of Haydock desires to express its continued confidence in the elected guard- lane." (Applause.)—Mr.R.Bradshaw seconded. He was 'satisfied of one thing that they had three guardians in Flaydock who promised to do their duty, ned they had done their duty, although they had net told them how many times they had been at Warrington and Newton during the last year, nor how many meetings they had missed. At any rate, they were cognisant of what was going on at Warrington, and throughout the Warrington Union. He gave some explanation of the reason of the calling of what had been termed the hele-and-corner meeting. At the meeting none of the overseers were nreaent to take the chair, and he was requested to pre- side, and there were very few present, and that showed what interest the rateparera took in the meeting. No- Hem had been issued as in previous rearm.and this ques- tion of the reduction of the rate came before the meet- ing. He thought some courtesy was due to the rate- navere who attended the annual meeting, but the three guardians did not submit any account of their exoenses f r the past year and the As- sistant-Overseer said he had asked the guardians to let him have a statement two or three times but none had been received. None of the Guardians chose to attend the meting, and he was certain if they had, the nropcsition which was made and carried would not have been put, and as a proper list had not been sent in they thought it best to stop the allowance until the next annual meeting. He had never heard the slightest ex- pression that the Guardians had neelected their duty. (Hear, hear.)—Mr. Johnson also spoke in supnort of the reaohition.—The Rev. Father Moore and Mr. Billings havine replied, the Chairman said the meeting had not been called to discuss the right or wrong of the thing, they had met to gay whether they wanted the Guardians to continue in office or not, and if they did not, someone would have to propose an amendment. No amendment being forthcoming, the resolution was put and unani- mousle earri.d.
