div.head: FASHIONABLE MA RRItIGE AT GRA PPENHALL.
div.p: FASHIONABLE MA RRItIGE AT GRA PPENHALL.

On Wednesday the village of Grappenhall, was en fete for the occasion of the marriage of Mr. Walter Mace Shipman, Cleveley,Altrincham, to Miss Marian Long, the only daughter of Mr. William Long. J.P., Thelwall Heys, Thelwall. At 2 o'clock, the time for the ceremony to be performed, there was a large crowd of people of both sexes, outside the Grappenhall Parish Church, many of whom had come from Warrington; a:I the villagers were there, and there was a strong representation of the county ventlemen, whose carriages stretched as far as the Post Office. The people were brightly dressed and there was a profusion of flowers, which toge- ther formed a brilliant scene. Atmospheric conditions were also fav"?urable. A large part of the Church, which for the occasion was improved by floral arrangements, had been reserved for the wedding guests, who num- bered 150, and these included Mr. and Mrs. J. C. Parr, Mrs. Thomas Gandy, the Misses and Mr. T. Gandy,Miss Shipman, Mr. and Mrs. E. Milner, Mr. James Tinsley, Miss Tinsley, Messrs. Tinsley, Mr. and Mrs. Richardson, Mr. and Mrs. Todhunter. the Misses Todhuntor, Miss Fell, Miss Milner, Mrs. Beard, Mr. and Mrs. Lewis Beard, Miss Gaskell, Miss Nellie Gaskell, Mr. and Mrs. Holbrook Gaskell. jun., Mr. and Mrs. J. B. Gaskell,Miss Valentine, Mr. and Mrs. V. B. Davies, Mr. and Mrs. F. Monks, Mrs. A. Milner and Miss F. Milner, Mr. and Mrs. Thorneley, Mr. E. Thornelgy, Miss Julian Adams, Mrs. Broadbent, Mr. C. H. Broadbent, the Misses Broadbent, Mr. John King,Miss King, Messrs. King, Mr. and Mrs., Stanley Pearson. Miss Powell,Rev. and Mrs. H. G.Sinith. Rev. W. H. and Mrs. Drummond, Mr. and Mrs. R. D. Dirbishire, Mr. Stewart, Mr. and Mrs. H. Rawson, Mr. Roger Gasket!. and Mrs. Greenall.

All the unreserved seats were also occupied, and many persons were, therefore, compelled to stand throughout the service, which was of a simple character ; no hymn was sune, nor were the choir in attendance. Mr. W. Asqnith Woods officiated at the organ, and he played an excellent selection of music, including the Bridal March from Loheneriu, " Mendelssohn's " Wedding March,and selections from Bach and Batiste. The bride, who tris given away by her father, entered the church promptly at to o'clock, the congregation rising as she did so. She wore a charming dress of white duchesse satin, trimmed with fichu of net, edged with Brussels lace, court train, with true lovers' knot of orange blossoms, and a tulle veil fastened with a wreath of orange blossoms. She also wore a diamond crescent, the gift of the bridegroom. Her bouquet was composed of white roses and lilies of the valley and her appearance was very favourably commented upon. Her bridesmaids, Miss Geta Milner (cousin of the bride), Miss Margaret Grundy (neice of the bridegroom), and Miss Ethel Rawson, carried shower bouquets of yellow daffodils with long yellow ribbons and trails of smilax and asparagus fern. Their dresses were composed of white duchesse satin, with fichus of mousseleine de soie, edged with butter-coloured lace, and yellow velvet neck-hands and waistbelts, black straw hats trimmed with yellow and white net and large bunches of daffodils. They wore pearl and enamel brooches, the gift of the bridegroom. The honeymoon will be spent in Devonshire and Corn- wall. The bride's travelling dress was of fawn cloth. ceat and skirt, the coat faced with white cloth and lined with pink brocade, with a waistcoat of the same material, with white straw and black net toque trimmed with pink roses. Site carried a long travelling coat made of fawn faced cloth. The officiating clergymen was the Rector of the parish. the Rev. Richard Greenall, and the " best man" was Mr. Frank Gaskell, Wooltoa Wood, Liverpool. The approach to the church was covered with red cloth, and lined with the people, while the gateway through which the bridal party had to pass was over- arched with evergreens and daffodils. At intervals along the road leading to Grappenhall Heys were multi- coloured flags suspended, and at the lodge entrance to the grounds was another handsome arch which upheld the words " Long life and prosperity." There was still another arch further up the drive and this coatained the wishes of "Good health to the bride and bridegroom." The porch of the house was also decorated and had on the words " Good Luck." These decorations were the spontaneous work of the workmen at Mr. Long's tannery and the employe's at the house, who thus displayed their pleasure at the event and their goodwill to the par- ties. In the evening some 230 of the workmen, vil- lagers, their wives and friends were treated to a capital entertainment in the Temperance Hall, which was lent for the purpose by Mr. R. A. Naylor. Musical and in- strumental selections were given, and Mr. Wilson Black- ledge, the humorist, gave some of his popular sketches which were greatly enjoyed. Messrs. Thomas and C. H. Tinsley had control of the arrangements, which were highly satisfactory, and they were ably assisted by some of the workmen themselves. The following is a Hat of the presents :

WARRINGTON VESTRIES.
(Continued from page 6.) PARISH CHURCH.—A LARGE DEFICIT.

The Rector presided at the annual vestry meeting in connection with the Parish Church, held in the National schools, on Tuesday evening. Amongst those also pre- sent were the Revs. A. A. Markham and H. R. M. Hutt, Mr. R. T. Fairclough (rector's warden), Councillor Woods (people's warden), Mr. E.A.White (vestry clerk), Messrs. A. Browne, William Gill, F. Taylor, J.Walton.T. Mason,R.lsherwood,and May. After devotional exercises, Mr. Woods read the annual statement of accountseabiee showed that the total receipts from special offertories were £212 10s. 5d., from general or church expenses, offertories £261 163., making a grand total of £474 63. st, being £l5 less than the total offertory of the year befce e. The expenditure on parochial needs was £599 ss. 9d., and on extra parochial £79 4s. 5d., leaving an adverse balarce of £287 93. 11d., or practically an increased debt of £25 on the year's work, and which would not have been had they had the parochial tea Party, which produced £33 the last year it was held. Owing to the great pressure brought to bear on the parish by the bazaar for the schools the Rector thought it advisable to adjourn the tea party to a more con- venient season. In order to reduce the expenses, the Rector, his warden (Mr. Fairclough) and himself (Mr. Woods) had had a meeting, when they went into every item of expenditure, and they felt that by making cer- tain alterations, which would not interfere with the efficient conduct of the church and parish, they should' materially reduce the debt. He would like to remind the vestry of the beautiful addition to the choir furniture and decoration, viz., the oak choir stalls and brass memorial tablets to the memory of Mr. Joseph Davies, late churchwarden of the church, given by his widow and family. They were a splendid addition to the church as well as being a lasting memorial to one who worked leard for the town and the church of which he was war- en. Mr R T Fairclough wasperfectly satisfleld with the accounts with the exception of the adverse balance. It was rtoo large, but he hoped they would be able to reduce it during the coming year. Last year all their efforts were devoted to the reduction of the debt on the schools. Since the Rector had come amongst them they htd spent about £ll,OOO on these buildings. They had I five entirely new schools, and these had taxed their ' resources as a parish t the utmost. All the expenses in connection with them had been paid with the exception of £2OO or £3OO on St. George's schools. They had renter overspent themselves on the schools, but it had , been with a good object, and he thought the ratepayers I generally had every reason to be obliged to the Rectorfor what he had done. (Applause.) If a School Board I were established there would be a large addition to the rates, which were heavy enough already. He was sorry there was an adverse balance, but he did not see how they could have wiped that off and liquidated the debt on the schools as well. —Mr. Arthur Browne,eadd he was most dissatisfied with the adverse balance. He thought it was a shame that the Parish Church should have such a debt. He did not know how it was accounted for. He was supposed to be a people's eidesinan but he did not know how it had come about. They had never had a meeting to consider it. When they were so much in debt he thought the congregation should do without what was unnecessary. —Mr. Woods, proceeded to explain certain items of the accounts, pointing out several where they exnected to be able to reduce the amounts in the forthcoming year. The collector was paid £4O a year, and she earned it.— (Hear, hear.) This year she would be paid from another source, and would thus relieve the church expenditure from that amount. There was ancther point. The sick and poor funds were very heavy, and this year those would be reduced very considerably. That would mean that two extra offertories which had been previously for the sick and poor fund would go to the church expenses. The church house had cost the wardens £2O daring the last year, but in the future he understood that would be reduced to £lO. They had also paid this year an old debt incurred at the time of the death of the Duke of Clar- ence when the church was lavishly decorated. The gas and coke account had also been larger, caused by a new arrangement with the Training College, but in future it was expected that it would not be so large. They had had to repair the turret clock, an expense he did not think would occur again in his lifetime. The wardens did not want the church to go to " rack and ruin" for want of repair, and they had spent certain sums upon it. Other items of expenditure were also mentioned by Mr. Woods, including the increase of the salary of the organist. the St. George's mission grant, clergy fund, the repair of the stained glass windows,etc. They were compelled to give every Sunday school in their district £lO each to prevent themselves from being fined by Government, who required a proportion of the rent of a school—used as a day and Sunday school—to be paid by the Sunday school. If they had not paid that £lO for each of their Sunday schools, he believed there was a clause in the Education Act which would have deprived them of the Education grant. In conclu- sion he referred to the falling off in the general offer- tories, which somewhat accounted for the deficit. But this year they expected to reduce it by about £9O or £loo.—Mr. Browne: But £lOO reduc- tion will not be sufficient. They would be still going on year after year in debt.—After a short discue- sion the Rector said he believed the financial statement would be accepted as generally satisfactory under the circumstances. They were all very sorry as Mr. Browne was that they should have such a large deficit. When they considered the immense amount raised for the schools,he thought they would see there had been a great difficulty to give to the offertory to the same extent as to the schools. The reduction of the sick funds was only temporary, but they though:, they should be just before they were generous. He did not think they hould give to the sick and poor when they were in debt. They therefore thought it right to reduce he number of offertories for that fund.—Mr.'Browne sail, whilst dissatisfied with the debt, he would propose the adoption of the accounts. If the debt were not reduced next year he should have something to say upon the matter.—Mr. J. Walton secondad,and the accounts were passed.—A hearty vote of thanks having been accorded to wardens, sidesmen, and auditors for their past ser- vices, the Rector re-appointed Mr. R. T. Fairclough as his warden; and the meeting.on the motion of Mr. Fair- clough, seconded by Mr. Fred Taylor, re-appointed Mr. Alfred Woods as parishioners' warden.—Mr. Fairclough appointed Mr. John Walton as his sidesman, and Mr. Woods appointed Mr. Arthur Browne.—The following gentlemen were appointed sidesmen by the meeting : Messrs. William Gill, Thomas Moores, W. Price, James Craile, Thomas Mason,John Dewhurst, John E. Wright, and James Wood.—The following were appointed sides- men for the Missions :—St. George's. Sergeant Price ; Bank-street. Mr. Whittle.—Messrs. J. D. Buckton and William Gill were elected as lay representatives to the ruri-Jecanal conference.—Mr. H, B.White was re-elected vestry clerk, and Messrs. Fred Taylor and Samuel Davies were appointed auditors.—Mr. Thomas Mason,in proposing a vote of thanks to the ladies of the parish for their services during the past year, observed that they owed as a congregation a debt of gratitude to them for the enereetic and willing manner in which they had worked.—Mr. John Walton seconded the motion,and the motion was heartily agreed to.—Mr. Woods, in highly complimentary terms, proposed a vote of thanks to the , Rector.and referred to the sum of £lOO which, he said, had been presented to the Rector, but instead of making use of it himself he had handed it over to the funds of the church. • (Applause.)—Mr. Fairclough seconded the motion,which was unanimously agreed to.—The Rector, in reply,said that there were nearly 500 communicants on Easter Sunday, an increase of nearly 100 compared with the previous Easter. ST. THOMAS'S, sroacrox HEATH.

At noon on Tuesday, the Rev. T. S. -T—ef-ts-,-;icar, pre- sided over the annual vestry meeting. There were pre- sent Messrs. W. Richardson (people's warden), E. W. Woods (vicar's warden), W. B. Roberts, Clarke, Butter- worth, Jackson, Lee, Pearson, T. Ince, Weighy, F. Tim- perlev, J. Robin, E. Bradshaw, A. Down, T. Warburton, F. Rose, Massey, C. Sewards, &c.—Mr. William Richard- son submitted the church warden's statement of accounts which showed a credit balance of £1 3s. 11id. after ell demands had been paid.—On the motion of Mr. Lee, seconded by Mr. Clarke, the balance sheet was adopted. —The Vicar said he was pleased to inform them that his friend Mr. Woods, who had in previous years acted as warden, had consented to take the post for another year. Mr. W. B. Roberts eroposed, and Mr. Warburton seconded. that Mr. Richardson be re-apoointed people's warden.—The motion was carried. Mr. Woods remarked that the gentlemen who acted as sidesmen last year were Messrs. Bobert Davies, Charles Sowards, Vere B. Davies, A. Down, T. J. Lee, and William Phillipson. He was sorry to say that the last-named gentleman had :eft the parish, and that Mr. Vero B. Davies had sent in his reel- nation.—The four remaieing gentlemen were re-elected sidesmen.—Messrs. Richardson and Woods, were appointed to represent the church at the next ruri-clecanal conference at Chester, on the motion of Mr. Roberts, seconded by Mr. Pearson. Mr. F. Rose made an application on behalf of Mr. Her- bert Spence. the organ-blower and bellringer, for an in. ' crease of salary. After some discussion it was proposed by Mr. Lee, and seconded by Mr. Pearson that Mr. Spence's salary be increased to £6.—The propmition was carried.—Mr. Woods presented the financial state- ment of the Curate Fund, which he said he had received from Mr. Robert Davies, who bad been kind enough hitherto to act as treasurer. Mr. Davies had intimated that he was no longer able to keep the accounts, and suggested that they might be given into the custody of the wardens.—The Vicar, being asked to explain the present position relative to the appointment of curate, replied that the matter was really in his own hands. He nominated a gentleman to assist him owing/to his in- ability to perform the work, and that gentleman re- ceived what the friends in the parish were kind enough to subscribe. He thought now that they were on this subject, that it would be well, and indeed he felt he was in duty bound, t ) tell them that he had been advised by his medical adviser to retire from the parish for a time. He had been bound to accept this advice, and had con- sulted those in authority, and also the Bishop of Chester in the matter, who had agreed to the suggestion. Of course he would still he the vicar of the parish, but the Bishop would see that a suitable gentleman occupied the post.—lt was asked if the parishioners would hay

MAKE LIFE ENJOYABLE. Loss of health means loss of all which makes life en- joyable ; for, in addition to the bodily pain and suffering which it cause:, it entails a vast amount of mental pain and anxiety, especially in the homes of the working classes. It brings in its train a ' host of discomforts which retard the recovery of the sufferer, and hinder, instead of assisting, Nature to perform her functions. When a working man suffers from any ailment which prevents his following his daily avocation, he is natur- ally filled with anxiety regarding the maintecance of those depending on him for their daily sustenance. His very love for his family retards and hinders his speedy recovery, and his spirits become depreged at the antici- pation of the gloomy prospects before them in the event of a long continuance of his illness. It is well known that depression of spirits often proves a serious bar to a speedy recovery. • These results arise in addition to the various incon- veniences and discomforts which the sufferer and his family experience as direct results of his illness, such as additional expenses for luxuries for the sick, with in- creased difficulty to obtain those luxuries, or even the necessities of life. • Most of the various forms of disease which trouble the labouring classes of the country, and which are often attributable, more or less, to some unhealthly condition of their daily work, may be classed under a few leading heads. ~ To avoid the discomforts arising from various forms disease,every working man should seek the aid of THE VEGETABLE TONIC, Which has gained a world-wide renown as the most wonderful medkinal discovery of the age; and as un- failing remedy it is prescribed by many leading physi- cians in various ailments.
